name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Democratic candidates push for term limits at Polk County Steak Fry
description: Two national Democratic lawmakers endorsed Josh Turek for U.S. Senate on Saturday and called for term limits for U.S. Supreme Court justices and lawmakers. Nearly 700 Iowans gathered at Des Moines Water Works Park for the 2026 Polk County Steak Fry to hear from 10 current legislators and hopefuls. They were joined by headliners U.S. […]
text:
About 700 Democrats rallied for Iowa party candidates Saturday at the Polk County Democrats' Steak Fry Aug. 29, 2026 in Des Moines. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)Two national Democratic lawmakers endorsed Josh Turek for U.S. Senate on Saturday and called for term limits for U.S. Supreme Court justices and lawmakers.
Nearly 700 Iowans gathered at Des Moines Water Works Park for the 2026 Polk County Steak Fry to hear from 10 current legislators and hopefuls. They were joined by headliners U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island and U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland.
U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, spoke Aug. 29, 2026 at the Polk County Democrats’ Steak Fry in Des Moines. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Whitehouse, who currently serves as the ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, said Turek reminded him of former Iowa Sen. Tom Harkin.
“I would say I was an early believer in Josh’s race. I served in the Senate with Tom Harkin. I know what Iowa can deliver because I saw Tom Harkin in action,” Whitehouse said. “And when I took a look at Josh, I saw a lot of Tom Harkin in him. So please send Josh to the Senate.”
Electing Turek, Whitehouse said, will do several things. First, it will “put a check on the crazy people that Trump is putting into office. Second, it will address issues with the Supreme Court. And third, get the dark money out of U.S. elections.”
Whitehouse said there are three great fights that need to happen in Washington. “We need to get rid of dark money in our politics because it’s rotting our politics. We need to back off the climate denial fraud and corruption operations of the fossil fuel industry because our children deserve a better future than what the fossil fuel industry will provide them. And we need to clean up the mess at the Supreme Court.”
The Supreme Court, Whitehouse said, needs to be investigated. They need a proper ethics program that has proper fact finding – there can’t be an exception for the nine, he said. He also wants to see retroactive term limits.
“Those are the things we can do if you send Josh Turek to the Senate,” Whitehouse said. “That will change America. Josh is the right guy.”
Iowa State Sen. Renee Hardman, left, and Josh Turek, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, spoke Aug. 29, 2026 at the Polk County Democrats’ Steak Fry in Des Moines. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Turek took the stage to a standing ovation and hundreds of waving Turek signs. He stressed how Iowans across the state are struggling to put food on the table, a roof over their head, pay electric bills and access healthcare. He highlighted Iowa’s declining educational system, record-level farm bankruptcies due to tariffs and war and the state’s rising cancer diagnoses and ongoing water quality crisis.
“And really, Iowa, we have hit the bottom,” Turek said. “This is not the state that we know. This is not the state we grew up in.”
Pointing to the voting record of his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, Turek said she stands for cuts to healthcare and food programs, support of tariffs and war and tax breaks to billionaires.
“This is not what Iowans want. Iowans want to have a senator that is going to fight for them,” Turek said. Fight for Iowa. Fight for Iowans. Fight for the middle class. Fight for our workers. Not just look out for the billionaires and the large corporations.”
Turek said he also agreed there’s a need for term limits.
“If we can win this seat, we will not only make a generational change to this state, we will be able to flip the Senate, and we’re going to be able to change this country,” Turek said. “All of us together, we’re going to do it.”
U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland speaks Aug. 29, 2026 at the Polk County Democrats’ Steak Fry in Des Moines. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Raskin, who serves as the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, also endorsed Turek. He gained national recognition for serving as the lead impeachment manager during the second impeachment trial of Donald Trump and is a key member of the January 6th Committee.
Raskin, who received a standing ovation as he approached the podium, said this was first trip to Iowa. “Been here for 17 days and in the state longer than Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn,” he joked, drawing effusive clapping, whistling and cheering. He added that Iowans can tip the House and Senate back in the direction of democracy and freedom.
Raskin said Democrats stand for democracy. “The only party in America that will stand up to your right to vote, even if you’re not going to vote for us. We are the party that stands up for constitutional democracy and freedom for everybody in America.”
He invoked the “last great American Republican President Abraham Lincoln, who spoke of government of the people, by the people and for the people.” This is the proposition, Raskin said,  that is being tested in the November election. “Our party, says the government, must be an instrument for the common good and public interest of all.”
People must go to the polls, he said, to take the government back again. “You know, everything is under attack. Our whole Constitution is under attack. The preamble is under attack. It’s not even enforceable in court, and it’s under attack.” He said separation of church and state is also under attack.
Agreeing with Whitehouse’s call for term limits for the Supreme Court, he said freedom of speech is under attack. “It’s gotten so bad that Donald Trump’s masked paramilitary soldiers are shooting down American citizens exercising their First and Second Amendment rights in the streets of America,” Raskin said, and promised Americans will see justice for the cases of those killed by federal agents  in states such as Minnesota.
Sand calls for conversations and common sense
Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said politics is supposed to be about making state government work for ordinary people — not a small number of people with too much power for too long. He threw in his support for term limit legislation that many other candidates are calling for on both a federal and state level.
Sand said two things are missing in Iowa: common sense and conversations. With his town halls, he is listening, he said, and having discussions about solutions that would bring people together and force state government to work for ordinary people.
“That’s what I want us to get back to in the Capitol building. Common sense, listening to each other, being willing to recognize when even the person that’s mostly wrong actually has a point to make. We are having none of that in Des Moines,” Sand said.
He discussed his varying viewpoints to his opponent Lahn and reminded the crowd that his campaign is focused on bringing people together with real solutions.
“That’s why we had over 100 Republicans announce endorsements, including people who are in elected office right now as Republicans,” Sand said. “Because people across the state of Iowa are fed up with the direction of the state. They want change.”
Sand concluded, “Let’s remake this state and turn it back into an Iowa that is not about being redder or bluer, but one about being better and truer.”
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, running in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, also cited her support for term limits. 
She said she filed a term limits bill in the Iowa Senate that many of her colleagues in the Legislature didn’t like. “We can see that things are not working. We need new voices and new perspectives coming up through the process. And so, we need to find a way to make sure that we can have those new perspectives and new leadership that we need to lead us in a better direction. I will do that in Washington,” she said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sen. Ted Cruz criticizes Democrats as ‘Marxists and Islamists’ at Hinson event in Iowa
description: U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz said Saturday Iowans would play an important role in keeping “Marxists and Islamists,” who he said have taken over the Democratic Party, out of power by electing Ashley Hinson to the U.S. Senate in November. Cruz, alongside other Iowa Republican elected officials and candidates on the November ballot in the state, […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz spoke with Iowans before speaking at Republican Ashley Hinson's Annual "BBQ Bash" fundraiser held at the Horizon Events Center in Clive Aug. 29, 2026, supporting her run for U.S. Senate in the upcoming midterms. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz said Saturday Iowans would play an important role in keeping “Marxists and Islamists,” who he said have taken over the Democratic Party, out of power by electing Ashley Hinson to the U.S. Senate in November.
Cruz, alongside other Iowa Republican elected officials and candidates on the November ballot in the state, joined Hinson for her annual fundraiser, Ashley’s BBQ Bash, at the Horizon Events Center in Clive. More than 1,000 people attended the event, which included remarks from the GOP leaders and music from country music singer Lee Greenwood — as well as a performance from Hinson herself, who played violin alongside other performers at the beginning of the event.
Hinson, who is seeking the open seat now held by Sen. Joni Ernst and currently represents Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, will face Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, in the general election. Cruz, who delivered the keynote address, contrasted the views of Hinson and other Republicans running in the midterm elections with the political positions — and religious backgrounds — of some Democrats who have won primary elections around the country this year.
“We’re seeing the Democrat Party taken over by communists and by Islamists,” Cruz said. “That green-red alliance is frightening. Right now, today, Comrade Mamdani is the most dangerous and the most powerful Democrat in America. And you’re seeing it in race after race after race — open Marxists. I’m not calling them communists; they call themselves communists. Winning primaries in New York City, in Michigan, in Colorado, in Florida, in Oklahoma.”
Cruz was referencing candidates who have won primaries in several states this election cycle who are affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America. He was also referencing the 2025 election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the more recent victory of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s U.S. Senate Democratic primary. Mamdani is affiliated with DSA while El-Sayed has rejected the label of democratic socialist, but both politicians are Muslim.
“Let me say about the Islamists: Sharia law has no place in the United States of America,” Cruz said, going on to speak about El-Sayed’s appearance on Fox News with host Jesse Watters.
Cruz said not all Democrats are in these categories, and did not link Turek with these movements. However, he said “every Democrat in the House and Senate is terrified of the communists and Islamists in their party, because that’s where the energy, the money, the passion” lies.
“That brings me to why I’m here and why we’re all here, because the state of Iowa is a battleground,” Cruz said. “Because we need Ashley Hinson to win this race. … Control of the House and control of the Senate both run through Iowa.”
Speakers at the event repeatedly warned attendees Hinson is in a competitive election. The Cook Political Report, an election forecaster, recently shifted ratings for the Iowa Senate race from “leans Republican” to a “toss up,” and a recent Suffolk University poll found Hinson was leading Turek 45% to 41% among likely Iowa voters, within the poll’s statistical margin of error.
The U.S. Senate seat is not the only hotly contested race on the ballot this year — the elections for Iowa governor and the state’s 1st and 3rd Congressional Districts, all currently held by Republicans, are also seen as potential pick-ups for Democrats in 2026.
Hinson criticizes Turek immigration ad
Hinson said her opponent, Turek, was misrepresenting himself as “moderate” on the campaign trail to win voters’ favor in Iowa. She criticized Turek’s campaign ad, titled “I-35,” released Friday, in which he said he would work with anyone, “including President Trump, to secure the border, stop the flow of drugs into Iowa.”
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, running for the U.S. Senate in 2026, played violin at her annual BBQ fundraiser Aug. 29, 2026 held at the Horizon Events Center in Clive. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The advertisement points to Turek’s vote in 2024 supporting Senate File 2340, a law allowing Iowa law enforcement to charge people with an aggravated misdemeanor if they have been denied admission, deported or otherwise removed from the U.S., or if they currently have an order to leave the country.
The measure, which was heavily criticized by Democrats and organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union of Iowa, also gave state courts the ability to order the deportation of undocumented immigrants, and state agencies and law enforcement the ability to transport migrants to U.S. ports of entry to ensure they exit the country. Individuals who do not comply with an order to leave can be charged with a felony under the law.
When Turek was criticized during the Democratic primary for this vote, he defended his support for it, saying, “I am someone that believes that we can recognize that we need safe and secure borders — but it’s also not a mutually exclusive issue, that we also need an easier pathway to citizenship and fundamental immigration reform.”
When Hinson brought up Turek’s statement in the ad that he would work with President Donald Trump on border security, the audience laughed.
“I’d laugh too if it wasn’t so egregious, right?” Hinson said.
She brought up Turek’s votes on other legislation in the Iowa House related to immigration law enforcement. She said his vote on House File 946, a measure that stated law enforcement officers who “knowingly and intentionally” fail to comply with state laws on federal immigration enforcement would be subject to investigation by the attorney general, was a vote “to restrict Iowa law enforcement from working with ICE to protect these criminal illegals from deportation.”
Hinson also claimed Turek “wanted to defund federal border security and immigration enforcement.” Turek said in April he would not support funding for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security “without serious reforms to ICE,” but he has not called for defunding border security.
“What we’ve seen here is the tale of two Tureks, right? One Josh in the primary, another Josh in the general election,” Hinson said. “So the only thing that I think is consistent here about Josh Turek is how shamelessly willing he is to say or do anything to get himself elected. So the fact is, the illegal immigration crisis was created by left-wing liberals like Josh Turek, and he is the last person that Iowans should trust to fix it.”
Democrats criticize Hinson over ‘Epstein files’ votes
Iowa Democratic leaders held a news conference before Hinson’s event, where speakers criticized Hinson for not voting to release the “Epstein files” — U.S. Department of Justice documents and information on the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Democrats, alongside some Republicans like U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, had voted to compel the DOJ to release more information on Epstein, specifically after news reports of Attorney General Pam Bondi telling Trump his name appeared in government documents related to Epstein. Hinson, alongside other members of Iowa’s all-Republican federal delegation, have said they support releasing more information on Epstein and related co-conspirators, but said they trusted the Trump administration’s approach to releasing information.
Iowa Rep. Jennifer Konfrst said Hinson “has been fighting firmly on the side of the Epstein files, not Iowans.”
“For months last year, she publicly opposed and blocked the release of the Epstein files, she alone could have at any time decided to join the bipartisan effort in Congress to release the files, but she chose to stand in the way,” Konfrst said. “… As a mom, I can’t believe Ashley Hinson would sooner go to bat for the awful individuals named in the Epstein files than the young survivors Jeffrey Epstein sexually abused. It is disgusting, and it is disqualifying. It is not something we’re going to forget come November. Because while she was blocking the release of the Epstein files, she was voting to cut our healthcare and raise our prices. She was fighting harder for the Epstein class than for Iowans.”
Earlier in August, the Gazette reported Hinson was asked by three callers during a telephone town hall about not supporting the 2025 effort to force a House floor vote on the issue through a discharge petition. In the town hall, Hinson called the effort “a Democrat floor procedure” while saying she supported releasing the documents.
“Democrats are desperate,” Billy Fuerst, a campaign spokesperson for Hinson, said in a statement Saturday. “Ashley voted to release the Epstein files and wants every creep who hurt women and children to be behind bars for the rest of their lives.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Your teenager is still figuring out who they are. Big Tech’s algorithms act like they already know.
description: At precisely the age when young people are still figuring out who they are, an algorithm optimized for engagement should not be shaping the possibilities.
text:
MY CHILD doesn’t have a smartphone or use social media. Until they turned 13, I thought that meant they were protected from its influence. I was wrong. 
I’m watching the culture of social media reach my child secondhand, both as a mother and the wife of a public school teacher. Online vocabulary travels offline, including increasingly precise categories young people use to understand differences in attention, personality, sexuality, gender, politics, and mental health. 
Some of this can be enormously valuable. A teenager with undiagnosed autism can discover an explanation for their differences. A gay or transgender teenager can discover that others feel the same way. But social media doesn’t simply provide access to information. It continuously classifies our behavior to predict what to show us next, including content we never asked for. 
Last week’s landmark multistate settlement with Meta will limit how much time teenagers can spend on its platforms, but it largely leaves personalized feeds intact, requiring only that Meta give parents and teens the option to turn them off.  
Massachusetts should go further by passing S.3175, “An Act Protecting Children from Addictive Social Media Feeds.” The bill would disable certain algorithmically personalized feeds for minors across all social media platforms, while still allowing teenagers to search for content, follow creators and groups, and otherwise tell the platform what they want to see. In other words, it would preserve teenagers’ ability to explore while limiting the platform’s ability to direct that exploration.  
Algorithmically personalized feeds can be addictive by design, but there is another reason to think twice about them: They may also influence how teenagers come to understand themselves.  
Developmental psychologists have long studied “social essentialism” —our tendency to see categories as revealing deep and meaningful differences between people. Research with children has found that categorical language can make characteristics seem more intrinsic and categories more rigid, as though they represent distinct kinds of people. Put simply, a label can make an attribute feel less like something about you and more like something you are. This is especially consequential during adolescence, when forming a sense of self is a central developmental task. 
That should give us pause in an information environment built around classification. Online platforms infer demographic characteristics, interests, and other attributes to decide what content and advertising to put in front of us.  
Research on TikTok has described how recommendation systems can turn users’ behavior into increasingly specific profiles and then reflect those inferred identities back to them through the content they see. The algorithm may therefore be putting teenagers into ever-smaller boxes at precisely the age when they should still be forming—and revising—ideas about themselves. 
Imagine a teenager wondering whether she has ADHD. She watches several ADHD videos. The algorithm hasn’t learned that she has ADHD; it has learned that she engages with ADHD content, so it supplies more.  
Troublingly, fewer than half of symptom claims in the 100 most popular #ADHD TikToks aligned with clinical diagnostic criteria. Beyond the risk of inaccurate self-diagnosis, researchers studying autism have documented how users who encounter diagnostic frameworks online can reinterpret their lives through them. 
Obviously, TikTok doesn’t cause ADHD or autism. But algorithms can shape the path of exploration and self-reflection. Repeated exposure can make one characteristic disproportionately present in someone’s information environment, making it seem increasingly central to who they are. 
This can also run counter to one form of social progress: making our differences matter less. I grew up believing equality meant gender should tell us less about a person, not more. Girls should be allowed to be masculine without needing to explain themselves, and boys should be allowed to be feminine without needing to explain themselves. 
Not every difference needs to define your identity. Algorithms may undermine that progress by increasing the salience of the very characteristics Americans have spent generations fighting over, deepening cultural divisions that cut across shared economic interests. 
That should concern both sides of our culture wars. Progressives worried about algorithms pulling teenage boys toward increasingly rigid ideas about masculinity and conservatives concerned about the growing list of identity categories may be seeing different manifestations of the same underlying system. We don’t have to agree about the categories to agree we should be suspicious of the machinery that makes them more salient. 
The goal shouldn’t be to prevent teenagers from exploring or changing their identities, but to protect their freedom and intellectual independence as they do so. Teenagers should remain free to search for information, encounter unfamiliar ideas, and decide for themselves what those ideas mean for who they are, without an algorithm constantly mediating that process.  
We cannot expect teenagers to protect that freedom on their own. And parents cannot solve this individually. I keep my child off social media, but their peers use it, shaping what they discuss at school and how they understand themselves and one another.  That is why the House should pass S.3175. 
The bill would put reasonable limits on how platforms can direct minors’ attention while preserving their ability to choose what they explore. And it can do so without requiring teenagers to surrender their privacy. Its age-assurance system must include a method that requires neither government identification nor biometric data and allows users to remain anonymous to the platform.
At precisely the age when young people are still figuring out who they are, an algorithm optimized for engagement should not be shaping the possibilities. Particularly when that system is susceptible to manipulation and capable of fragmenting us along increasingly granular lines. 
Elise Rapoza is a New Bedford resident and senior research associate at the MassINC Policy Center.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tyrin Johnson was shot in the back. Memphis deserves the truth.
description: Tyrin Johnson was shot in the back. That is not speculation. It is the finding of an autopsy performed by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center. The report shows that a bullet entered the right side of Johnson’s back and exited through his upper chest. A forensic pathologist who reviewed the findings said the bullet’s […]
text:
Officers with the Memphis Safe Task Force have cited the "buffer law" to prevent locals from viewing some of their interactions. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tyrin Johnson was shot in the back.
That is not speculation. It is the finding of an autopsy performed by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center. The report shows that a bullet entered the right side of Johnson’s back and exited through his upper chest. A forensic pathologist who reviewed the findings said the bullet’s upward trajectory was consistent with Johnson running away from the person who shot him.
That evidence directly contradicts the account authorities gave the public after Johnson was killed by members of the Tennessee National Guard in downtown Memphis on July 5.
Memphis police initially said Johnson turned toward the soldiers with a handgun during a foot pursuit. A National Guard report similarly claimed he “rounded on” the soldiers and pointed a gun at them. The autopsy establishes that Johnson was not shot in the chest as those initial descriptions suggested. He was shot from behind.
This discrepancy cannot be explained away with another press release.
Johnson was 20 years old. His family has spent nearly two months demanding the evidence that would show what happened during the final moments of his life. They have reportedly not been shown video of the shooting. Now, the physical evidence has raised even more serious questions about the government’s version of events.
The public deserves answers.



We were told the National Guard would provide support. Instead, Guard members pursued Tyrin Johnson through downtown Memphis and opened fire. A military deployment promoted as a way to make Memphis safer ended with a young Black man shot in the back. 


Every available recording must be preserved and released, including surveillance footage, vehicle-camera recordings, police radio communications and video from the body-worn cameras of Memphis police officers who responded to the scene. The identities of the soldiers who fired must be disclosed. The public should be told how many shots each soldier fired, where each soldier was standing and why two soldiers reportedly discharged their weapons when the autopsy documents a single gunshot wound.
Memphis police officers were involved in the response and should have been operating their body cameras. If footage exists, officials should not hide it behind a vague appeal to an “ongoing investigation.” If no footage exists, the public deserves to know why.
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation says its investigation remains open. But an investigation conducted behind closed doors cannot by itself repair the damage caused when the government’s initial account conflicts with medical evidence. This case requires a genuinely independent, transparent investigation, followed by a public accounting of the evidence.
The medical examiner classified Johnson’s death as a homicide. That classification does not by itself establish criminal culpability. 
But neither does a uniform place someone beyond the reach of the law. If the evidence establishes probable cause that Johnson did not pose an imminent threat when he was shot, the person or persons responsible must be charged. The same legal standards that apply to every other Tennessean must apply to members of the National Guard.
Anything less would amount to a separate system of justice for agents of the state.
Man fatally shot in second Memphis Safe Task Force use-of-force incident this week

I raised concerns about Johnson’s killing before the autopsy became public because his death cannot be separated from the larger militarization of public safety in Memphis. The Memphis Safe Task Force has placed National Guard troops alongside federal, state and local law enforcement personnel, giving military forces an expanding presence in ordinary civilian policing.
We were told the National Guard would provide support. Instead, Guard members pursued Johnson through downtown Memphis and opened fire. A military deployment promoted as a way to make Memphis safer ended with a young Black man shot in the back.
That reality should force us to reconsider not only this shooting but the entire political project that made it possible.
Supporters of the Memphis Safe Task Force repeatedly cite arrest totals, traffic stops, citations and firearm seizures as proof of success. The White House has claimed that the operation “crushed” violent crime. Yet Memphis crime was already declining before Guard patrols began, and a recent analysis found no measurable evidence that National Guard deployments reduced violent crime, homicide or gun victimization in the cities examined.
Smart City Memphis recently highlighted an estimated $319 million cost for the Memphis deployment through the end of 2026. At that price, Tennesseans should demand more than political theater, inflated claims and carefully selected enforcement totals. They should demand evidence that the deployment has made communities safer — and an honest accounting of the harm committed in its name.
Public safety cannot be measured only by how many people the government stops, cites or arrests. It must also be measured by whether government agents respect constitutional rights, whether families receive the truth when their loved ones are killed and whether those who misuse state power are held accountable.
A government that demands obedience while refusing transparency is not producing safety. It is producing fear.
That is why elected officials at every level must do more than offer condolences. They must demand the release of the footage, insist upon an independent investigation, hold public hearings and refuse to expand or fund this deployment without meaningful civilian oversight. Silence in this moment is not neutrality. It protects the institutions withholding answers.
There is also an election approaching.
This November, Tennesseans must pay close attention to the officials and candidates who champion the militarization of our communities while resisting transparency and oversight. Anyone asking for the power to govern should be required to explain whether they will protect the public from abuses of state authority — or simply protect the authorities.
Those who want more militarized law enforcement with less public accountability should not be elected or returned to office.
This is not a partisan abstraction. It is a question of life and death. Johnson’s family is living with the consequences, and every Black family in Memphis understands what is at stake when the government can kill one of us and then control the evidence, the investigation and the story told afterward.
Black lives are literally hanging in the balance.
Justice for Tyrin begins with the truth. It requires the release of every pertinent recording, a full and independent investigation, and criminal charges if the evidence establishes that his killing was unlawful.
Tyrin Johnson was shot in the back. No elected official should be permitted to look away.

name: Mississippi Today
title: After decades of overhunting and habitat loss, black bears are slowly recolonizing the lower Mississippi River basin
description: A black bear with tags in its ears lounges on a tree branch in Tennessee. Black bears were once common across the basin, but overhunting and habitat changes diminished the population, leaving most of the remaining bears in mountainous and other remote regions. Now, black bear sightings are increasing in many parts of the basin.
text:
On the Fourth of July, a picture of a black bear sitting on the edge of a Tennessee cornfield sparked a social media flurry.
It was the beginning of a deluge. Over the next month, bears would be recorded running through yards and sprinting through a golf course on a rainy day. 
Reactions ranged from bewilderment to humor. Many responded with shock — mainly over the location. Because these bears were not being observed in the rolling mountains and hollows of East Tennessee. They were hundreds of miles away, on the opposite side of the state, in the flatlands of West Tennessee. 
But these sightings did not surprise Dan Gibbs, black bear coordinator at the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency. While most black bears in Tennessee are concentrated in the east, reports from Middle and West Tennessee residents have steadily streamed in over recent years.
The recent sightings are likely several bears that probably came from bordering states with expanding populations, like Kentucky, Mississippi, Arkansas and Missouri.
“It will be a slow process, but bears are going to recolonize Middle and West Tennessee,” Gibbs said. “You can’t stop it … they’re going to be in northern Mississippi, they’re going to be in eastern Arkansas, eastern Missouri, western Kentucky. That’s just their historical range, and they’re going to reclaim it.”
Mississippi Alluvial Valley was ‘breadbasket’ for black bears
Black bears were once abundant across most of the United States, including the lower Mississippi River basin. But decades of habitat destruction and overhunting in the 1800s and 1900s threatened to wipe out the population altogether. In Tennessee, the animals’ range shrunk to just 10 secluded, mountainous counties along the state’s eastern border by the early 1970s.
In Mississippi, the population was estimated at just 12 bears when the Mississippi Game and Fish Commission (now Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks) was founded in 1932.
One of the biggest misconceptions about black bears is that they are a mountain species.
They’re really “generalists” that can survive — and thrive — in a variety of ecosystems, including swamps and wetlands. In Tennessee, European settlement and hunting pushed bears into the Great Smoky Mountains and the Cherokee National Forest, large areas of conserved land and places that were harder for people to reach. But wetlands are rich, productive ecosystems that make great food sources for black bears.
“The whole Mississippi Alluvial Valley … the historical floodwaters that used to flood miles and miles before the levee system, that was kind of the breadbasket of the black bears in this part of the Southeast,” said Anthony Ballard, black bear program leader for the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks.

Mississippi’s core black bear population is concentrated along the Mississippi River in the bottomland hardwood systems — frequently flooded, low-lying areas where oak, hickory and old-growth cypress trees are common. Increasingly, bears are colonizing the state’s southeast corner, establishing home ranges in a very different habitat: pine stands with thick underbrush, Ballard said.
Another myth about black bears is that they form their dens in caves, according to Janelle Musser, TWRA’s assistant black bear coordinator. In reality, caves are damp and not particularly attractive.
“They are great at finding dens in the habitat that they are living in,” Musser said. 
In southern Alabama, bears often create dens in shallow depressions in brush on the ground. In the Mississippi Delta, dens can be found in cane thickets and tree tops, Ballard said, sometimes as high as 50 feet off the ground in old-growth cypress.
Black bear populations take decades to recolonize.
Female black bears don’t begin to have cubs until they reach 3 years of age, and if they’re eating natural foods, they’ll have a couple of cubs every other year. Young males begin to move away from their mothers at around a year and a half old, sometimes traveling tens or hundreds of miles to establish their own home range, Ballard said. “It’s kind of nature’s way of making sure that there’s not inbreeding.”
Male black bears can have home ranges anywhere from 25 to more than 60 square miles, depending on the availability of food and presence of female bears. Females’ home ranges are much smaller, and a female cub’s home range may overlap with her mother’s. 
These large home ranges and frequent movement make it difficult to survey bear populations, Gibbs said.
A population of black bears is generally considered “established” if there are breeding females in the area. 
Tennessee has received cub sighting reports in counties just east of Nashville, Gibbs said. But it will probably be another 10 to 15 years before Middle and West Tennessee have a bear population large enough to survey.
Bear hunting
Hunting black bears was a “part of life” in the Southeast in the 1800s and early 1900s, Ballard said. “It was as much a part of the hunting world as whitetail deer are today.”
Davy Crockett wrote about killing dozens of bears in a personal account of his life published in 1834. “Of all the hunting I ever did, I have always delighted most in bear hunting,” he wrote. When Crockett arrived in Lincoln County, just north of the Alabama-Tennessee border, around 1809, he noted an “abundance” of deer and smaller game, “but the bear had been much hunted in these parts before, and were not so plenty as I could have wished,” Crockett wrote. He had better luck along the Obion River in the western-most part of the state.
Almost a century later, President Theodore Roosevelt went on a storied hunting trip in Mississippi in 1902, failing to find a bear. When assistants located a bear, tied it to a tree and suggested he shoot it, Roosevelt refused. The story led to the invention of the Teddy Bear. 
Mississippi put protections in place preventing black bear hunting in 1932, when the estimated population dropped to around 12 bears. 
Arkansas — once called the Bear State — was home to an estimated 50,000 black bears before settlement began, according to the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission. The state banned black bear hunting in 1927 due to declining populations. By the 1950s, an estimated 40 to 50 bears remained in the state, according to an article published in The Mountain Echo in 1979. 
Arkansas officials trucked in more than 250 black bears from Minnesota and Manitoba, Canada, to the Ozark and Ouachita Mountains in western Arkansas in the 1960s in an attempt to bolster their population. Today, the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission estimates there are around 5,000 black bears in the state.
Louisiana’s Wildlife and Fisheries Commission closed all bear harvest seasons temporarily in 1956 as the population there plummeted. The state similarly brought 161 bears from Minnesota to the Mississippi and Atchafalaya River basins from 1964 through 1967, but continued habitat destruction as agriculture replaced forest land contributed to continuing population decline, according to Louisiana’s Black Bear Management Plan. 
The state banned bear hunting in the late 1980s, and the Louisiana black bear was listed as a federally threatened species in 1992.
At least two dozen of the bears relocated to Louisiana were recorded as killed, according to a 1968 article in The Times-Picayune. Others wandered far from their release sites, with one recorded traveling 260 miles. Musser said moving bears away from their home range is not considered effective practice now, because bears frequently attempt to find their way back, increasing the chance that they are killed on the journey.
A 2003 study found that bears in the Arkansas mountains have genetics indicating they descended from bears released in the reintroduction program.
After population growth, the Louisiana black bear was removed from the federally threatened species list in 2016, and the state opened a limited December hunting season in 2024. Louisiana issued 26 tags to hunters in 2025, allowing each to bag one bear. The number of tags increased to 42 this year, and the state’s wildlife department expanded hunting boundaries. The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries estimates there are now around 1,500 black bears in the state.
Black bears were thought to be all but wiped out in Missouri by 1931, but sightings began to tick up after Arkansas began its reintroduction program in the late 1950s. Missouri opened a limited, highly regulated hunting season in 2021, and the University of Missouri Extension now estimates there are around 1,000 black bears in the state.
Tennessee closed its hunting season from 1970 through 1972, and partnered with North Carolina and Georgia in 1976 to share management information, ultimately adding Kentucky, South Carolina and Virginia to the fold. Tennessee’s black bear hunting regulations are focused on reducing poaching and protecting breeding females. Bear hunting is prohibited in more than 450,000 acres of bear sanctuary reserves, including the Great Smoky Mountain National Park. Tennessee estimates its current population at around 6,000 bears.
Mississippi has yet to reopen a hunting season for black bears. The state has been studying its black bear population in a standalone program since 2002, initially collaring individual bears to document their home range habitat and reproduction. The population has since grown to the size that it’s no longer feasible to track each individual. 
The program is expected to release its most up-to-date population estimates in the coming weeks. (The state typically waits 10 years between estimates to measure a full generation.) The most recent estimate from 2012 put the bear count between 150 to 300.
“Obviously, there’s a lot more now,” Ballard said.
A bill that would have forced a hunting season in 2027 passed through Mississippi’s Senate last year but stopped in the House. Ballard said there’s no set bear population that the state needs to reach before granting hunting licenses, but there are many considerations, including different management objectives for different populations and parts of the state. 
“We don’t shy away from the fact that we want to have a season, because that’s a natural outgrowth of having a sustainable population,” Ballard said. “We just want to make sure that we’re not doing it at the risk of potentially over-harvesting an animal that’s just made a recovery to a point where we can harvest.”
Mississippi wouldn’t want to over-harvest its “core population” along the state’s western edge, he said, but in the Southeast, where there are more human developments and less ideal habitat, there may be a different hunting strategy.
Coexistence
Black bears are typically associated with forest and mountainous habitats, but they were once abundant throughout the Southeast, including in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley and the Atchafalaya Basin.  Credit: Courtesy Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
Residents and visitors to areas with black bear sightings should start preparing now to live alongside established bear populations, Musser said. 
“We don’t know exactly how long that will be until it’s more common per se, but if they continue to wait (to adjust), that’s when we’re going to see those (human-) bear conflicts,” she said.
That means learning more about black bears using resources like bearwise.org and transitioning to using bear-resistant trash cans in residential and public areas.
“We have many people in East Tennessee living with bears, and throughout the country, living in areas with bears, and it’s not a huge safety risk as long as you do a few simple things,” Musser said.
One of those things is preventing bears from eating human food. In Tennessee, it is now a Class B misdemeanor to feed a black bear or fail to secure trash in areas where the state fish and wildlife commission prohibits it.
“I try to impress upon people just how good of a sense of smell that bears have. It’s about seven times better than a bloodhound,” Ballard said. “Anything that a dog can get into, a bear is going to be able to smell better and is going to be much more able to get into that.”
Farmers may see bears attempting to eat crops, mostly corn, Ballard and Gibbs said. But populations in West Tennessee and Mississippi are not dense enough to make a noticeable difference.
Compared to other animals like deer, Ballard said, bears cause much less crop damage. Gibbs said people have had success using herd dogs to keep bears, coyotes and other animals away from livestock and crops. 
For smaller-scale farms and chicken coops, electric fences may be a solution, Musser and Ballard said.
And then there’s hazing — using loud noise deterrents or paintball guns to scare bears away.
“Stuff that doesn’t cause long-term harm, but enough that it makes that bear uncomfortable,” Musser said.
Chris Dowdy, 52, grew up in Paris, Tennessee. He has a picture of his grandmother from the 1950s standing next to a bear in her yard. He describes himself as an outdoorsman and hunter. “Ironically,” he said, “my grandmother … and myself are descendants of Davy Crockett.”
He now lives in Dover, which has had several recent reported bear sightings. Dowdy said he welcomes the animals’ return to their original habitat. 
Their presence in West Tennessee is literally written into the region’s maps, he said: Dover abuts the Cumberland River, and has an area called “Cub Creek.” To the east, an unincorporated town called Bear Spring was named for the place where the supposed last bear in Stewart County was killed, according to a 1928 article in the Nashville Banner.
“It’s not abnormal (for bears to coexist with people), it’s just abnormal to us because it’s not something we’re used to having,” he said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana GOP makes controversial endorsements for Congress. More could follow.
description: The Republican Party of Louisiana’s leadership faced backlash this week after endorsing candidates in Louisiana’s two competitive congressional races using an opaque, private process.  The Louisiana GOP’s eight-member executive committee initially voted Sunday to back New Iberia state Sen. Blake Miguez over the five other Republicans in the 6th Congressional[...]
text:
Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell speaks with reporters Feb. 11, 2026, at the State Archives after qualifying to run for the 5th Congressional District. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)The Republican Party of Louisiana’s leadership faced backlash this week after endorsing candidates in Louisiana’s two competitive congressional races using an opaque, private process. 
The Louisiana GOP’s eight-member executive committee initially voted Sunday to back New Iberia state Sen. Blake Miguez over the five other Republicans in the 6th Congressional District election. It followed with a second endorsement Thursday for the other major GOP candidate in the race, state Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge.
At the same Thursday meeting, the party’s executive committee endorsed Monroe’s Misti Cordell in the 5th Congressional District race. Brent Littlefield, with Cordell’s campaign, said she had been working on securing the state party’s backing for months. 
“This endorsement means so much to me because it came from the grassroots — the men and women who have spent years doing the hard work of building our Republican Party in communities across Louisiana,” Cordell said in a news release Friday morning. 
A state party endorsement can come with huge financial advantages for the chosen candidate. Groups such as the Republican National Committee will assist a candidate’s campaign only after they receive the state party’s approval. The state party can also help their endorsed candidates with access to discounted rates for direct mail advertising and supplying crucial voter profile information. 
Cordell is a healthcare business owner who has never served in elected office. She’s the chair of the Louisiana Board of Regents, the state’s higher education oversight body. 
Cordell is running against three other Republicans with more political experience: state Sen. Stewart Cathey of Monroe, state House GOP Caucus Chairman Mike Echols of Monroe and state Rep. Gabe Firment of Pollock.. 

Echols and Firment said Friday they had been told the GOP was going to withhold its endorsement until after the Nov. 3 primary because of the large number of qualified Republicans running.
“I don’t know that it makes a huge amount of difference to the average voter or citizens. I’m not terribly upset about it,” Firment said in an interview about the Louisiana GOP’s nod to Cordell. 
Echols expressed more frustration. He said the Republican Executive Committee’ endorsement process “smells to high heaven” and likened it to a smoke-filled, secretive deal put together by the former Democratic Gov. Huey Long. 
“I’m running to win votes, not win a backroom popularity contest of 8 in a secret emergency meeting,” Echols wrote in a text message. 
It’s possible Cordell won’t be the only candidate in the 5th District race to receive the party’s endorsement. 

Louisiana GOP Chairman Derek Babcock said Cordell was endorsed because she’s so far the only candidate in the 5th District field to submit signatures from Republican State Central Committee members required for endorsement consideration. The executive committee may take up additional endorsement requests if other candidates turned in signatures. 
“I’m not going to say that we’re finished” with endorsements, Babcock said Friday. 
Babcock, who is on the Republican Executive Committee, said he did not personally vote to endorse Cordell because there are too many strong GOP candidates in the 5th District to choose one. 
“My opinion and my vote was that we stay out of that race,” he said. 
Landry has not endorsed candidates in the 5th or 6th Districts races, but the state party preferences for Edmonds and Cordell likely pleased him. 

Landry and Miguez had a falling out two years ago when Miguez publicly criticized the governor’s plan for overhauling Louisiana’s tax and budget system. Last year, the governor took some not-so-subtle shots at Miguez when he vetoed a nutrition bill the senator had authored. Landry’s rejection came less than two weeks after Miguez had announced he was running for U.S. Senate, though he eventually qualified for the 5th District contest.    

The governor and first lady Sharon Landry are personal friends with Cordell, who he appointed to the Board of Regents. Some longtime Landry’s campaign staffers are now working on Cordell’s election effort.

In an interview Friday, Babcock said he wants to see the party endorsement process overhauled after this election cycle. The rules for how to seek the party’s endorsement should be displayed clearly on the party’s website in the future, and there need to be firm deadlines for candidates to submit signatures for endorsement consideration, he said. 

Firment said he would like to see any future party endorsement process involve a more extensive vetting of candidates’ backgrounds and interviews. Candidates should have to articulate a “vision” for their time in office, he said. 
Babcock said some of the confusion around party endorsements should be resolved by the new semi-closed party primary process that applies to elections for Louisiana Supreme Court, Public Service Commission, Board of Elementary and Secondary Education and U.S. House seats moving forward. For these races, voters will pick which Republican candidate they want to receive the party’s backing, not the executive committee, Babcock said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Kansas City’s habit of dismissing the voters who say no
description: Kansas City leaders can seem contemptuous of the voters they answer to. The Royals stadium deal, pushed through without a public vote, is the latest example. That hostility goes back more than a decade — and former Mayor Sly James’ recent column is the latest reminder. James begins an Aug. 23 essay by chastising those […]
text:
Sly James, mayor of Kansas City, after speaking about leadership, political activism and public investments last year at the Dole Institute of Politics at University of Kansas in Lawrence (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector).Kansas City leaders can seem contemptuous of the voters they answer to. The Royals stadium deal, pushed through without a public vote, is the latest example. That hostility goes back more than a decade — and former Mayor Sly James’ recent column is the latest reminder.
James begins an Aug. 23 essay by chastising those he calls CAVE people — citizens against virtually everything — a slight he has used since at least 2012. Readers aren’t told what they’re against or why they’re wrong. James just waves them off. It seems to be his preferred approach to public policy: dismiss, distort and dominate.
He seems unaware that his insult is one of Missouri’s nicknames — we’re the Cave State. The irony is compounded because the state’s better-known nickname, the Show-Me State, is exactly the type of discourse James is dismissing.
James then turns to his real task: buttering up the Kansas City Streetcar Authority and assailing streetcar skeptics. This, too, goes back to 2014, when he smeared opponents of extending the streetcar south along the trolley trail into Brookside and Waldo. James was also dismissive of his own advisory board, which had not yet even met when the city filed its petition to create the taxing district.
Even before 60% of voters rejected the initial streetcar district in August 2014, then-Councilman Russ Johnson said, “[T]he streetcar is going to be expanded whether we like it or not, because I know 50 people that will figure out how to draw a boundary to get it passed.”
To dismiss and dominate is strong-arm politics: “I’m right, you’re wrong.” But to distort facts requires skill, and James’ column gets several things wrong.
First, James cites Kansas City’s “vision and momentum” as the reason it was “selected for Google Fiber’s flagship experiment.” But Kansas City, Missouri, wasn’t chosen. It lost. Google chose Kansas City, Kansas. A vice president for Google said, “Kansas City [Kansas] has great infrastructure and Kansas has a great business-friendly environment for us to deploy a service in.”
Second, James refers to KC as “a booming metropolis.” But from April 2020 through July 2025, Kansas City, Missouri’s population grew 2.6%. That’s slower than Overland Park (+3.3%), Lenexa (+5.4%), Olathe (+6.2%), Lee’s Summit (+6.3%) and North Kansas City (+25.7%). Kansas City’s growth is behind the national average (3.1%), yet ahead of Missouri’s (1.9%). Far from booming, we aren’t even keeping up.
Third, James claims, “Sales tax receipts generated within the Transportation Development District surged by more than 65% following the line’s opening — far outpacing citywide growth.” He appears to be citing a 2019 article by the head of the KC Streetcar Authority. The authority’s own materials say sales tax receipts grew 58% from 2014 through 2016, versus 16% citywide. Nobody explains why the numbers differ. James doesn’t even tell us what years his data covers
James wants readers to believe the streetcar is driving economic growth. But the figures aren’t just a decade old — they’re misleading.
The downtown TDD is a tiny district that has received all manner of taxpayer subsidies. One or two successful venues could swing the TDD’s sales tax receipts without producing a noticeable change in citywide collections — and without proving the streetcar caused the increase.
For a substantive analysis of the streetcar’s economic development effect, read this comparison of property valuations within the TDD and the county. The TDD’s total market value grew at the same rate as the county in each year between 2014 and 2023, meaning zero economic benefit by the metric that’s hardest to cherry-pick.
Fourth, James calls the streetcar’s zero-fare policy “forward thinking” and an example of economic equity. Yet the bus system, which serves low-income riders citywide, just reinstated a $2 fare. The streetcar, a slow and expensive Main Street party bus, is free. Where is the equity in that?
Fifth, he makes claims about the streetcar’s role in winning the NFL draft, the World Cup and NCAA events. He says others call it the “best in the nation.” This is impossible to verify, and it echoes James’ claim that Kansas City lost the 2016 Republican National Convention to Cleveland because it had too few hotel rooms. Yet Kansas City had roughly 10,000 more hotel rooms than metropolitan Cleveland and nearly identical downtown inventory.
James ends by arguing that expanding the streetcar routes east and west will build a “unified, inclusive city” for generations to come. But when Kansas City voted on that same eastward extension along Linwood Boulevard in 2014, neighborhoods along the route rejected it. Freedom, Inc. called it “a regressive tax scheme,” and the pastor of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, whose parish sat on the route, warned the assessment would be “a huge and unfair burden on the poor.”
None of this makes James uniquely careless with the truth, but it does make him the latest example of how Kansas City leaders tend to operate. The city has real strengths and substantial challenges, and no single project, stadium or streetcar will solve them. City Hall seems more interested in hardball politics — dismiss, distort, dominate — than in understanding problems and crafting solutions that gather support.
And it appears to be habit forming.

description: People share their opinions on data centers and artificial intelligence when a North Dakota legislative committee meets again Monday to address those topics.  The Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meets at 9 a.m. Monday at the Capitol with an agenda that includes presentations by policy experts, the energy industry and state utility and pollu[...]
text:
The meeting room for a new legislative committee to study artificial intelligence and data centers was standing room only on July 15, 2026. More than 70 members of the public were in attendance.  (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)People share their opinions on data centers and artificial intelligence when a North Dakota legislative committee meets again Monday to address those topics. 
The Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meets at 9 a.m. Monday at the Capitol with an agenda that includes presentations by policy experts, the energy industry and state utility and pollution regulators. Public comment is scheduled for 11:15 a.m. 
The committee, announced in June, has taken testimony on the pros and cons of artificial intelligence and the impact of data centers that are being built to generate AI. Multiple data center projects are proposed in North Dakota, with developers attracted by the state’s cool climate, access to power and abundance of land for development. 
Previous meetings have explored AI regulation, AI use in education and risks to youth, and concerns about data centers.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In Dolly Parton’s life and death, lessons in life and love and devotion to what really matters
description: The queen is dead. Long live the queen. That queen, of course, would be legendary country entertainer Dolly Parton, who slipped the surly bonds of Earth on Aug. 25 at the age of 80. A Tennessee native, she nonetheless visited Kansas three years ago to celebrate the expansion of her Imagination Library literacy program. The […]
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly joined singer and child literacy advocate Dolly Parton to an event marking statewide expansion in Kansas of a program donating a book each month to children 0-5. (Photo by Kansas Governor's Office)The queen is dead. Long live the queen.
That queen, of course, would be legendary country entertainer Dolly Parton, who slipped the surly bonds of Earth on Aug. 25 at the age of 80. A Tennessee native, she nonetheless visited Kansas three years ago to celebrate the expansion of her Imagination Library literacy program.
The preternaturally talented Parton had much to teach those of us in the Sunflower State — and every other state besides, if we bother to pay attention.
Notably, she remained in the region where she was born, raised and achieved international fame. She invested in the people and places that she came from, even though those people and places might not always have agreed with how she presented herself or how she chose to live her life as a fiercely independent entertainer.
In mid-August, I marked five years at Kansas Reflector as opinion editor. I too, have chosen to live in my home state. In my inaugural column, I wrote about how important it was that good people, caring people, keep pushing for positive change.
Parton proved that could be done. For real, and for the long term.
For those of us who are LGBTQ+, politically progressive or just a little bit quirky, the fact that Parton stayed and earned not just the respect and love of those in Tennessee but those across the nation proves that the traditional red vs. blue dynamics of this country do not explain the wonder and kindness of its people.
Parton was famous for saying that it cost a lot of money to look as cheap as she did, but the truth of the matter was, she never looked cheap. Flamboyant yes. Extravagant even. But aside from a handful of bouts with overzealous makeup artists, she never looked like anything other than what she was — an enthusiastic musician, humanitarian, and creative adventurer.
She wrote thousands of songs, recorded dozens of albums, appeared on film and TV, donated millions to charity and ran a theme park that transformed her poverty-stricken community. She stayed true to herself and helped others along the way.


 
A fading past
Few others share Parton’s cultural importance and dedication to do good. Some try. Rock stars Bruce Springsteen and Elton John have spoken up for admirable civic causes and raised money for charity, but both have reached their late 70s.
As our society’s common cultural touchpoints recede, so too does our shared sense of civic understanding.
Both the Democratic Socialists of America and President Donald Trump paid tribute to Parton. She was warmly remembered on social media by both rapper Eminem and the Nashville musicians’ union. Millions felt touched by her spirit and warmth.
Parton made a conscious decision in her later decades to be an unproblematic celebrity. Her public statements about social issues were carefully calibrated to support liberal fans while not offending conservative ones. She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom when offered by both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.
She understood, with the keen intelligence that followed her career as a performer and businesswoman, that she had become a common cultural cause. She likely sacrificed her own freedom of expression to do so.
I don’t know who can fill Parton’s tiny, high-heeled shoes today. Modern entertainers cultivate devoted, narrow fandoms. Musicians and writers and actors and standup comics work harder than ever to reach fewer and fewer people. If another Dolly Parton set out from Locust Ridge, Tennessee, today, would she have the same opportunities to become internationally beloved?
Let’s not think about that. For now, at least.
 
Family and friends
Throughout her eight decades, Parton proved that core values of humanity — love, family, friendship — matter no matter what you look like or where you live.
As one of 12 children, she tended to an enormous extended family, recording albums and writing cookbooks with them. She featured her parents and siblings on a TV broadcast from 1976. You can see how the presence of the family delighted her (and the musical talents of her mother, Avie Lee.


 Monday Night Variety
She was married to her husband, Carl Dean, for almost 60 years. Although the couple did not have children, they helped raise several of Parton’s younger siblings and stayed in close touch with the extended family.
Dean stayed out of the spotlight, telling his effervescent wife that he had no use for publicity. He still listened to her albums, watched her movies and visited Dollywood to keep an eye on things. When he died last year at age 82, Parton issued a heartbreaking yet optimistic song, “If You Hadn’t Been There.”
As different as those of us living in Kansas can be — liberal or conservative, Republican or Democrat, Christian or Muslim or Jewish, man or woman, black or white or every race in between, gay or straight, transgender or cisgender, married or single, introvert or extrovert — we all share similar desires.
We love our spouses and significant others. We care about our friends. We watch over our families. Like Parton, let us all try to do our best.
As she sang in her 1991 song “Family”:

When it’s family, you forgive them
For they know not what they do
When it’s family, you accept them
‘Cause you have no choice but to
When it’s family, they’re a mirror
Of the worst and best in you
And they always put you to the test
And you always try to do your best
And just pray for God to do the rest
When it’s family 
 
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” comes out Sept. 29 from the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.
