name: Washington State Standard
title: WA governor met with state worker protest at hospital construction ceremony
description: Washington marked a milestone Friday with the final structural beam placed on a new psychiatric facility on the Western State Hospital campus in Pierce County.  Along with the pomp came protest. “This is really a chance to honor the hundreds and hundreds of workers who are working so hard every single day to build this […]
text:
State employees protest near an event commemorating the construction of a new psychiatric facility where Gov. Bob Ferguson was speaking on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)Washington marked a milestone Friday with the final structural beam placed on a new psychiatric facility on the Western State Hospital campus in Pierce County. 
Along with the pomp came protest.
“This is really a chance to honor the hundreds and hundreds of workers who are working so hard every single day to build this really critical structure,” Gov. Bob Ferguson told a crowd that included hundreds of construction workers. As is tradition, the governor signed the final beam before it became part of the building.
A few yards away, on the other side of a 6-foot chain-link fence, a different group of workers was not there to celebrate.
The handful of state employees loudly chanted their displeasure with the progress of talks on a collective bargaining agreement with negotiators from Ferguson’s budget office.
“No contract! No peace! No contract! No peace!” they shouted, with some calling out the governor by name. 
Washington Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson speaks at the topping ceremony for the new 350-bed facility on the Western State Hospital campus on Aug. 28, 2026. The event marked the signing and placement of the final beam in the structure. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
Ferguson didn’t visibly acknowledge their presence during the event. Afterward, when asked for his message to them, he said, “It’s an interesting choice to come protest an event where we’re honoring workers.” 
“We’re negotiating,” he said. “I don’t have anything else to add.”
Negotiations between the executive branch and unions representing tens of thousands of state workers are intensifying. State law sets an Oct. 1 deadline for agreements to be ratified by unions in order to be considered for funding in the next two-year budget.
The Washington Federation of State Employees, which represents 54,000 state government, higher education and public service workers, is organizing walkouts Monday to demonstrate their frustration with the state’s proposals.
Friday served as a warm-up. A half dozen of the union’s members marched on the other side of the fence from where Ferguson headlined the ceremony.
A barrier between them and the stage couldn’t prevent their voices from being heard.
Eric Olson, senior vice president of Clark Construction, the final speaker of the program, walked to the podium, paused briefly and glanced their way before saying, “We’re going to go forward now.”
A couple minutes into the demonstration, Charles Southerland, chief executive officer of the hospital’s Civil Center of Excellence, approached the members, asking them to stop. 
They did not. 
“Just to be clear, our issue is not with hospital administration,” said Mike Yestramski, president of the Washington Federation of State Employees and social worker at the hospital. “The issue is above them.”
Yestramski has been at odds with Ferguson in the past, helping lead a protest at the Capitol during the 2025 legislative session as Ferguson and lawmakers discussed the possibility of furloughs. The union leader drew attention at that time for calling Ferguson a “ratfink.” 
This year, with a looming budget shortfall, union leaders braced for bare-bones wage offerings from state negotiators. But Yestramski said Friday it is worse than expected, with the rejection of every one of their proposals.
Mark Camacho, union member, uses a megaphone to lead chanting workers at a ceremony for a new psychiatric facility at the Western State Hospital campus. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)
Several construction workers approached and chatted with the governor after the event.
The state broke ground on the 500,000-square-foot, 350-bed facility in October 2024 and construction accelerated last summer. The nearly $1 billion undertaking is expected to be completed in mid-2028. It’s part of a court-ordered state effort to reduce wait times for mental health treatment and evaluations for criminal defendants who are incompetent to stand trial. 
As the ceremony wrapped up, Ferguson and his wife were escorted in the opposite direction of the protesting employees.
“If state workers (are) so important as you said when you came and talked to us the first time to become governor, then put more stake in the state workers,” said Mark Camacho, union member and behavioral health specialist at Western State Hospital.
Yestramski said that to say contract negotiations have not been going well “would be an understatement.” 
“We figured if we could come to this,” he said, “maybe (the governor) would talk to workers.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Forward Party makes its case for ballot access before a federal judge
description: Attorneys for the New Mexico Forward Party on Friday told a federal judge that New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver held minor party candidates to an unfairly burdensome standard to qualify for the upcoming Nov. 3 general election ballot.
text:
New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls stands outside U.S. District Court in Santa Fe on Aug. 28, 2026, after his attorneys argued that New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver enforced unfair ballot access requirements on minor party candidates. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Attorneys for the New Mexico Forward Party on Friday told a federal judge that New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver held minor party candidates to an unfairly burdensome standard to qualify for the upcoming Nov. 3 general election ballot.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Even though the state Forward Party officially qualified as a minor party in New Mexico earlier this year, its small voter base has meant that its statewide candidates — such as Party Chair Bob Perls, a former state lawmaker who filed to run for U.S. Senate this year — had to collect as many signatures as independent candidates: more than 14,000. By comparison, Democrats and Republicans seeking statewide office have to collect 2,500 and 2,350, respectively.
In June, Perls failed to make the ballot in the race against incumbent U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Forward Party candidate Michael Vigil failed to qualify as a challenger to State Auditor Joseph Maestas.
Perls filed his lawsuit against Toulouse Oliver in U.S. District Court in July.
“New Mexico’s political status quo has been frozen,” Oliver Hall, an attorney and executive director of the Washington, D.C., Center for Competitive Democracy representing Perls, argued in court Friday. He added that he believes New Mexico has the most stringent requirements in the nation for minor party candidates.
Former presidential candidate Andrew Yang launches NM Forward Party

Attorneys for Toulouse Oliver responded that the Forward Party’s local candidates successfully qualified for the general election, and that the current signature requirements for statewide candidates are meant to keep “frivolous” candidates off the ballot.
They called on Lindsey Bachman, the Secretary of State’s communications, legislative and executive affairs director, to testify remotely via Zoom. Perls’ attorneys alleged that he and other Forward Party candidates did not have the proper access to the state’s online voter signature portal for a portion of the summer and argued that it put them at a significant disadvantage compared to candidates who could gather signatures electronically.
Bachman responded that nothing was stopping them from continuing to gather voter signatures with a pen and paper.
“We continue to receive petition filings that include paper and online (signatures),” she said, adding that there “likely is an ease” to gathering signatures digitally, but has had “candidates tell me they don’t like using the online form.”
U.S. District Court Judge Margaret Strickland told attorneys on both sides that she would issue a written ruling “quickly.”
After Strickland left the courtroom, Perls told reporters he thought much of Friday’s hearing focused on the minutiae of Bachman’s testimony and not his lawsuit’s allegations of First and Fourteenth Amendment violations.
As for the assertion that higher signature requirements keep “frivolous” candidates off the ballot, Perls noted that New Mexico typically suffers from “empty ballots,” pointing to the lack of contested primary races for the state Legislature and beyond. The Republican nominee for Luján’s U.S. Senate seat, for example, ran unopposed as a write-in candidate in the June primary. 
“All we want to do as the Forward Party is bring competition, bring choice to voters, in some small way solve the problem of lack of choice,” he said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Front Range cities will vote on tax measure to fund Colorado Connector rail service
description: The fate of a decades-long effort to restore intercity passenger rail service to the Front Range is now in the hands of Colorado voters. The board of the Front Range Passenger Rail District voted 14-1 Friday to refer a sales tax measure to the November ballots of voters in 30 municipalities along the planned route […]
text:
A next-generation Amtrak Airo train carries Colorado state and local officials for a ride on the test track at the federal Transportation Technology Center near Pueblo on Friday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The fate of a decades-long effort to restore intercity passenger rail service to the Front Range is now in the hands of Colorado voters.
The board of the Front Range Passenger Rail District voted 14-1 Friday to refer a sales tax measure to the November ballots of voters in 30 municipalities along the planned route of the Colorado Connector rail service between Pueblo and Fort Collins. If approved by voters, the measure would raise an estimated $295 million annually by levying a district-wide 0.333% sales and use tax, equal to about 33 cents added to a $100 purchase.
Under a multi-phase plan announced by the FRPR district earlier this summer, the operation of a Colorado Connector “starter service,” between Fort Collins and Denver, is already on track to launch with three daily round trips by 2029 — with or without the additional tax revenue.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The funding from a successful ballot measure would go towards the full build-out of the Colorado Connector system, which spans 12 planned permanent stops along the Interstate 25 corridor. District officials say that service on the full Fort-Collins-to-Pueblo line would begin by 2032, with the potential for future expansion north to Cheyenne and south to Trinidad and New Mexico.
John Putnam, a longtime state and federal transportation official and chair of the FRPR board, called I-25 “a single point of failure for our economy, for our way of life, for emergency response.”
“We are overdue in creating redundancy and resiliency, providing options and getting cars off the road,” Putnam said just prior to the board’s vote, which came at a special meeting held at the Transportation Technology Center, a federal rail testing facility east of Pueblo.
“All transportation is subsidized right now — highways are heavily subsidized,” he added. “There’s no reason to hold passenger rail or transit or another form of transportation to a double standard.”
Following the vote, state and local officials celebrated by boarding a next-generation Amtrak Airo train undergoing testing at the TTC for a ride around the facility’s test loop. The first trains in the Airo fleet are slated to enter service on Amtrak intercity routes like the Cascades line in the Pacific Northwest by next year — and with Amtrak highly likely to operate the Colorado Connector as one of its state-supported routes, Colorado officials hope they’ll soon be traveling up and down the Front Range as well.
John Putnam, chair of the Front Range Passenger Rail District board of directors, speaks at an event at the federal Transportation Technology Center near Pueblo on Friday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, a Democrat from Lafayette, called it a chance to “see the future of passenger rail in the state of Colorado, and really a way forward for the nation.”
“What an exciting development it is, how exciting it will be when all of you have collectively together made this dream a reality,” he added.
Years in the making
Aside from several stops on long-haul Amtrak routes, Colorado hasn’t had regular intercity passenger rail service since the early 1970s. Interest in a revival waxed and waned over the years, with multiple false starts, feasibility studies and proposals that stalled amid high projected costs.
A state commission established in 2017 finally took formal steps towards a service development plan, before the Legislature in 2021 created the FRPR district and gave it the authority to refer a tax measure to voters once a plan had been completed.
In addition to Colorado Connector and Amtrak’s seasonal Winter Park Express, the state is also planning to launch a “Mountain Rail” service between Denver and Granby by the end of this year, with future expansion planned as far as Steamboat Springs.
The Colorado Connector’s full delivery plan calls for a gradual expansion to 10 daily round trips north of Denver and eight round trips on the southern segment. Permanent stations would be located in Fort Collins, Loveland, Longmont, Boulder, Louisville, Broomfield, Westminster, Denver, Littleton, Sterling Ranch, Colorado Springs and Pueblo. The plan also envisions special-event stops at the Broncos’ future home at Burnham Yards and the planned Denver Summit soccer stadium at I-25 and Broadway.
The Front Range Passenger Rail District’s board of directors voted 14-1 to refer a sales tax to the 2026 ballot at its meeting Friday, held at the Transportation Technology Center near Pueblo. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
State officials had considered moving forward with a ballot measure as early as 2024, but ultimately delayed a vote to allow additional time for service and financial planning. State lawmakers earlier this year shrank the district’s boundaries to align with the few dozen urban and suburban municipalities most directly served by the route — and those, based on past results, most likely to vote for a tax hike. The “Colorado Connector” brand, meanwhile, received a splashy rollout after Coloradans were invited to vote on the service’s name, which shortened is CoCo.
Those involved with the project have been candid about one major motivating factor behind the extra planning and outreach — the long shadow of FasTracks, the Regional Transportation District expansion plan that was approved by voters in 2004, only to face extended delays on projects like the B Line between Denver and Boulder, which is currently slated for completion in 2042.
The timeline for that commuter-rail service was pushed back decades in large part due to the unexpectedly high costs of leasing the tracks along the route from freight rail giant BNSF. District officials say that with Amtrak’s involvement, diligent planning work and a long-term access agreement already signed between Colorado and BNSF, the Colorado Connector won’t be similarly derailed.
“A lot of that was done (because of) concerns about how FasTracks didn’t exactly come to pass as was promised,” Claire Levy, a Boulder County commissioner and the area’s representative on the FRPR board, said before Friday’s vote. “We wanted to make sure when this went to a vote that we had a very transparent financial plan, so that people would have confidence that a ‘yes’ vote would actually provide the funding to to do what is being promised.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Sullivan goes on attack in first post-primary faceoff for Alaska’s U.S. Senate race
description: In their first faceoff since the Aug. 18 primary election, Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan used the term “Lower 48 liberal” or some variation of it 16 times to attack his opponent, Democrat Mary Peltola. Speaking at a candidate forum held Thursday at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association’s annual conference in Anchorage, Sullivan used […]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, listen to a question at a candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. The Alaska Senate race is considered critical to control of the body, which currently has a Republican majority. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)In their first faceoff since the Aug. 18 primary election, Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan used the term “Lower 48 liberal” or some variation of it 16 times to attack his opponent, Democrat Mary Peltola.
 

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at ae U.S. Senate candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association Conference in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Speaking at a candidate forum held Thursday at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association’s annual conference in Anchorage, Sullivan used nearly every question as an opportunity to tie Peltola, a former U.S. House member, to former Democratic President Joe Biden, whom he accused of maliciously trying to destroy Alaska’s economy.
“My opponents’ liberal Lower 48 anti-Alaska allies in the Congress and the White House were focused on completely shutting down Alaska oil and gas and killing thousands of jobs,” he said.
Sullivan and Peltola are the front-runners among four top vote-getters advancing to the general election. The winner will represent Alaska in the U.S. Senate for a six-year term. 
Sullivan claimed Peltola “consistently voted with Lower 48 liberal allies of hers against our interests, and that is why this election is so important.”.
And he warned that a Peltola victory would allow Democrats and environmentalists to resume what he described as deliberate attempts to harm Alaska. They would continue their efforts to block oil development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and impose environmental restrictions on development elsewhere in Alaska, he said.
“If my opponents’ liberal Lower 48 allies get power again, the Democrats, if (Senate Minority Leader) Chuck Schumer is in charge again — she’s committed to supporting them — they will,” he said. “If elected, she would once again empower, vote with, and be beholden to the same far-left politicians who for decades have worked to crush our state.”
The primary election results indicate that Sullivan is facing headwinds as he runs for a third term in the Senate.
 

Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, speaks at the U.S. Senate candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association Conference in Anchorage.
 

	In the nonpartisan, open primary, Sullivan had about 42% of the total vote, 7 percentage points behind Peltola, who was at about 49%, according to the most recent count, released on Wednesday.
The race is considered pivotal to control of the Senate, where Republicans currently hold the majority.
Peltola voices support for oil and gas development
At Thursday’s event, Peltola largely refrained from attacking Sullivan directly.
She described herself as pro-development and a champion for the oil industry.
Peltola was the first Alaska Native woman elected to U.S. Congress in 2022, and served a two-year term before being defeated by current U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III in 2024. 
At the event, she took credit for winning approval for ConocoPhillips’ huge Willow project on the North Slope from a reluctant President Biden.
She is “proud of the work that I did within the Biden administration to talk about Willow in a way that they could understand,” she said. “And we moved Willow forward, thanks to me.”
Sullivan took issue with that statement, pointing out that Willow development had been approved in the first Trump administration, before Peltola was elected to the House. However, a court ruling in 2021 overturned that Trump approval, finding it to be based on flawed analysis that violated federal law. That left the decision about Willow approval up to the new Biden administration.
Peltola, in line with a message common among Alaska Republicans, used several remarks at the forum to criticize Lower 48 regulators whom she said do not understand Alaska conditions. Among those conditions are seasonal restrictions, she said.
“Our construction windows are so short in Alaska. They’re like nowhere else. Developing in the Arctic is so unique,” she said. “If we miss a barge, that can cause a year’s delay or two years’ delay. if we miss a shipping window that can have devastating effects for the life of the project.”
Overall, Peltola lauded the Alaska oil industry as critical to the state and its economy.
 

Mary Peltola listens to a question posed by moderator Michelle Egan at a candidate forum held by the Alaska Oii and Gas Association on Aug. 27, 2026. Next to Peltola is i Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola, a Democrat and former U.S. House member, is challenging Sullivan. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“You know, over 80% of the oil revenues, of the revenues that state of Alaska operates with are generated by oil and gas and in large part the Trans Alaska Pipeline,” she said.
That percentage is outdated, however. Oil royalties, taxes and fees once provided as much as 90% of the money used for state government operations, that percentage has diminished over time. As of December, oil royalties, taxes and fees provided only about a quarter of the unrestricted general funds, according to the Alaska Department of Revenue. Investment earnings of the Alaska Permanent Fund, the state’s sovereign wealth fund, actually provide the majority of unrestricted-use revenues, and that has been the case for several years.
In many of her remarks at the AOGA forum, Peltola echoed Sullivan somewhat. She lobbed a bit of criticism at the Biden administration. Her specific target was former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland.
Peltola faulted Sullivan for voting to confirm Haaland, the first Native American to serve in that position. She claimed Haaland was “one of the biggest stumbling blocks Alaska has ever seen.”“We need to make sure that we’re confirming secretaries that are going to understand our mission and not be roadblocks and not be activists,” she said.
Haaland, a Laguna of Pueblo tribal member, is now running for governor in New Mexico. While serving as Interior Secretary, she visited Alaska and spoke at the Alaska Federation of Natives conventions and was celebrated by that organization.
Most of the AOGA event focused on issues directly related to the oil industry. High-profile issues like inflation, healthcare policy and the Iran war and their effects on Alaskans were not discussed.
Peltola did slip in a mention of fisheries issues, which have become a hot debate topic in this year’s election.
She said she worked to prevent an Endangered Species Act listing for Alaska Chinook salmon, and that such a listing would have had unintended ripple effects on other fisheries. Other species of salmon, such as sockeyes and chums, swim with Chinook salmon, she said. “If we preclude Alaskans from being able to harvest Chinook, that means we’re precluding them from harvesting just about everything during the summer,” she said.
Trump administration impacts
Peltola also voiced a specific criticism of the Trump administration.
The mass federal government firings carried out through the administration’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, exacerbated staffing shortages that were already slowing needed federal services in Alaska – including permitting for development projects, she said.
 

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright confer during a panel discussion at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association annual convention iin Anchoroage on Aug 27, 2026. Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“DOGE impacted Alaska more than any other state, and no other state is more impacted by our federal agencies and our federal employees in Alaska,” she said. “No other state is as dependent on the decisions and the work of our federal employees as Alaska is. We’ve got to fully staff all of our agencies from top to bottom.”
Sullivan has tied himself closely to the Trump administration, delivering effusive praise for the president and his cabinet members. As he has elsewhere, he spoke at the forum of his close relationship with Trump and said he has helped the president focus on pro-development Alaska policies. 
“We were able to get the Trump administration, who issued an executive order on day one to unleash Alaska’s extraordinary resource potential,” he said, referring to an order that overturned Biden-era environmental protections around the state.
Trump administration cabinet members, in turn, have praised Sulivan in their recent visits to Alaska and described him as a close Trump ally.
One was U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, a keynote speaker at the AOGA conference. In his speech to the industry audience on Thursday, he said Sullivan has been a staunch ally of oil developers and the Trump efforts to reverse past environmental policies and deemphasize renewable energy in favor of oil, natural gas and coal.
He said Sullivan and the other two members of Alaska’s all-Republican congressional delegation. With their defense of fossil fuel production and  “have been there in a battle to try to roll back some of these choosing-expensive-energy policies that have so burdened Americans.” 
Earlier in the month, at an airport stop during a tour of Alaska, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also praised the senator.
“No one advocates for Alaska and what is the need today and the future buildout of what it’s going to look like down the road than Dan does,” Mullin said during a brief airport news conference on Aug. 11 with Sullivan and the commandant of the U.S Coast Guard. “It’s amazing, because he’s got such a good relationship with the president, which that’s vital to be able to get something done.”
But support among voters has declined. Recent polling puts Trump’s approval rating below 40% and indicates that he has net disapproval in almost all states, including Alaska.
U.S. House candidates speak
Candidates in Alaska’s other federal race, the contest for the state’s sole U.S. House seat, met later in the day for what turned out to be a more congenial and low-key forum.
 

U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, R-Alaska, listens to a question at an Anchorage candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. Next to him is his challenger, independent candidate Bill Hill. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Incumbent Rep. Nick Begich III, R-Alaska, and independent challenger Bill Hill delivered largely similar messages on what they said was a need for regulatory certainty, development opportunity and the benefits of oil and gas production in the state.
Begich used the forum to talk about what he said were his successes during his first term in office. Begich has also aligned closely with President Trump and his administration.
“I’m only one member of the United States House out of 435, but we have delivered historic wins for our great state,” he said.
He cited numerous bills that mandate more oil drilling and other resource development on public lands in Alaska. Those successes, he said, included opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil development and winning a higher share of future royalties from oil produced on federal land. Those victories “are 50-year objectives” that generations of Alaskans have tried to achieve, he said.
“I’m also proud to report that I’ve passed more legislation into law than any other member of Congress in the 119th Congress,” he said. “I’m also proud to report that we have passed more legislation, had more legislative wins than any freshman in House history.”
Begich, though a Republican and an ally of President Trump, is a member of a Democratic family active in Alaska politics. His grandfather, also named Nick Begich, was a Democratic U.S. House member who died in a plane crash in 1972. One of his uncles, Mark Begich, was Anchorage’s mayor and served one term as a Democratic U.S. senator. Another uncle, former state Sen. Tom Begich, is currently a Democratic candidate for governor.
Hill, a former teacher and school superintendent whom polls indicate is not well known among a wide swath of Alaska voters, used the forum to describe his biography.
He is a Dena’ina Athabascan from the Bristol Bay region and has fished commercially since he was 8 years old, he told the AOGA audience. He worked as a construction worker, spent 25 years working in education and is the owner of a small business, he said.
Hill said he is grateful for the benefits that oil development has brought to the state.
“As a young kid, I worried about the idea that I would have to fly out of my home community of Kokhanok to attend high school,” he said, naming the Iliamna Lake village where he grew up. “But then the oil and gas industry came to Alaska. It transformed Alaska. It transformed opportunities in Alaska.”
 

Independent candidate Bill Hill, a former teacher and school superintendent from Bristol Bya, speaks at a U.S. House candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Oil revenues paid for schools, services like water and sewer systems and produced a Permanent Fund dividend program that has transformed Alaskans’ lives, he said.
“So I am a product of the oil and gas industry,” he said.
As an independent, he would be in position to work effectively if control of the administrative or legislative branches switched in the midterms or later, he said.
“We can weather the swings between administrations. Part of that requires having somebody who can work across party lines, and I would like to do that work for you,” he said.
The forum ended on a friendly note, with both candidates naming their preferred fish — red salmon for Begich, Bristol Bay salmon for Hill — and discussing their affinities for muktuk and pilot bread, two iconic Alaska food items.
But the morning after the forum, the National Republican Congressional Committee issued a news release attacking Hill as an anti-fossil fuel “radical” who wants Alaska to transition from its oil dependence.
“Liberal Bill Hill wants to bring back Biden’s failed energy policies and put D.C. Democrats ahead of Alaskans. Hill’s radical agenda would raise costs, crush Alaska’s economy, and kill jobs. Liberal Bill Hill will be resoundingly rejected this fall,” committee spokesperson Zach Bannon said in the statement.
As of Wednesday, Begich had 45.2% of the vote in the open primary, while Hill had about 32%, according to the Division of Elections. Matt Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his campaign in July and threw his support to Hill, had 8%, according to the results. In third place is Eric Hafner, a Democrat currently serving a federal prison sentence in New York, with 3.77% of the vote. Democrat John Williams got 2.6% of the vote and fourth place, advancing to the general election in November.
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and his wife, Julie Fate Sullivan, listen to the U.S. House candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. On the stage are independent candidate Bill Hill, iincumbent U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, and moderatoro Tara Sweeney. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Cox appoints 2 more justices in year of major changes to Utah’s Supreme Court
description: Gov. Spencer Cox on Friday announced he picked a judge and an attorney for two open seats on the Utah Supreme Court, the latest changes in this year’s reshaping of the state’s highest court.  Cox appointed 5th District Judge Matthew Bell and civil litigator Michael Menssen to fill the seats vacated by retiring Chief Justice […]
text:
Utah Supreme Court nominees Matthew Bell and Michael Menssen, sitting with Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman, react to remarks from Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Utah Capitol. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)Gov. Spencer Cox on Friday announced he picked a judge and an attorney for two open seats on the Utah Supreme Court, the latest changes in this year’s reshaping of the state’s highest court. 
Cox appointed 5th District Judge Matthew Bell and civil litigator Michael Menssen to fill the seats vacated by retiring Chief Justice Matthew Durrant and former Justice Diana Hagen, who stepped down in May after a dismissed complaint of misconduct against her was made public. 
In a press conference at the Capitol Friday, Cox told reporters that “originalism is very important to me and to these justices as well,” referring to the judicial philosophy focused on the text of the constitution and its meaning as intended by the Founding Fathers.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There is no place for judicial activism in the system,” Cox said. “If you want to make laws, then get another job.”  
Earlier this summer, Cox tapped lawyers to fill a two-seat expansion of the Supreme Court under a new state law. The expansion followed a string of legal setbacks the court dealt the Legislature, including in a redistricting lawsuit. Lawmakers backing the change insisted growing the bench would help the court review cases more efficiently. 
After all four open seats are filled, the governor will have appointed six out of seven justices. 
Hagen’s resignation came after the Utah House of Representatives released the dismissed complaint in response to a public records request. The complaint alleged Hagen had an extramarital affair with an attorney involved in the state’s redistricting case. Both denied the allegations, and Hagen said she stepped down to avoid dragging her family and friends into the controversy once the governor and top Republican state leaders sought an independent investigation into the allegations. 
The governor called Durrant “a towering figure in Utah’s legal community” who has spent more than 25 years on the state’s high court, with 14 years as chief justice.
“And to say his shoes are not easy to fill is certainly an understatement,” Cox said. 
In another change, the governor, rather than the justices, will appoint the new chief justice for the first time under a 2025 measure he signed into law. 
“I’m going to take my time on that,” Cox said of the process Friday. “We want to make sure we have a fully-staffed court before I make a decision like that.”
He pledged to reach out to each justice for their perspective on the matter and said he anticipates making a decision in six to eight weeks. He noted that upcoming appointment, like the ones he announced Friday, is subject to approval by the Utah Senate. 
Bell, the current presiding judge for the 5th District encompassing Washington, Iron and Beaver counties, was previously an assistant U.S. attorney and a trial attorney in the U.S. Department of Justice’s antitrust division. He began his career as a corrections officer and police officer, Cox said. 
“It is hard to imagine another candidate so well prepared to consider and rule on the issues that impact every level of our system,” Cox said. 
The Utah Supreme Court inside the Scott M. Matheson Courthouse in Salt Lake City is pictured on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The governor described Menssen, who specializes in complex commercial and labor law, as “one of the finest civil litigators in our state” and praised his work with groups helping to expand legal aid for low-income Utahns.
Bell said the oath he’ll take if confirmed “means applying the law faithfully and objectively as it is written, not as we wish it to be.”
Menssen agreed.
“In determining what the law is, a judge must be open-minded and be guided by neutral, objective decision-making, not the judge’s own policy preferences,” he said.
Menssen received his law degree from the University of Virginia; Bell graduated from Brigham Young University. 
The Appellate Judicial Nominating Commission put forward a list of three women and nine men for Cox to consider. The list also included three Utah Court of Appeals judges.
Utah Senate confirms 2 new Utah Supreme Court justices despite concerns over one’s residency

The Utah Senate in June confirmed his earlier picks of justices Stephen Dent, a former prosecutor, and Jay Jorgensen, a prior attorney for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Cox also named Justice John Nielsen to replace former Associate Chief Justice John Pearce last year. 
The series of changes has meant the Utah Supreme Court is no longer a majority of women.  
Cox previously pushed back on criticism that not enough women were considered for the two expanded seats, filled earlier this summer, noting he’d appointed both Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman and Hagen. He said his focus was on finding the best legal minds for the job. 
On Friday, Cox recalled telling the new appointees that “I hope that they will rule against me and against the Legislature whenever they feel like that is necessary, that nothing in this process should make them feel beholden to me for appointing them, beholden to the Senate for confirming them. It is the exact opposite.”

name: WyoFile
title: National Elk Refuge plan calls for feeding Jackson Hole elk, even if CWD transmission skyrockets
description:
The proposal leans into hunting to reduce the population to 5,000, but it doesn’t require steps to end feeding, which wildlife disease experts predict is best for the elk population.
The post National Elk Refuge plan calls for feeding Jackson Hole elk, even if CWD transmission skyrockets appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A long-range plan for the National Elk Refuge released Friday afternoon proposes continuing to feed elk for the long haul in the Jackson Herd, even as deadly chronic wasting disease propagates across the landscape. 
Long-awaited, the refuge’s draft environmental impact statement includes a “proposed action” calling for a “range of strategies” to reduce the number of overwintering elk on the 24,700-acre U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service property to 5,000 animals over the next 10 years. That’s the same numeric goal listed in the 2007 plan the refuge is operating under currently — a goal the service has, thus far, been unable to achieve.
Strategies that the draft plan highlights include increasing and modifying hunting seasons, adjusting the feeding season start and end dates, and redistributing elk across the landscape — the last of which has proven to be a persistently difficult task. 
Additionally, the plan calls for using hunters to more effectively target “suburban” elk that only migrate short distances and spend summers on nearby ranchland and in subdivisions between Wilson and Grand Teton National Park. 
A multi-agency “Cooperative Elk Studies Group” will meet annually in June to determine if the strategies are working and if changes are needed, based on the “best available science.” 
There was anticipation that the National Elk Refuge’s plan would include rigid management designed to address the spread of chronic wasting disease, an always-lethal malady that showed up in Jackson Hole in 2020, was detected on the refuge for the first time this spring and again in July. 
More than 900 elk nibble at the hay on the sleigh within the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Black Butte Feedground in 2021. Infectious chronic wasting disease prions are spreading throughout the elk feeding region, including on to the National Elk Refuge. (Angus M. Thuermer, Jr./WyoFile)
Federal wildlife disease experts who’ve modeled CWD transmission on the refuge predict that feeding in the face of the disease will result in the worst-case scenario for elk populations and elk hunting for the Jackson Herd.
While the National Elk Refuge plan was in the works, federal scientists studied what, at the time, was described as the forthcoming proposed action. It called for feeding elk until rates of the ugly prion disease reach 7%, and feeding bison for the long haul. 
But those triggers were stripped out of the “proposed action,” Alternative D, included in the draft EIS. 
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik, who ultimately calls the shots at the refuge, is a former Wyoming Game and Fish Department director who in 2020 described elk feeding as a “wicked problem” that isn’t going away in the “short or mid-term.”
Feeding has occurred at the National Elk Refuge since 1912, and it’s intended to keep wapiti off of private land, prevent the spread of brucellosis to cattle and prop up populations to support hunting. But it’s also a disease-spreading practice that unnaturally concentrates animals, truncates migration routes and is seen by many experts as an antiquated way of managing wildlife. 
“Feeding only occurs in a handful of counties in northwest Wyoming,” former National Elk Refuge manager Brian Glaspell said in 2019. “Everybody else thinks it’s a bad idea, let’s just be honest about that.”
National Elk Refuge staff were not granted clearance to discuss the plans on Friday. A press release sent out by the Fish and Wildlife Service that afternoon came from an unnamed email account. WyoFile’s inquiry about an interview did not receive a response before this story was published. 
The public can comment on the updated plan and draft EIS until Oct. 13. 
A virtual meeting — join by clicking here — has been scheduled from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Sept. 15. An in-person meeting is also scheduled for 5 to 7 p.m. on Sept. 22. The location has not been announced.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers walk out during Wyoming Business Council reform talks
description:
Though two separate legislative committees each found agreement, some objected to mixing committee duties.
The post Lawmakers walk out during Wyoming Business Council reform talks appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
At least five lawmakers walked out of a rare combined hearing of two separate legislative committees this morning after convening to compare notes on overlapping bills aimed at reforming the Wyoming Business Council. 
The future of the state’s top economic development shop has stakes for how prepared Wyoming communities are to host economic development from Gillette to Kemmerer.
A handful of other committee members failed to attend entirely, but it was unclear whether their absences were in protest or for other reasons.
Ten Sleep Republican Sen. Ed Cooper, Cheyenne Republican Sen. Tara Nethercott and Casper Republican Sen. Jim Anderson, who all serve on the Joint Minerals, Business and Economic Development Committee, were among the first to walk out about 25 minutes into the meeting. Appropriations Committee members Jackson Democrat Sen. Mike Gierau soon followed and Riverton Republican Sen. Tim Salazar left shortly after.
Both committees had met separately on Thursday to advance a legislative effort to reform the Wyoming Business Council — along with other state-level economic development strategies — highlighting a long list of programs to trim or completely remove from the business council based on consultations with the agency itself and business leaders across the state.
Though both committees struck a mostly cooperative tone among themselves and their stakeholders during their separate meetings Thursday, several members expressed opposition to and frustration with combining the two panels on Friday.
The duplicative nature of working almost identical bills and then trying to hash out the differences outside of a legislative session was “out of order” and in violation of committee assignments, Nethercott said just before departing the joint hearing.
“We don’t come together and have joint meetings every time different committees have topics that intersect with each other,” she said. “This is an unusual course. It’s an unproductive course, and I do believe the taxpayers have a better use of their time, including that of their elected officials.”
How we got here
After years of both criticism and accolades for the business council, the Freedom Caucus-led Joint Appropriations Committee in January moved to defund and dismantle the agency just ahead of the Legislature’s budget session.
Lawmakers and stakeholders alike clashed over whether the agency is fulfilling its mission — defined by some 93 pages of state statutes accumulated over 25 years — and whether it was even necessary to help advance the state’s economy. Though the business council avoided complete elimination, legislators ultimately reduced its biennium budget from the governor’s recommended $54.6 million to about $15 million — enough to sustain the agency as lawmakers reexamine its role and contemplate potential reforms.
The reform effort began this past spring under direction from the Legislature’s Management Council, which assigned the Minerals Committee to examine the business council’s structure and guiding principles and instructed the Appropriations Committee to reimagine the agency’s budget matters, including its management of vast federal and state grant and loan programs.
Reform, so far
Both committees took up bill drafts earlier this week that overlap. 
The Minerals Committee on Thursday voted to sponsor a consensus block grant local funding program bill draft and the Wyoming business council-program amendments and repeal bill draft. The Joint Appropriations Committee, meantime, advanced almost identical measures, but did not vote on them because it will meet one more time in October before the full Legislature convenes this winter.
While the Appropriations Committee tailored its consensus block grant bill draft as a likely replacement for the business council’s controversial Business Ready Community grant program, the Minerals Committee generally regards it as complimentary to the Business Ready Community program. The primary difference between the two, according to lawmakers and business insiders, is that the Business Ready Program tends to advantage communities already in a position to attract new businesses, while the consensus block program addresses dire needs and roadblocks to attracting new businesses, like crumbling infrastructure.
Though not in total agreement, local-government officials and economic-development advocates across the state say both programs serve legitimate needs, and many expressed anxiety if pressed to choose between the two. While communities like Gillette, Cheyenne and Casper are good investments to attract new industries, towns with fewer resources like Rawlins and Kemmerer could do the same, but they struggle with basic infrastructure like roads, sewer and drinking water.
The Kemmerer post office and, in the background, the original JCPenney in downtown Kemmerer. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
While discussing the astronomical and continually rising costs of basic infrastructure needs, Wyoming Association of Municipalities Executive Director Ashley Harpstreith suggested that no matter the funding mechanism, the state is going to struggle to meet the need.
“The poster child that comes to mind is Kemmerer,” Harpstreith told the joint committees. “We’re looking at nuclear development there. We’re redeveloping old coal [facilities]. It’s pretty exciting stuff. But we kind of put the cart before the horse because we have a $60 million deficit in sewer there.”

title: Idaho Behavioral Health Council identifies at-risk areas for targeted spending of opioid funding
description: An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds.  The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve[...]
text:
An advisory group is recommending Idaho use its opioid settlement funds to focus on at-risk populations and communities. (Getty Images)An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. 
The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. 
The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. 
The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. 
Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding

The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. 
Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment.
“This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” 
The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What areas are at high risk for opioid use? 

Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said.
The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey, the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center.
The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. 
The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. 
Brooke Green represents Idaho’s Legislative District 18 in the House. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Legislature)
In general, people ages 26-49 are at the greatest risk of opioid misuse and overdose, the summary said. And men die from opioid overdose at a rate nearly 50% higher than women. 
The advisory group’s recommendations will go to legislators and the governor, and ultimately the Legislature will decide how to use the state’s settlement funds. 
“I really appreciate the visual that you guys put together,” Boise Democratic state Rep. Brooke Green said at the meeting Friday. “(It) really highlights some of our vulnerabilities throughout the state.”

title: Voting rights struggle continues, advocates say at March on Washington anniversary
text:
WASHINGTON — Just over two months from midterm elections and four months removed from a U.S. Supreme Court decision that gutted Voting Rights Act protections for majority Black U.S. House districts, and 63 years after Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech there, thousands gathered again at the Lincoln Memorial Friday.Organizers focused the anniversary march around a “Defend the Vote” message. The event, co-chaired by civil rights leader Rev. Al Sharpton and King Jr.’s son Martin Luther King III and daughter-in-law Arndrea Waters King, featured appearances from union leaders, interfaith organizers, people whose parents attended the iconic 1963 march.Elected leaders also spoke, including Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a possible 2028 presidential contender.Demonstrators who traveled from across the country with various organizations marched from the Lincoln Memorial to the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial following a four-hour program of speeches.From behind bullet proof glass, King Jr.’s granddaughter Yolanda Renee King, 18, told the crowd she never met her grandfather, or grandmother Coretta Scott King, but she is carrying their legacy forward.“Sixty-three years ago, my grandfather told America, ‘I have a dream.’ Today, I want my generation to say something back — ‘We hear you,’” she said. “We know the dream was never finished, and we know you were never asking us to simply remember you. You were asking us to continue, so we will. We will pick up the baton.Yolanda King highlighted Civil Rights Movement icons, including John Lewis, who later represented Georgia’s 5th Congressional District from 1987 until his death in 2020.“This is a marathon, run as a relay,” she said. “That means nobody is expected to run the whole race. My grandfather did it. My grandmother did it. John Lewis did it. Fannie Lou Hamer did it. … The countless people whose names we will never know did it. They ran their leg.”

 







Family of the late civil rights icon Martin Luther King Jr., from left to right, son Martin Luther King III, granddaughter Yolanda Renee King and daughter-in-law Arndrea Waters King, along with an American Sign Language interpreter, at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, commemorating the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

Lewis shared the stage with King Jr. speaking to roughly a quarter-million civil rights demonstrators at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963. Organizers also convened that demonstration to pressure President John F. Kennedy to develop robust civil rights legislation with Congress. At the time, Lewis was a leader with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.  King III said his ancestors “woke up with courage and faith to speak truth to power and get into the kind of good trouble that the late John Lewis talked about, that helped to open doors for the marginalized across the country, regardless of race, age, agenda.” Callais decisionSeveral speakers criticized the U.S. Supreme Court’s late April decision in Louisiana v. Callais that overhauled Section 2 of the 1965 Voting Rights Act that protected against diluting the voting power of minority citizens.“The fact that we still have to fight to maintain and renew voting rights in this country is beyond abysmal and a truly national disgrace,” King III said.Rep. Yvette Clark, D-N.Y., chair of the Congressional Black Caucus likened the ruling to “opening the door to a coordinated attack on the Black political power and fair representation across the South.”“Since the Callais decision came down, Republicans across the country have wasted no time in their zealous pursuit for unbridled power,” Clark told the crowd, highlighting mid-decade voter map redistricting efforts and a bill, titled the SAVE America Act, that is championed by President Donald Trump and would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.Marc Morial, president and CEO of the National Urban League, told the crowd, “It's time to send the SAVE (America) Act to the graveyard.”

 







Gary Roush, 73, of College Park, Maryland, carried a sign protesting a new rule issued by the U.S. Postal Service. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

Postal Service ruleGary Roush, 73, of College Park, Maryland, carried a sign protesting a new rule issued by the U.S. Postal Service mandating new requirements for mail-in ballot envelopes, which states say would pose serious challenges before November’s midterms. Additionally, the new USPS rule forbids the agency from delivering or collecting ballots from people who are not confirmed to be eligible voters on lists newly mandated from states by the federal government.A federal district judge on Thursday night issued a temporary restraining order on the rule after the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the administration to implement the policy. USPS appealed the order Friday.Roush, who was among the crowd at the “Defend the Vote” march, said he believes Trump has “made it crystal clear: He plans to use the post office to try to stop most mail-in ballots.”Roush’s sign featured a USPS promotional character from the 1960s used in ad campaigns to encourage people to write ZIP codes on the envelopes. A message on his sign read, “Trump plans to use us to rig the election.”“He's going to create as much havoc as possible,” said Roush, who added he’s “extremely worried” about the upcoming midterms.

 







Swani Keelson, of Baltimore dressed as the late voting and women's rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at the 63rd anniversary event of the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)

Building a movementSharpton’s National Action Network and the King family’s Drum Major Institute coordinated the day, along with nearly 100 partner organizations including sorority and fraternity chapters from historically black colleges and universities, and other national and local activist groups.Ocasio-Cortez, who has been on a speaking tour with Sanders ahead of the midterm elections, said, “Brothers and sisters, these drum majors for justice, just as you all and countless others today, were not handed a movement. They have always had to build one. “And when they came here 63 years ago, they came with demands,” she continued. “They demanded the right to vote, an end to segregation, and fair housing. They demanded a federal jobs program, a higher minimum wage, and an end to discrimination in employment… Freedom is both political and economic.”Organizers evoked numerous founders of the Civil Rights Movement, and other anniversaries since, including the 37th commemoration of the March on Washington in 2000 when Coretta Scott King, the late widow of the slain civil rights leader, urged attendees to continue her husband’s and other leaders’ missions.That anniversary march at the turn of the millenium, dubbed “Redeem the Dream,” was also co-organized by Sharpton and King III, and focused on ending racial profiling and police brutality following high-profile abuse cases in the previous decade in Los Angeles, New York City and Philadelphia.“My mother, Coretta Scott King, said that nonviolence is really the only credible response to the violence that we are seeing around the world. She was right about it both then and now,” King III told the crowd.Attendees in United Auto Workers t-shirts lined the seats at the foot of the memorial steps, another nod to the history of the movement.The UAW, including its then president Walter Reuther, was among the coalition of activists, labor unions and religious organizations that supported the landmark 1963 march. Other speakers and performers at the original march included folk singers Bob Dylan and Joan Baez, and Little Rock, Arkansas, civil rights activist Daisy Bates. King and other leaders met with Kennedy and Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson following the march to discuss bipartisanship around civil rights legislation, according to the Martin Luther King Jr., Research and Education Institute at Stanford University.Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in July 1964, less than a year after Kennedy was assassinated in November of 1963. Johnson subsequently signed the Voting Rights Act in August of 1965.

name: VTDigger
title: Urban trees are often planted just to die. Montpelier wants to change that.
description:
About 80% of Montpelier’s downtown trees are in decline thanks to poor site conditions and pests.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Urban trees are often planted just to die. Montpelier wants to change that..
text:
About 80 percent of the trees planted in downtown Montpelier are not faring well, facing urban challenges that don’t support their longterm health and growth. The city is taking steps to try to improve the longevity of its trees. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Montpelier residents have a particular attachment to some of the trees that line their streets. Each year, the fall colors of the century-old Barre Street ginkgo tree elicit social media posts and calls to come admire the foliage. 
But according to Alec Ellsworth, the city’s tree warden, Montpelier’s trees are not faring well. About 80% of the 50 trees downtown are in decline. Ten are actively dying, and 12 are at “high risk” due to the emerald ash borer, a pervasive pest targeting ash trees. 
It’s not just Montpelier facing this problem. Ellsworth said it’s part of an all-too-common pattern of cities planting trees in ways that don’t allow them to grow and thrive. 
“Trees are just plunked in a little four-by-four tree well … and then, let’s say eight years later, the tree has died, and you replant it, and then five, eight years later it dies again,” he said. 
“But maybe by that point the person in charge of the trees has moved on, and so there’s no institutional knowledge, so they think, ‘Oh, something must have gone wrong.’ So they replant it again and again, and so this cycle just repeats itself, where it’s just a giant waste of time and money,” he said. 
Montpelier is trying a new approach, the Stockholm planting method, that’s becoming more common around the world, as urban arborists look to improve the longevity of trees and respond to increasingly common stressors like heat, pollution and pests. 
“There’s definitely a big national movement in urban forestry to do more thoughtful planting processes,” Ellsworth said. 
The method involves creating a “structural soil” that includes rocks and biochar, according to the Stockholm Tree Pits website. It is meant to provide more water, air exchange and space for roots to grow, allowing trees to stay healthier and reach their full potential as shade providers. 
Urban planners of decades past were able to plant trees in small spaces, in part because two particular tree groups — ashes and elms — were able to thrive in those conditions. But Dutch elm disease almost completely wiped out urban elm trees in North America, and the emerald ash borer has threatened to do the same for ash trees.  
Along with pests, urban trees have seen rising threats from climate change, construction damage and road salt. “There’s not as much variety of trees that can handle the semi-punishing environment of a downtown urban landscape,” Ellsworth said. 
Ellsworth said that better planting methods can also save money for cities in the long run. Montpelier spends an average of $10,000 to plant a single tree, which he said was on the cheaper side because they do so much work in-house. 
“If you buy a tree at Gardener’s Supply, it’s going to be $600 or something, and then you pay somebody $500 to put it in,” he said. “You can get a tree in the ground and it might live five, even 10 years, but it will never grow big, and then you just repeat the cycle. So, is it cheaper just to plant a tree for $1,000 that’s gonna live for only 10 years?” 
He gave the example of a tree he recently removed from its location outside of Capitol Grounds on State Street. The tree was roughly 25 to 30 years old, but it had barely grown since the day it was planted in 2002. 
“Your businesses, your pedestrians, your visitors, people want to see big, beautiful shade trees,” he said.  
Shade trees can provide direct cooling to sidewalks, roads and store fronts, making downtown areas more comfortable to be in. Ellsworth has gone around the city with a heat gun and seen the drop in temperature of more than 10 degrees between the sidewalk in the summer sun and a bench sitting in the shade. 
Montpelier is also partnering with the University of Vermont to study nine tree wells planted using the Stockholm method to see if they help filter or collect stormwater. If the study is successful, tree wells could be added to the state’s guidance on stormwater treatment practices, Ellsworth said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: The debate over the debate, and Magruder steps down from green bank, in political notes
description: A gubernatorial debate between GOP nominee Dan Cox and Gov. Wes Moore (D) sparks more debate, about how many debates there should be and who should be included, and "green bank" director Kathy Magruder steps down, in political notes.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox, right, and Gov. Wes Moore (D) will share a stage for their only debate of the election on Oct. 6 on Maryland Public Television. (Photos by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) and two-time Republican nominee Dan Cox (R) are set to square off during a televised debate about a month before Election Day.
In a news release Wednesday, Moore’s campaign spokesman Carter Elliott said the campaign is “glad” that Cox accepted “our challenge to debate Governor Moore this fall on Maryland Public Television.” Marylanders will see firsthand the MAGA agenda Dan Cox threatens to bring to Maryland, and a reminder of why they overwhelmingly rejected him four years ago,” Elliott wrote.
But Moore’s opponents aren’t satisfied with the debate, which is scheduled for Oct. 6 on Maryland Public Television.
Cox didn’t just accept the MPT invitation, he urged Moore to schedule two additional debates, suggesting Maryland universities as potential hosts.
Green Party of Maryland gubernatorial nominee Andy Ellis. (Photo courtesy Andy Ellis)
“What is he afraid of? Let’s let the people hear from both candidates,” Cox said in the news release.
Cox isn’t the only one. Green Party candidate Andy Ellis has called for a four-candidate debate focusing specifically on data centers, already a central issue this campaign season.
Ellis took issue with a candidates’ forum hosted by the Maryland Association of Counties earlier this month. It only featured Moore and Cox — who were never on the stage at the same time — not Ellis or Working Class Party candidate Cathy White, who will also appear on the ballot in heavily Democratic Maryland on Election Day.
“If Dan Cox thinks data centers are a key part of his campaign, and Wes Moore thinks they are key to Maryland’s future, then they should show up on a stage with all four candidates for governor and have an in-depth debate about this,” Ellis said. “We can do it in Adamstown, or Lusby, or Landover, or Newburg. We should have an audience and questions informed by the communities’ concerns.”
Magruder retiring after 17 years at green bank
When Kathy Magruder took the helm of Maryland’s new statewide green bank in 2009, it was an organization with “a broad mission” — and an “itty bitty little budget,” she says.
During Magruder’s tenure, the Maryland Clean Energy Center has grown tremendously. During the 2025 fiscal year alone, it earned more than $35 million in federal and state grants for renewable energy projects.
And now, Magruder is calling it a career.
She told the organization’s board back in May that she would be stepping down, though she plans to stay on while the center searches for a new executive director. Magruder said she expects to leave MCEC by the end of the fiscal year in June 2027.
Katherine Magruder, executive director of the Maryland Clean Energy Center.  (Courtesy photo)
Magruder said her proudest accomplishments include helping to establish numerous dedicated funding streams for the green bank to help grow clean energy businesses in Maryland.
“The state has always had a very clear vision for the environment, and the desire to protect the environment, but less of a strategy for how to finance the desired outcomes,” Magruder said in an interview.
That list of funding streams includes the Climate Catalytic Capital Fund, established in 2022 with the passage of major climate legislation in Maryland, which committed over $41 million to the center for green energy initiatives.
“That was a lift of government. But now that those things are in place, the boat should be able to sail on,” Magruder said.
The center has also received numerous federal grants, but some were lost amid pullbacks by President Donald Trump’s administration, including $62 million from the Environmental Protection Agency’s “Solar for All Program,” and millions in funding for electric vehicle chargers. Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown has filed or joined suits challenging the federal decisions.
Magruder said receiving the grants was “a proud moment, and it was just as devastating to have those funds pulled back by the Trump administration.”
Her retirement announcement earned words of praise from Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Senate’s Education, Energy and the Environment committee.
“Kathy has the unique expertise to blend technical policy with economic solutions. Her work has earned her bipartisan respect from my colleagues in Annapolis,” Feldman wrote. “Kathy’s legacy will serve Marylanders for decades to come.”
