name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas librarian fired after opposing book ban efforts to receive $275K in settlement
description: A central Arkansas county agreed this week to pay $275,000 to the former library director who was fired after speaking against local conservatives’ push to limit children’s access to books. Saline County announced Thursday it had reached a settlement with Patty Hector, who had been the county library’s executive director when she was fired in […]
text:
Patty Hector, director of the Saline County Library, listens during public comment on a resolution that would restrict children's access to books that contain "sexual content or imagery" at a Monday, April 17, 2023, meeting of the county Quorum Court. The court adopted the resolution. At left is Leigh Espey, library manager. Hector was fired Monday, Oct. 9, 2023, and Espey appointed as interim library director. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)A central Arkansas county agreed this week to pay $275,000 to the former library director who was fired after speaking against local conservatives’ push to limit children’s access to books.
Saline County announced Thursday it had reached a settlement with Patty Hector, who had been the county library’s executive director when she was fired in October 2023. County Judge Matt Brumley’s firing power came from an ordinance approved by the all-Republican quorum court, which previously urged Hector to move books with “sexual content or imagery” out of children’s reach.
Hector alleged in her 2025 legal complaint that her firing was retaliatory and violated her First Amendment right to free speech. The case was set to go to trial next week before Monday’s settlement hearing. U.S. District Judge James Moody signed off on the settlement Wednesday.
Hector said she hoped the settlement would send a message to librarians and other public servants that their constitutional rights matter.
“Standing up for the freedom to read cost me a job and a career I loved, but I never believed that staying silent was the answer,” Hector said in a news release from the American Civil Liberties Union of Arkansas, which represented her in the litigation. “Libraries belong to everyone, and librarians should be able to serve their communities according to professional standards without fearing political retaliation.”

Saline County judge: Library director’s statements cause “high degree of concern”

 

Brumley, a Republican, said in a statement that he disagreed with Hector’s allegations and was prepared to go to trial, but “ultimately determined the responsible decision is to resolve this matter rather than spend years in a costly legal battle at the expense of the taxpayers.” 
The county will pay $225,000 in damages and $50,000 in legal fees from the Association of Arkansas Counties Risk Management Fund.
A few months before firing Hector, Brumley told her and the county library board that he had a “high degree of concern” about her statement to the quorum court that “there is nothing wrong with” the books some citizens wanted out of children’s reach.
The books in question pertained to LGBTQ+ topics, sex education and systemic racism, which Saline County conservatives called “indoctrination” and inappropriate for children. Others said that such books reflect the community and that trying to restrict access to it is censorship.
 Uncertainty over library law remains

The settlement comes as librarians have raised questions about how to enforce a state law that would impose criminal penalties for distributing content considered “harmful to minors.”
A federal appeals court in July said the 2023 law could take effect, overturning a lower court ruling blocking its enforcement.
John Adams, lead attorney for the 18 plaintiffs that challenged the law, told the Central Arkansas Library System’s governing board Thursday that he plans to ask the appeals court for clarification on compliance. CALS and its executive director, Nate Coulter, are among the plaintiffs.
Without clarification, librarians are unlikely to know what the law does and doesn’t allow “until someone actually gets charged and prosecuted,” Coulter said. Violating the law is a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by a maximum prison sentence of one year.

Central Arkansas Library System Executive Director Nate Coulter (standing) addresses CALS board members and administrators at the board’s monthly meeting on Aug. 27, 2026. From left are board President Karama Neal of Little Rock, system collection development manager Leslie Blanchard, and board member Alexis Sims of Maumelle. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Loni Bean, a bilingual specialist at the Dee Brown Library in southwest Little Rock, told the CALS board that supporters of Act 372 could “make an example of” an employee of the state’s largest library system.
Bean urged the board to pass a policy at next month’s meeting affirming that CALS leadership will provide legal representation and job security for any employee who faces legal challenges “arising from actions taken in good faith in the course of their job duties and in accordance with library policies.”
Coulter said he supported putting such a policy in place for his to-be-chosen successor, since he plans to retire at the end of October.
 Potential library funding cuts

Hector’s lawsuit is part of a larger fight over library restrictions playing out in Arkansas and other Republican-led states. 
The Arkansas Department of Education is considering new rules that hinge public libraries’ funding on ensuring patrons age 16 or younger cannot check out materials that depict or describe sexual contact and behavior.
The department is taking public comment on a revised draft of the rules until Sept. 13. Dozens of Arkansans expressed opposition to a previous version.
An Arkansas county’s voters will decide whether to slash library funding by $1.4M

Saline County voters will also decide in November whether to cut about one-third of the county libraries’ operating budget.
“Any librarian who opposes this cut should feel free, like Patty [Hector], to speak out against it in their personal capacity,” said John Williams, legal director of the ACLU of Arkansas and Hector’s attorney in her lawsuit.
Williams promised that the ACLU “will defend any librarian whom Saline County tries to punish” for speaking against the proposal, which the quorum court put on the ballot in May by passing an ordinance.
Two years ago, Brumley rejected a similar citizen-led effort on technicalities.
Craighead County voters cut local library funding in half in 2022. Supporters of the cut included vocal opponents of the Jonesboro library’s LGBTQ+ Pride display in 2021.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee campaign slams new poll saying he’s down 38 points days after another survey found gap closing
description: Has Gov. Dan McKee closed the gap with his Democratic primary opponent, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, as a WPRI-TV 12 poll published Tuesday indicates? Or, is the incumbent trailing by an even more significant margin while Foulkes picks up support from previously undecided voters? The latter is the finding of a University of New Hampshire poll […]
text:
Gov. Dan McKee arrives at WPRO in East Providence for a gubernatorial debate on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current) Has Gov. Dan McKee closed the gap with his Democratic primary opponent, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, as a WPRI-TV 12 poll published Tuesday indicates? Or, is the incumbent trailing by an even more significant margin while Foulkes picks up support from previously undecided voters?
The latter is the finding of a University of New Hampshire poll published Thursday. 
The online survey of 851 voters — including 446 likely Democratic primary voters — conducted Aug. 20 to Aug. 24 shows Foulkes leading McKee by 38 points, with a 4.6% margin of error. It’s the widest gap between the gubernatorial rivals of any poll to date, including prior iterations of the same UNH survey. 
When the same survey was last conducted in June, Foulkes led McKee by 20 points, with nearly 1 in 3 likely primary voters undecided. The new survey shows fewer voters have not made up their minds (23%) while more than half back Foulkes. Fewer than 1 in 5 support McKee.
The WPRI poll showed a 15-point gap between the two candidates.
Gov. Dan McKee trails Democratic primary challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes by 38 points, according to an August survey by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. (Courtesy of University of New Hampshire Survey Center)
McKee’s campaign dismissed the poll as “bogus.”
“UNH has been an unreliable pollster across New England for years, and this is not an accurate reflection of the current state of the race,” Sophie Mestas, a campaign spokesperson said. “Governor McKee will close this campaign on a message of fighting for working families and delivering the results Rhode Islanders need and deserve — and that’s a message that wins.”
Andrew Smith, director of the UNH Survey Center, defended the poll’s methodology, which relies on the same probability model used by other leading scientific survey groups like Gallup and Pew Research Center. 
But Smith acknowledged the difficulty of accurately projecting results in primary races due to low turnout and last-minute decisions by undecided voters.
Primaries are a different animal,” Smith said. “You tend to get a lot of people saying they’re going to vote and they don’t.”
Smith also pointed to McKee’s consistently low approval rating, including among Democrats, as further evidence of his lackluster support in the primary race.
“He’s kind of burned his bridges with the Democratic base there,” Smith said. “That, to me, is the real problem.”
Foulkes’ campaign took the results as further evidence of her traction with voters. 
“Poll after poll shows Rhode Islanders are ready for change,” Angelika Pellegrino, a campaign spokesperson said. With early voting underway, the momentum in this race is with Helena.”
Foulkes trumped McKee in nearly every demographic category of primary voters, including every age bracket, geographic area, party affiliation and education level. Her support was highest among self-described progressive voters, men, and voters ages 18 to 34. McKee’s support came from self-identified conservative and libertarian voters, those 50 to 64 years old, and voters who supported Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Already dogged by low approval ratings, McKee’s favorability worsened compared with the June survey. Eight in 10 voters surveyed disapprove of his job performance, including more than 7 in 10 Democrats. Infrastructure, specifically roads and bridges, was the top source of voter frustration with McKee, a recurrent theme in the wake of the late 2024 closure of the westbound Washington Bridge.
Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes bested Gov. Dan McKee in nearly every demographic category in the new UNH poll. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)
Foulkes, who has frequently criticized the governor for his handling of the rebuild process, has gained favorability compared with two months ago. More than one-third of primary voters view her favorably, 8 points higher than the share of voters who view her unfavorably. And more survey participants know who she is — unsurprising given TV ads by the campaigns and three live debates since the survey was taken in June.
Despite their frequent headbutting on policy and professional track records, the primary rivals share one thing in common: both candidates’ supporters say the No. 1 reason to vote for them is that they are better than the other. Roughly 3 in 10 voters back McKee as the better of the two, with nearly as many Foulkes’ supporters naming the same reason for their support.
However, another 28% of Foulkes voters say she “represents change,” while 20% are won over by her competence or qualifications. Just over 10% of McKee voters cite his qualifications or policies, respectively, as reasons for their support.
On issues, housing topped the list of concerns for survey respondents, named by 1 in 5 participants across the political spectrum. Cost of living was also a top priority, followed by jobs and the economy. 
The poll also asked participants about the controversial three-year charter school moratorium signed into law by McKee in June. More than one-third of respondents overall support the new law, rising to 50% among registered Democrats. But nearly as many Republicans and independents oppose the ban on new charter schools.
Similar ideological divides characterize attitudes toward the state’s property on high-value second homes, known as the “Taylor Swift tax.” The surtax, approved by lawmakers in the fiscal 2026 budget with a July 1, 2026, start date, was backed by 8 in 10 Democrats, while 6 in 10 Republicans opposed the higher tax. Independent voters were nearly equally split, though slightly more opposed the tax hike.
The margin of error for questions open to all voters, regardless of party affiliation, is 3.4%.

name: WyoFile
title: After abrupt move to governor’s office, former Wyoming Game and Fish boss moves on to private lands nonprofit
description:
Angi Bruce will start in late September as chief programs and policy officer for the Denver-based Western Landowners Alliance, the organization has announced. 
The post After abrupt move to governor’s office, former Wyoming Game and Fish boss moves on to private lands nonprofit appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Angi Bruce’s stint working in a newly created policy job with Gov. Mark Gordon’s team is shaping up to last only a matter of weeks.
The former Wyoming Game and Fish Department director abruptly resigned Aug. 7 and “effective immediately” took a job with the governor’s office as the newly created director of special policy initiatives. Her departure from the state wildlife agency followed a controversial two-year tenure. There are indications the resignation was involuntary: When she left, Bruce had a calendar filled with upcoming Game and Fish duties, and she took a significant pay cut, according to public records acquired by WyoFile.
Now, Bruce is on the professional move again. On Thursday, Western Landowners Alliance announced that the nonprofit had hired the Game and Fish’s first-ever female director as its chief programs and policy officer, and that she starts in late September. 
“I have had the opportunity to collaborate with Angi over the past decade,” Western Landowners Alliance CEO Lesli Allison said in a statement. “She is a big-picture thinker who also understands the politics and practical realities of getting things done on the ground.”
Bruce will oversee the alliance’s work on sustaining working lands, connected landscapes and native species in the new role. In a statement, she said her new employer is giving her the opportunity to combine her “two loves,” which are “landowners and wildlife.” 
“Growing up on a farm, I learned early on the land ethic of landowners and how valuable their contributions are to maintaining healthy wildlife populations and connected landscapes,” Bruce said.
Western Landowners Alliance, which lists a Denver address and was formed in the early 2010s, has a mission statement that seeks to advance policies and practices that “sustain working lands, connected landscapes and native species.” 
“WLA provides a collective voice, a peer network and a shared knowledge base for landowners striving to keep the land whole and healthy,” the organization’s website states. 
Well-known Wyoming resident Bob Budd, who directs the Wyoming Wildlife and Natural Resource Trust, sits on the group’s board.  
WyoFile reached out to Allison and Bruce for this story, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: A second Des Moines priest sues Homeland Security over work authorization
description: A second Roman Catholic priest from the Diocese of Des Moines has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over alleged delays in work authorization permits. Father Nipin Thakidipurathu Scaria, a citizen of India who now resides in Des Moines, is suing Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration [[...]
text:
Father Nipin "Nivin" Thakidipurathu Scaria, the rector at St. Ambrose Cathedral in Des Moines, has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over alleged delays in work authorization permits. (Photo by Kathie Obradovich/Iowa Capital Dispatch)A second Roman Catholic priest from the Diocese of Des Moines has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over alleged delays in work authorization permits.
Father Nipin Thakidipurathu Scaria, a citizen of India who now resides in Des Moines, is suing Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Director Joseph Edlow, and Thomas Schuurmans, the director of CIS’s Nebraska Service Center, in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
According to the lawsuit, Scaria — known to parishioners as “Father Nivin,” was admitted to the United States several years ago on an R-1 visa, which is a temporary visa for foreign nationals entering the country to work in a religious capacity.
According to court records, Scaria’s employment authorization to work in the United States was initially set to expire on March 30, 2025, but in October 2024, he received notice of an automatic 540-day extension — meaning his authorization would expire on Sept. 21, 2026, unless U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services first acted on his application for a work permit.
Since then, no action has been taken, the lawsuit asserts.
“If Father Nivin loses work authorization, he will be unable to perform his religious duties to his parish as a priest of the Roman Catholic Church,” the lawsuit states. “If Father Nivin loses work authorization, he will be required to stop work at the Roman Catholic Diocese of Des Moines in his position as rector of St. Ambrose Cathedral in Des Moines. This abrupt halt to his work authorization will interfere with religious services for the diocese.”
Federal law suggests the processing of such an application should be completed no later than 180 days after the initial filing of the application.
“Clearly, Congress did not contemplate an adjudication time of over a year,” the lawsuit states. “There is no reasonable justification for these delays and inactions… It is unreasonable for (Scaria) to abruptly stop his work for the Catholic Church and this impairs the free exercise of religion for the church (and its) parishioners.”
The lawsuit asks the court to assume jurisdiction over the matter, set the matter for an expedited hearing, and order U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to process his application.
The U.S. Department of Justice has yet to file a response to the lawsuit on behalf of the defendants.
Other priest’s lawsuit is dropped
In July, a priest from Nigeria, Father Sylvester Okoh, filed a similar lawsuit against the same defendants.
According to that lawsuit, Okoh was initially admitted to the United States on an R-1 visa. In November 2022, with his previously granted employment authorization set to expire on January 25, 2025, Okoh allegedly filed an application to adjust his residency status. In September 2024, CIS issued a notice indicating Okoh’s work authorization would be automatically extended 540 days to July 19, 2026.
With that expiration date only three days away, Okoh sued, citing the threat to his religious duties as a priest in the Roman Catholic Diocese of Des Moines.
That lawsuit contended that CIS had delayed action on Okoh’s application based on the agency’s December 2025 policy memoranda placing an indefinite hold on pending benefit applications from nationals of Nigeria and 38 other countries the Trump administration designated as “high risk.”
Earlier this week, Okoh’s attorney dismissed the lawsuit, informing the court that the defendants, without ever responding to the lawsuit itself, had processed Okoh’s application.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG sues feds for records related to drug agents’ fentanyl tactics in the state
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Thursday filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Justice seeking records related to allegations that Drug Enforcement Administration agents knowingly let fentanyl flow into the state.
text:
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez announced on Aug. 27, 2026 was suing the U.S. Department of Justice for records related to allegations that federal drug enforcement agents knowingly let fentanyl flow into New Mexico. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Thursday filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Justice seeking records related to allegations that Drug Enforcement Administration agents knowingly let fentanyl flow into the state.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Federal whistleblowers in June detailed how agents would employ the controversial tactic known as “fentanyl walking” to monitor drug shipments — without seizing them — in hopes of catching higher-up traffickers in criminal operations. Torrez subsequently opened a “thorough and aggressive investigation” into the allegations and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said she wanted the state to pursue civil damages from the federal government.
Torrez in July announced he was seeking federal records such as DEA policies, communications between agents and prosecutors and whistleblower complaints. In August, he said the agency had wrongfully denied his request.
On Thursday, he said in a statement that the federal government failed to provide the records or respond when he responded to their denial and produced additional information.
“Fentanyl is devastating families across New Mexico, and we deserve to know the truth about the DEA’s practice of allowing that poison to flow into our communities,” Torrez said. “Rather than come clean with the public, the U.S. Department of Justice is once again stonewalling our efforts to get to the bottom of this unconscionable practice, to determine who is responsible for endangering our families and to hold those responsible to account.”
New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham calls for restitution amid allegations that feds let fentanyl into NM

The U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While overdose deaths have decreased nationally, they’ve increased in New Mexico. State leaders have spent nearly $844 million in recent years to rebuild the state’s behavioral health system, often prioritizing programs that address addiction and overdoses.
Torrez’s lawsuit argues that the government’s denial of his records request unlawfully interferes with his ability to investigate potential violations of state law. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court, asks a judge to order the federal government to turn over the records or reconsider its denial.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Community gathers in Minneapolis to remember Annunciation victims a year after shooting
description: Dozens gathered at Pearl Park in in Minneapolis on Thursday to drop off food, plant trees and assemble care packages for homeless youth in memory of the children and families scarred by the deadly mass shooting at the Church of Annunciation one year ago. The public remembrance took place a mile from Annunciation Catholic Church […]
text:
A memorial grows in front of Annunciation Church Wednesday, Sept. 3, 2025, days after a mass shooting left two children dead and more than two dozen others injured. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Dozens gathered at Pearl Park in in Minneapolis on Thursday to drop off food, plant trees and assemble care packages for homeless youth in memory of the children and families scarred by the deadly mass shooting at the Church of Annunciation one year ago.
The public remembrance took place a mile from Annunciation Catholic Church and School in the southwest part of the city. The Annunciation community attended a private service in the church, which rang its bells at 8:26 a.m. — to mark the moment the attack started — to honor 8-year-old Fletcher Merkel and 10-year-old Harper Moyski, who were killed in the shooting.
The shooting wounded 29 other people, and the shooter died by suicide at the scene.
Christine Anderson, whose two grandchildren were at Annunciation the day of the attack, said she spent all Thursday morning at Annunciation helping students decorate cookies for first responders before she went to the public remembrance to join others in healing.
“We have a hopeful path into the future,” Anderson, 73, said. “We are all in this together, and the connectedness I’ve felt with this community has been important to me.”
Fletcher Merkel (left) and Harper Moyski were killed in the shooting at Annunciation Church in Minneapolis on Aug. 27, 2025. (Photos provided by the families)
Angela Anschel, 45, and her daughter Coraline, 6, joined volunteers in breaking up soil near the park to plant trees.
“Something that comes out of devastating events is, it brings people together,” said Anschel, who lives less than a mile from Annunciation. “It starts a conversation. It has allowed us to talk about really hard things in community.”
The mass shooting rocked the community and the state of Minnesota, driving some Annunciation parents whose children were injured to publicly advocate for better school safety measures and for stringent gun control laws.
Hours after the shooting, Minnesota Democrats and families of Annunciation victims began to publicly call for a ban on assault-style weapons and other gun control measures. Gov. Tim Walz said he would call a special session to pass gun control measures, but Republicans and some Democrats resisted, and Walz backed down.
During the regular legislative session earlier this year, Democrats renewed their gun control campaign. The Minnesota House is tied between Republicans and Democrats, and House Speaker Lisa Demuth — who is also the Republican nominee for governor — used legislative procedure to block the legislation. The parents of one of the slain Annunciation students accused Demuth of breaking a promise to allow a gun control vote on the House floor.
Some Annunciation parents have pledged to continue pushing for stricter gun control measures at the next legislative session. Additional gun control bills, like an assault weapons ban, are unlikely to pass unless Democrats win majorities in the Minnesota House and Senate and win the governorship in November.
“I didn’t feel like we got far enough” on gun policy change, said Anschel, whose three young kids don’t attend Annunciation but who is close to several families directly impacted.
In a break between digging into soil, Anschel said that, for her, being “in action is always better versus sitting making calls” — though she’s also made calls to the Legislature.
J.J. Pelkey, an incoming kindergartner at Annunciation Catholic School, breaks up soil to plant trees near Minneapolis’ Pearl Park at a remembrance event on the anniversary of the Annunciation Church shooting, Thursday Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)
Retired educator Katie Johnson, 75, attended the remembrance because she said it was so painful to see young people hurt after working with students for decades.
“We wanted to honor everyone involved and everyone who will continue to suffer this trauma for the rest of their lives,” Johnson said.
Elected officials were also in attendance, including state Rep. Emma Greenman, Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey and Minneapolis City Council Member Jamison Whiting.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi State student ‘shell-shocked’ after being detained for an alleged threat
description: Mississippi State University in Starkville, Miss., on Monday, Aug. 18, 2025.
text:
Mississippi State University campus police detained a student Wednesday after an employee reported that he had threatened to blow up the financial aid office, an allegation the student and his attorney deny. 
Zayden Leonard, 21, a junior majoring in biological sciences, was trying to resolve an issue with his financial aid. 
He went to the university’s financial aid office to get his questions answered in person, and while waiting for help, six campus police officers approached him, handcuffed him and took him into custody, said civil rights attorney Harry Daniels, who is representing Leonard.  
Campus police detained Leonard for less than an hour, and officers later told him an employee in the financial aid office had reported that he threatened to blow up the office, Daniels said. If true, conviction for that crime could result in up to 10 years in federal prison. 
Leonard was not charged, university spokesman Sid Salter said in an email. 
The university has a responsibility to maintain a safe environment for students, faculty, staff and visitors, Salter said. When concerns are reported involving potential threats to campus personnel or operations, the university follows safety and reporting procedures, he said. 
“The university cooperates with appropriate law enforcement authorities while also ensuring that students have access to applicable university resources and support services,” Salter said. 
Daniels said the incident was dangerous and unjustified. 
“People who weaponize law enforcement to show power should be held accountable for their actions,” Daniels said. “The situation could have ended up deadly.” 
Daniels said Leonard and his family are “shell-shocked” and considering legal action. 
MSU declined to provide additional details, citing ongoing legal and student disciplinary processes. Salter reiterated that Leonard has not been charged. Campus law enforcement said it is directing questions about the incident and investigation to the university’s communications department.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: When ‘Ethical AI’ becomes part of the CCSU brand
description: How can a public university promise that students will use AI “responsibly and ethically” while tying its future to Big Tech and military contractors?
text:
What does it mean for a public university to promise that students will use AI “responsibly and ethically” while tying its future to Big Tech, military contractors, and the security and carceral state? 
That contradiction sits at the center of Central Connecticut State University’s proposal to remake itself as a polytechnic research university.

Timothy Scott 

CCSU says this transformation will remain grounded in humanistic values. Its materials describe graduates as “ethical analysts” and assign the liberal arts and social sciences a role in connecting technology to ethics, policy, and community partnership. This sounds reassuring, but CCSU never explains what ethics requires of the university itself —even as it builds ties to ethically fraught industries.
CCSU presents responsible AI as a student skill: understand its limits, evaluate its output, and avoid misuse. But this responsibility begins only after harmful technologies have been developed, sold, and embedded in education, work, public services, and state authority. It evades larger questions: what these systems collect, whose interests they serve, who profits, and whether they should exist at all.
This framework pushes responsibility downward. Students are held accountable under vague and inconsistent rules, while CCSU selects vendors and pursues partnerships with corporations that further entrench AI —including surveillance technologies—across public institutions, law enforcement, and the security state. Ethics becomes a burden imposed on users rather than a restraint on institutional power.
University-approved technology can still cause harm. More accurate biometrics can expand warrantless surveillance and persecution. Transparent predictive software can still sort people by alleged risk. Sometimes the ethical problem is not misuse. It is the intended use.
That matters because CCSU is building its vision around AI, cybersecurity, Industry 4.0, applied research, and corporate partnerships. Its plans promote corporate-sponsored research, workforce pipelines into “priority sectors,” the possible co-location of companies within the Central Applied Learning and Industry Corridor, and CCSU’s National Security Agency-validated cyber programs.
Terms such as “aerospace” and “advanced manufacturing” conceal the political character of this alignment. CCSU’s strategy includes Pratt & Whitney, Sikorsky, and Electric Boat —subsidiaries of RTX, Lockheed Martin, and General Dynamics. These companies are pillars of U.S. militarism and prominent participants in CCSU’s workforce strategy. Pratt & Whitney maintains engines for Israel’s F-15I and F-16I fleets, while Sikorsky has supplied Israel with CH-53 military helicopters and is building their replacements. Their parent corporations have supplied Israel with weapons and military systems during what leading human-rights organizations have identified as its ongoing genocide in Gaza.
Calling these relationships “workforce development” does not erase their function. The fields and technologies CCSU is expanding are integral to war profiteering, mass surveillance, and border militarization. Yet CCSU has not said what projects it would reject regardless of profit or political connections, how it would review dual-use research, or whether faculty and students could decline military work. “Ethical AI” makes this alignment appear socially responsible before meaningful boundaries exist.
Big Tech is already embedded in the project through NVIDIA hardware, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Copilot, GitHub, and an autonomous drone. CCSU also plans research with multinational corporations and government agencies. These companies control much of the AI infrastructure, and several hold military, intelligence, policing, and immigration-enforcement contracts. Their systems turn human thought, expression, behavior, movement, and relationships into raw material for profit and institutional control.
ICE uses cloud databases, facial recognition, location tracking, social-media monitoring, and AI-assisted analysis to identify, detain, and deport people. These systems extend racist immigration enforcement into the digital sphere, drawing people’s homes, workplaces, movements, and relationships into a deportation dragnet. CCSU’s strategy helps feed this apparatus by constructing a publicly subsidized pipeline for an AI economy centered on automation, data extraction, and predictive control. Yet CCSU confines ethics largely to bias, privacy, and appropriate use. A public university cannot credibly claim to govern AI while relying on platforms it cannot inspect or control.
The environmental and labor costs remain ignored. Generative AI depends on energy- and water-hungry data centers, mining, semiconductor production, and rapid hardware replacement. It also relies on exploited workers who label data, moderate disturbing content, manufacture equipment, and maintain data centers. Once deployed, AI can diminish professional autonomy, eliminate entry-level jobs, and leave fewer employees overseeing more automation.
CCSU celebrates servers, robot dogs, and autonomous drones without binding standards for energy use, sourcing, labor conditions, or disposal. It is not simply preparing students for the future but helping construct one shaped by automation, monitoring, and corporate control.
Weak shared governance reinforces the danger. Forums, surveys, and appointed task forces do not replace access to contracts, faculty deliberation, and a formal vote. CCSU holds students responsible under unclear rules while declining to impose binding limits on its own purchases and partnerships. It has not established independent partnership review, identified applications it will reject, or guaranteed faculty authority over technology adoption.
Its “ethical and responsible AI” is therefore not merely vague but duplicitous: moral restraint in words; corporate dependence, mass surveillance, racist policing, military alignment, environmental harm, and labor exploitation in practice. Until CCSU accepts enforceable limits, public accountability, and real shared governance, “ethical AI” is not a safeguard. It is moral cover for the polytechnic brand.
Timothy Scott is an Associate Professor of Social Work at Central Connecticut State University, a tech industry researcher, and the author of the book, Schooling for Silicon Valley.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa likely voters closely split on income tax constitutional amendment, poll finds
description: Likely Iowa voters do not have a clear preference on a proposed constitutional amendment requiring two-thirds of state lawmakers to approve income tax increases, according to a new Suffolk University poll. The Suffolk University Political Research Center poll, released Wednesday, found roughly 33% of likely Iowa voters planned to vote “yes” on Amendment 1, w[...]
text:
The golden dome of the Iowa State Capitol in Des Moines. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Likely Iowa voters do not have a clear preference on a proposed constitutional amendment requiring two-thirds of state lawmakers to approve income tax increases, according to a new Suffolk University poll.
The Suffolk University Political Research Center poll, released Wednesday, found roughly 33% of likely Iowa voters planned to vote “yes” on Amendment 1, while 36% planned to vote against the amendment. An additional 30% said they were still undecided, while 1% refused to answer the question.
The poll, conducted by the Suffolk University Political Research Center, largely focused on the Iowa gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races. But the poll also asked likely voters about other subjects, including their top priorities for Iowa’s K-12 education system and agricultural economy and the constitutional amendment.
The proposed amendment to the Iowa State Constitution would require any future increases to the state’s personal income or corporate tax rates to gain supermajority approval at the Iowa Legislature in order to pass. The language specifies this requirement would not apply taxes imposed by local governments.
In Iowa, amending the state constitution is a multi-year process. Lawmakers had to pass Senate Joint Resolution 11 through two consecutive sessions for it to appear on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot. A simple majority of voters must approve the language included in the ballot question to amend the state constitution.
The poll of 500 likely midterm voters was conducted between Aug. 20 and 23 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. This means the three-point difference between approval and disapproval falls within the statistical margin of error.
The results also show there are a significant number of Iowans who still have to make up their minds on the ballot question. Organizations like Iowans for Tax Relief, an advocacy group that supports lower taxes and “less government,” launched an awareness campaign about the constitutional amendment in July.
When lawmakers discussed the proposed constitutional amendment, Republicans who supported the measure said requiring two-thirds of lawmakers approve raising income tax protects taxpayers. But Democrats argued the requirement would restrict future state lawmakers from being able to address a state budget crisis amid declining revenues.
Though Republican and Democratic lawmakers largely voted along party lines on whether to place the constitutional amendment on the ballot, Iowa voters’ opinions on the proposal were not as closely tied to their party affiliation.According to the poll, 39% of Republicans said they would vote to support the constitutional amendment, but 33% said they planned to vote against the measure and 28% remain undecided.
There was more opposition to the proposal among Democrats and independents, but the margins were still relatively close. The poll found 35% of Democrats opposed the constitutional amendment, while 27% supported it and 37% were undecided. For independents, 41% opposed the proposal, 31% supported it, and 27% were undecided.
In addition to the question on the constitutional amendment, the Suffolk University Poll also found Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson leading in the U.S. Senate race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek 45% to 41%, and Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand leading against Republican businessman Zach Lahn 48% to 44%. These results were also within the poll’s margin of error.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia cattlemen push back on Trump’s plan to import beef in bid to lower prices
description: A White House plan intended to help ranchers build up the nation’s cattle herd is causing consternation among Georgia cattlemen and generating beef in the Georgia governor’s race. A pound of ground beef cost the average Fourth of July grill master about $6.89 last month, up from $6.25 in July 2025 and $4.39 in July […]
text:
File photo of Maggie the cow, brought to the state Capitol in 2021 by representatives of Georgia's cattle industry to greet lawmakers. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderA White House plan intended to help ranchers build up the nation’s cattle herd is causing consternation among Georgia cattlemen and generating beef in the Georgia governor’s race.
A pound of ground beef cost the average Fourth of July grill master about $6.89 last month, up from $6.25 in July 2025 and $4.39 in July 2021, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The U.S. cattle herd, which includes beef and dairy cows, is at its lowest point since the 1950s, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. Ranchers say a number of factors, including droughts, rising costs for expenses like diesel and machinery, and market risk make expanding their herds an uncertain endeavor.
On Wednesday, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation allowing a total of 300,000 tons of lean beef trimmings for ground beef to be imported into the United States over 90 days without tariffs.
Lean beef trimmings are a form of beef made by separating smaller pieces of lean meat from large pieces of fat after larger steaks and roasts are cut.
“We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices,” Trump said in a statement on social media. “This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”
Ranchers express skepticism
But the plan drew swift criticism from representatives of Georgia’s cattle producers, who say it will undercut American ranchers and slow down the process of rebuilding the herd.
“What our producers need is confidence that if they invest in more cows, better genetics, improved pastures, equipment, and infrastructure today, there will be a fair market for the cattle they produce tomorrow,” said Kelley Owen, executive vice president of the Georgia Cattlemen’s Association. “The best way to increase America’s beef supply is to give American cattle producers the confidence to grow it.”
Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper, a Republican and Trump ally, broke ranks with the president over the beef plan.
“Increasing our reliance on imported food is not a long-term solution to Americans’ affordability concerns,” Harper said in a statement on social media. “We can lower costs for consumers while supporting the farmers and ranchers who produce our food here at home. A strong domestic food supply is essential to our economic and national security.”
Making hay?
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is Georgia’s Democratic candidate for governor, hopes to make the issue part of her campaign against businessman Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for governor.
“Georgia’s cattle producers power our agriculture economy and provide food for our state and our country,” Bottoms said in a statement. “I stand with Georgia producers against Donald Trump’s reckless plan to flood the market with imported beef.
“And while Donald Trump is selling out our state’s top industries, Rick Jackson refuses to stand up to him — even as cattle producers ring the alarm,” she added. “I encourage Rick to join me in a bipartisan stance against this damaging policy for our producers. As governor, I will be focused on growing Georgia’s economy, protecting our most important industries, and I will never be afraid to stand up to anyone on behalf of Georgians.”
A spokesman for Jackson’s campaign characterized Bottoms’ words as empty campaign rhetoric but did not directly address Jackson’s position.
“Governors do not set federal policy, but they can help support Georgians impacted by decisions made in Washington D.C., which is exactly what Rick is focused on,” said Jackson spokesman Garrison Douglas. “Unlike Keisha Lance Bottoms, he will deliver more than statements, he’ll deliver action, and he won’t run away from the problem like she did when she quit as Mayor.”
Douglas said Jackson’s platform for Georgia cattlemen will include efforts to increase processing capacity and biosecurity while lowering input costs and reducing property taxes.

name: Delaware
title: August Quarterly carries 212 years of faith, freedom and fellowship into festival weekend
description: Wilmington’s historic African American religious celebration concludes with music, worship, youth activities, food, vendors and the traditional Big Quarterly WILMINGTON — For more than two centuries, the final weekend of August has carried a special meaning in Wilmington. It is a time for worship and reunion, music and food, reflection and celebration. It is[...]
text:
Organizers expect more than 3,000 people to participate in Saturday’s Youth Day and Sunday’s Big Quarterly.
Wilmington’s historic African American religious celebration concludes with music, worship, youth activities, food, vendors and the traditional Big Quarterly
WILMINGTON — For more than two centuries, the final weekend of August has carried a special meaning in Wilmington.
It is a time for worship and reunion, music and food, reflection and celebration. It is also a reminder that the freedom to gather, worship and build independent institutions was once a courageous act for African Americans.
The 212th August Quarterly Festival will bring those traditions into the present this weekend with three days of events culminating in the Big Quarterly at Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park.
The remaining schedule includes an all-white party Friday evening, a full day of youth and family activities Saturday, and a worship service followed by the main outdoor festival Sunday.
Organizers expect more than 3,000 people to participate in Saturday’s Youth Day and Sunday’s Big Quarterly.
More than a festival
August Quarterly traces its roots to the Rev. Peter Spencer, the founder of the Union Church of Africans, now known as the African Union Methodist Protestant Church.
Spencer was born into slavery in Maryland in 1782 and later gained his freedom. After moving to Wilmington, he became a mechanic, educator, church leader and advocate for the city’s growing Black community.
In 1813, after rejecting white control over Black religious life, Spencer established the Union Church of Africans as an independent Black denomination. One year later, he began the annual gathering that became known as the August Quarterly.
The gathering traditionally took place on the last Sunday in August and served as both a religious revival and a homecoming. Free and enslaved Black people traveled to Wilmington from Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania and other areas to worship, sing, share meals and reconnect with relatives and friends.
That made the gathering more than a church service. It was a public demonstration of religious independence, community strength and the right of African Americans to assemble on their own terms.
The festival also became connected to Delaware’s abolitionist history. Spencer supported the Underground Railroad, and accounts of the festival’s history describe Wilmington as a place where enslaved people could make contact with abolitionists and plan journeys to freedom.
A tradition that continues to evolve
The August Quarterly has changed from the multistate religious homecoming of the 1800s into a weeklong celebration combining worship with gospel music, youth programming, cultural education, food and community resources.
Its underlying purpose, however, remains much the same: bringing people together around faith, freedom, family and African American cultural identity.
This year’s celebration began Aug. 23 with an opening service at Mother African Union Church and a memorial wreath-laying at Peter Spencer Plaza. Revival services continued during the week.
The festival now moves into its busiest weekend, giving families several opportunities to participate.
Friday celebration opens festival weekend
The AQ Liberation Fest will be held from 6 to 9 p.m. Friday, Aug. 28, at the Delaware Historical Society, 505 N. Market St.
Promoted as an all-white party, the evening will feature the Pieces of a Dream dance group and music from Best Kept Soul.
The event adds a social and entertainment component to the festival while keeping the celebration in the heart of downtown Wilmington.
Saturday belongs to young people
The AQ Youth and Young Adult Experience will take over Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park from noon to 8 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 29.
The day will feature children and youth performers, bookbag and school-supply giveaways, face painting, games and family activities.
By placing young people at the center of Saturday’s program, the festival connects a 212-year-old tradition with the generation that will be responsible for carrying it forward.
The event also helps families prepare for the new school year while offering young performers an opportunity to appear before a large community audience.
Sunday brings worship and the Big Quarterly
Sunday’s events begin with the August Quarterly Worship Service from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Chase Center on the Riverfront, 815 Shipyard Drive.
The service will feature the Rev. Carolyn C. Cavaness and the August Quarterly Festival Choir.
The Big Quarterly will begin at noon at nearby Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park and continue until 8 p.m.
The festival will feature local, regional and nationally known gospel groups performing throughout the day. Food and retail vendors will be joined by cultural, community and health organizations, while a children’s area will offer youth-oriented attractions.
The combination of worship, gospel music, food, vendors and family fellowship reflects many of the elements that have defined August Quarterly throughout its history.
For longtime participants, Sunday is an annual homecoming. For residents unfamiliar with the tradition, it offers an opportunity to experience one of Wilmington’s most important cultural institutions — and to learn why a festival founded in 1814 continues to matter in 2026.
TO GO

What: 212th August Quarterly Festival weekend
Friday: AQ Liberation Fest, 6 to 9 p.m., Delaware Historical Society, 505 N. Market St., Wilmington
Saturday: AQ Youth and Young Adult Experience, noon to 8 p.m., Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park, Rosa Parks Drive and Market Street, Wilmington
Sunday worship: 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., Chase Center on the Riverfront, 815 Shipyard Drive, Wilmington
Sunday festival: The Big Quarterly, noon to 8 p.m., Tubman-Garrett Riverfront Park
Information: Visit augustquarterly.org

title: Sales tax growth, drought and labor shortages shape SD’s budget outlook, economic advisers say
description: The South Dakota Governor’s Office is entering the state’s next budget-writing season with a rosier revenue picture than feared earlier this year, but advisers warned Thursday of uncertainty around federal policy, drought and workforce shortages. The Governor’s Council of Economic Advisors met by video conference to give state financial officials ground-leve[...]
text:
The South Dakota State Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Governor’s Office is entering the state’s next budget-writing season with a rosier revenue picture than feared earlier this year, but advisers warned Thursday of uncertainty around federal policy, drought and workforce shortages.
The Governor’s Council of Economic Advisors met by video conference to give state financial officials ground-level economic insight as they work to prepare the annual budget that Gov. Larry Rhoden will propose to lawmakers in December. The budget is influenced by economic factors that affect various tax revenues.
Revenue reports and sales tax growth
The state finished last fiscal year with revenue that was $29.7 million, or 1.08%, above predictions.
State sales tax revenue in July, the first month of fiscal year 2027, was up 12.8% compared to the same period last year.
Marnie Herrmann, of Rapid City and chief banking officer at Security First Bank, said average debit card transactions exceeded $50 for the first time this summer. Those payments generally reflect gas and grocery purchases, she said.
“That’s a little bit of a harbinger, if you will, of price pressures,” Herrmann said. 
Agriculture and manufacturing
Farm income has rebounded from a difficult stretch based on first-quarter 2026 reports, said Derek Johnson, state economist with the Bureau of Finance and Management.
Beef prices have risen, and grain prices have increased recently, creating some optimism among farmers, Herrmann said.
Governor celebrates surplus as Democratic lawmaker says state missed opportunities to help people

Other advisers warned that outside factors, especially shifts in federal policy and climate, are creating uncertainty.
Drought is affecting roughly 75% of the state, and extreme heat during corn’s pollination stage will impact yields, South Dakota economics professor Evert Van der Sluis warned. Federal farm program payments make up between 25% and 30% of net farm income, he added, and federal budget pressures could put those payments at risk.
“We’ve seen these federal payments fluctuate quite a bit in response to trade policies, especially,” Van der Sluis said.
Tariffs have cut into the agriculture and manufacturing industries. An ongoing dispute with Canada is increasing costs for some manufacturers and limiting sales for others, said Carla Gatzke, a former executive at Daktronics, a Brookings-based manufacturer of scoreboards and other electronic displays. Gatzke said the “swings in tariffs” over the last year discouraged development and capital investment in the Brookings area.
Labor force, housing and childcare
South Dakota’s unemployment rate was 2% in July, with roughly three job openings per unemployed person, Johnson said. But labor force participation is declining, and advisers tied that trend to childcare and housing challenges in the state.
People can’t work if they can’t find someone to care for their children or find a place to live, said Doug Sharp, owner of Sharp Automotive in Watertown.
South Dakota governor’s economic advisers bemoan Trump’s tariff policy

Several advisers shared stories of young family members staying home after having children. Sharp said a lack of data on childcare across the state makes it difficult to quantify the shortage or propose solutions.
Efforts to address the childcare shortage in recent years have stalled in the state Capitol, including a bill offering financial assistance to childcare workers that Gov. Larry Rhoden vetoed.
Housing, advisers said, is an easier challenge to address, though the costs remain a significant barrier to new single-family development. The cost of construction, said Karl Adam of the South Dakota Bankers Association, has “gone through the roof.”
“We still need single-family homes that are affordable in central South Dakota,” Adam said, “but we just don’t seem to be able to get that process started. The cost of construction is an impediment.”
Multifamily construction is making a “huge comeback” in Sioux Falls after a lag in recent years, city Finance Director Shawn Pritchett said.
Sharp said communities are working to incentivize builders.
“Every city will pull out all the stops to figure out how to build out the market,” Sharp said.

title: Execution date set for Oklahoma County killer
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma County killer James D. Pavatt is set to die Nov. 12 by lethal injection. The Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals on Thursday set the execution date. Inmates are put to death at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester. “This case should not be scheduled for execution given the material questions yet to […]
text:
Barbed wire and fencing surrounding the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester is pictured on Sept. 5, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma County killer James D. Pavatt is set to die Nov. 12 by lethal injection.
The Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals on Thursday set the execution date.
Inmates are put to death at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.
“This case should not be scheduled for execution given the material questions yet to be answered,” said Hunter S. Labovitz, assistant federal public defender.
Pavatt, who denies guilt, was sentenced to die for the 2001 shooting death of Robert D. Andrew, 39, an advertising executive, as part of what prosecutors allege was a murder-for-hire plot. 
Pavatt, 72, and Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew, 62, were having an affair, according to news reports.
The Andrews had two children and were going through a divorce.
Andrew was shot in the family home’s garage in Oklahoma City when he went to pick up the couple’s children, prosecutors said at trial.
Prosecutors believed a $800,000 life insurance policy was part of the motive.
Brenda Andrew was tried separately and also received the death penalty. She is appealing.
Brenda Andrew is being held at Mabel Bassett Correctional Center, a women’s prison in McLoud.
After Andrew’s death, Pavatt and Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with the children, but were later apprehended, according to news reports.
The execution is expected to be the fourth in Oklahoma this year.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Gun policy emerges as an early flashpoint in Florida governor’s race
description: Byron Donalds says that the choice between himself and David Jolly for Florida governor “could not be clearer,” and that’s certainly the case when it comes to comparing the two major candidates positions regarding the regulation of guns and the people who use them. Jolly is running on a gun safety platform that includes four tenets: He […]
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9 mm ammunition at a gun range. Several states have enacted laws that allow judges to temporarily remove guns from people in crisis, but a growing number of states are banning the measures. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Byron Donalds says that the choice between himself and David Jolly for Florida governor “could not be clearer,” and that’s certainly the case when it comes to comparing the two major candidates positions regarding the regulation of guns and the people who use them.
Jolly is running on a gun safety platform that includes four tenets: He wants to ban the sale of assault weapons, require universal and comprehensive background checks on gun purchases, explore licensing for firearm ownership, and preserve and expand the “red flag” laws passed in the wake of the 2018 school shooting massacre at Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public High School in Parkland.
Those red flag laws are officially called Risk Protection Orders (RPO). In Florida, only law enforcement officers or agencies can file an RPO petition in civil court which alleges that the respondent poses a significant danger of causing personal injury to him or herself others by having a firearm or ammunition in their custody.
That law was part of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public High School Safety Act passed by the Florida Legislature and signed into law by then Republican Gov. Rick Scott less than a month after the Parkland tragedy.
Donalds says that he is considering repealing that and other provisions of the law if elected in November.
The GOP gubernatorial candidate has proudly told audiences on the campaign trail for more than a year that he was one of the minority of Republicans in the Florida House who opposed the 2018 law. The measure includes a multitude of provisions: It raised the minimum age to buy a rifle or long from 18 to 21. The law also banned bump stocks; required a three-day waiting period for gun purchases; and created those risk protection orders.
When it comes to restricting the purchase of long guns to those 21 and over, Donalds says that “it’s gotta go.”
“We’re going to remove that provision,” he told the Phoenix on Tuesday night.
Senate a bulwark on 2018 gun law
However, the governor of Florida doesn’t have the ability to make that change on his or her own. Ron DeSantis has also been on the record supporting repeal of the measure, and the Florida House passed legislation that would do just that (HB 133) for the fourth straight year in January.
But it failed for the fourth straight year because Senate President Ben Albritton —just like his predecessor, Kathleen Passidomo — didn’t support the legislation.
The incoming Senate president is Manatee County Republican Jim Boyd. He did not respond to a request for comment.
“The Parkland gun safety law was bipartisan, it’s supported by law enforcement, and it should stay in place,” Jolly told the Phoenix.
Regarding repealing red-flag laws/risk protection orders, Donalds said Tuesday night that “we want to make sure without a shadow of doubt that constitutional rights are protected. So that’s what we’re going to aim for.”
In a video posted by earlier this month by Luis Valdes, the Florida state director with Gun Owners of America, Donalds vowed “we’re going to get those provisions undone in Florida.”
While Florida Republicans have passed legislation in the House to repeal the age limit on purchasing a long gun, this past session was the first time that a lawmaker filed legislation attempting to revoke the state’s red flag law. It never received a hearing.
Law enforcement’s concerns
A major factor holding off any repeals of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public Safety Act has been the opposition of law enforcement.
Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri just finished his role in chairing the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Commission, which ended its work last month. He is supporting Donalds, and introduced him at a campaign event in St. Petersburg on Tuesday night.
He declined to respond to a request for comment on the Republican gubernatorial remarks regarding repealing provisions of the 2018 law.
Opposition by law enforcement isn’t bulletproof, however.
For years, the Florida Sheriffs Association fought against allowing for the open carrying of firearms, and that opposition compelled previous Florida Republican leaders to oppose the measure. Albritton told reporters shortly after taking office as Senate president in December of 2024 that he had supported law enforcement his entire life and “I stand with them today in opposition” to open carry.
That opposition didn’t matter however after a three-judge panel of the Florida First District Court of Appeal ruled that the state’s ban on open carry was unconstitutional, a decision that Donalds celebrates.
“We now are essentially an open carry state because of the ruling,” Donalds said.
Yet the Florida Legislature never codified open carry into legislation during the 2026 regular legislative session.
Broward County Rep. Christine Hunschofsky, the incoming Democratic Leader in the Florida House, filed a measure last session that she said would have closed a perceived loophole in the current law by clarifying that all firearms remain prohibited in sensitive government and community spaces.
“I actually privately received a lot of support from the other side of the aisle and from law enforcement,” she said about the proposal, which never received a hearing in committee.
Uthmeier has already indicated that he wouldn’t defend Florida’s law banning individuals under the age of 21 from purchasing a long gun. Hunschofsky says that’s unfortunate.
“Last time I checked the role of the attorney general was to defend the laws of the state of Florida,” she says. “It wasn’t his job to decide which laws he felt were worth defending and which weren’t.”
Uthmeier has also intervened in several other cases involving the use of firearms during his short tenure as the state’s attorney general where he unilaterally declared that current state gun laws are unconstitutional.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska gubernatorial candidates highlight contrasting philosophies on oil and gas
description: At their first candidate forum since the Aug. 18 primary election, the four remaining gubernatorial hopefuls pitched visions for the state’s future that revealed sharp political divides. Speaking at the event, held at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association’s annual conference in Anchorage, were Democrats Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich and Republicans Ber[...]
text:
The four gubernatorial candidates emerging from Alaska's open primary gathered on the stage on Aug. 26, 2026 at the annual conference held by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. From left are Republican Bernadette Wilson, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins, Republican Dave Bronson and Democrat Tom Begich. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)At their first candidate forum since the Aug. 18 primary election, the four remaining gubernatorial hopefuls pitched visions for the state’s future that revealed sharp political divides.
Speaking at the event, held at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association’s annual conference in Anchorage, were Democrats Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich and Republicans Bernadette Wilson and Dave Bronson. Kreiss-Tomkins has been leading in the still-ongoing primary election vote count, with 22.2 %, followed by Begich at 20.5%, Wilson at 10.2% and Bronson at 8.2%.
The four emerged as the top vote-getters among 17 candidates for governor. Alaska’s election system uses open, non-partisan primaries and ranked choice voting in the general election.
Kreiss-Tomkins and Begich, both former state legislators, presented mostly similar positions. Wilson, a talk-show host, and Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor, also presented largely similar positions that contrasted with the Democrats’ views.
Oil and gas taxes figured prominently in the event.
 

Democrat Tom Begich speaks at an Aug. 26, 2026, forum held by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Both Democrats told the petroleum industry audience that they favored changes that would bring the state more revenues from oil producers. Their plans include a statewide corporate income tax on oil producers that are S corporations, also known as pass-through corporations, that currently do not pay them. 
The main company affected by such a tax would be Hilcorp, a privately held company based in Texas that is a major Alaska producer. As of 2020, Hilcorp had acquired all of BP’s Alaska assets when that oil giant left the state, and now it operates Alaska’s largest oil field in Prudhoe Bay, among others. Unlike BP, Hilcorp pays no corporate income tax to the state. Legislative leaders have been pushing to change that.
Hilcorp is also a main sponsor of the AOGA conference.
Begich said a tax on S corporations and other changes to the state’s tax system would bring in an extra $400 million to the treasury each year.
He acknowledged that the oil industry crowd might not like those changes at first. But ultimately, “it will be forward-thinking for private investment,” he said. “If we have that revenue coming in, we can improve our education system. We can improve our economy in general and make our energy significantly more affordable up here. In doing that, you’re going to attract people to this state.”
Kreiss-Tomkins said all sectors, including the oil industry, will have to contribute taxes to correct a structural deficit problem in Alaska that, for now, threatens to wipe out the state’s savings.
“I am pro-math, and math just doesn’t lie. And balancing a budget is ultimately a math problem, and I think you have to be clear-eyed about where the state is,” he said. Compromises will be needed to address that, including compromises from the oil industry, he added.
Wilson and Bronson, in contrast, said they adamantly oppose tax changes that would wring more revenue out of the oil industry.
Wilson called for deep slashes to the state budget.
 

Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, a Republican who finished fourth in the open primary election, speaks at a gubernatorial candidate forum held on Aug. 26, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. Next to him is former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins, a Democratic candidate who received the most votes in the open primary. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“We do not have a revenue problem in this state. We have a spending problem in this state,” she said. 
“The reality is we need to come into this budget, and we need to DOGE the heck out of it,” she said, referring to the mass firings and cuts imposed by the Trump administration through the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE.
Bronson said Alaska has made too many changes already to its oil and gas tax system, and that “changing the rules of the game and the tax structure midway through” scares off investment.
“The reality is we don’t have a whole lot of businesses that are lining up to do business with Alaska,” he said.
Both Wilson and Bronson accused the state legislature of blocking a proposed massive natural gas pipeline that would carry product from the North Slope about 800 miles to a yet-unbuilt liquefaction plant in Southcentral Alaska, known as the AKLNG project
There have been efforts over the past half century to build such a pipeline, but none have been economic. In pushing the latest version, Gov. Mike Dunleavy called the legislature into three  special sessions this summer to try to get them to approve sweeping tax concessions for the investment company now involved with the project, the Glenfarne Group. Lawmakers ultimately rejected Dunleavy’s demands.
Wilson said the Glenfarne plan pushed by Dunleavy, unlike all other plans over the past half century, made economic sense, but lawmakers blocked it.
“You had a couple of legislators specifically that are hell bent on seeing Alaska fail. That’s why you don’t have a gas line,” she said.
Bronson drew a similar conclusion.
 

Bernadette Wilson, a Republican candidate for governor, listens to a question at an Aug. 26, 2026, forum held by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“We’ve got personal animosities in Juneau, and it comes down to just a few people that are shutting that project down,” he said.
Glenfarne, like Hilcorp, is a sponsor of the AOGA conference.
Kreiss-Tomkins and Begich, in turn, criticized Dunleavy, describing his policies as a major reason why Alaska has had more people leave the state than move to it for 13 consecutive years – the most ever recorded. They were particularly critical of his policies on education.
Under Dunleavy, they said, Alaska has stagnated.
“This governor has just set a record for the most number of vetoes by any governor in Alaska history since we became a state,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “That is a sign of political failure, not political success.”
This year, Dunleavy set the record for the most vetoes by an Alaska governor in a single two-year Legislature, while the number of bills passed has also dropped significantly in recent years.
Candidates also discussed national politics at the forum. The two Republican candidates aligned themselves with President Donald Trump, and they portrayed themselves as hard-liners.
“I’m a hardcore conservative, and I’m proud of that,” said Bronson, who described the differences between candidates as stark.
“We’re at an inflection point in this country and in this state, in this election,” he said. “You can choose socialism. . .Or you can choose capitalism. That’s the choice in this race right now.
 

U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, listens to gubernatorial candidates at an Aug. 26, 2026, forum held by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. One of the candidate speaking was his uncle, former state Sen. Tom Begich, a Democrat. Tom Begich mentioned the family relationship during the forum. Nick Begich is running for re-election. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Wilson said the biggest danger to the state came from two of the three men who shared the stage with her.
“The greatest policy threat is, God forbid, this state elects a Democrat to this governor’s office.” she said. Wilson said Democratic Party policies regarding oil and gas “are the greatest threat to this industry.” She urged the audience to stick with Republicans and take advantage of the next two years of the Trump administration.
In contrast, the two Democrats emphasized consensus-building.
“Beyond a doubt, I disagree with Bernadette,” Begich quipped in comments directly following those by Wilson.
More broadly, Begich spoke about his approach to governing. While the governor has a responsibility to “be an advocate for the state of Alaska at all times,” including pushing back against the federal government, if necessary, that does not mean unrelenting combativeness, he said.
“What I won’t do is use the state’s power to attack people that are not even living in our state. I think that’s ridiculous,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins took a similar tone. He spoke of his time serving in a bipartisan coalition in the legislature that “set aside the more fringe and polarizing issues that I think often bring government and the legislature to a standstill” and prevent progress.
“That is a North Star principle for me. . .trying to find compromise, trying to work from a common-sense, common-ground agenda and get things done to move the state forward,” he said.
Ballots are still being counted, but the top four candidates for governor are unlikely to change. The Division of Elections’ primary election schedule calls for all absentee and questioned ballots to be counted within 10 days of the primary, resulting in a deadline of Aug. 28. The results are to be certified on Aug. 31, which is also the deadline for candidates to drop out.
