title: Postal Service pushes ahead on Trump order limiting vote-by-mail
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Postal Service took another step Thursday in implementing a Trump administration policy to restrict mail-in voting, even as a high-stakes legal battle plays out and midterm elections approach.The agency published an FAQ about its new rule that compels states to send their voter rolls to the federal government and only deliver mail ballots to voters who match federal citizenship data. The rule also updates standards for mail ballots that states have said would be difficult to implement before the Nov. 3 elections that will determine the balance of Congress.The controversial rule, which two dozen Democratic states and voting rights groups are challenging in federal court, increases the federal government's role in elections and voting. The states have argued the rule violates the U.S. Constitution, which grants them the power of administering elections.In a Thursday brief defending the rule, the U.S. Justice Department said it only contained “modest improvements and modernizations of the Postal Service’s infrastructure” and would have minimal effect on states’ election administration.“The Rule does not displace a single State election law,” the brief said. “And it need not and should not prevent a single voter from voting by mail.”Democrat-led states and voting rights groups re-filed lawsuits Wednesday to block the Trump administration from executing the rule after a Supreme Court ruling Monday that temporarily greenlit the policy on procedural grounds.USPS acknowledged pending litigation in the FAQ, and noted it would make any changes spurred by the suits. Republicans, including Trump, have long made the accusation that noncitizens vote in federal elections, which multiple studies have shown occurs rarely.   On Thursday, Trump said he believed states could implement the new rule, even in North Carolina where ballots are set to be mailed next week.  “North Carolina is great,” Trump said. “And they do some mail-in ballots. But basically they ruled on the legitimacy and the way we want to make them legitimate. And it was a great ruling for the Republicans.”Those states suing to block the rule are California, Massachusetts, Nevada, Washington, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, as well as the District of Columbia.Jennifer Shutt contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Mary Henry left a NH school district amid a $5 million deficit. Woodstock says she’s exactly who they need.
description:
The superintendent of Mountain Views Supervisory District said the hiring committee reviewed 17 applicants and chose Henry for her experience in public school finance.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Mary Henry left a NH school district amid a $5 million deficit. Woodstock says she’s exactly who they need..
text:
Woodstock Union High School in August 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 24, 2026.
Nine months after leaving a New Hampshire school district in the middle of a $5 million budget crisis, Mary Henry has a new job, a new state and a new administration standing firmly behind her.
Henry says she inherited the Claremont financial crisis, not caused it — and that she became the scapegoat for a problem she was brought in to fix.
Board members learned in August 2025 that Claremont’s SAU #6 was facing a multimillion-dollar deficit. Weeks later, the district placed Henry on unpaid suspension over what the interim superintendent at the time described only as “additional concerns” about her performance. Henry left in November after she and the district negotiated a separation agreement rather than go through a termination hearing.
In July, Henry started as director of finance and operations for the Mountain Views Supervisory District, which serves Woodstock and several surrounding Vermont communities.
Henry remains “one of the finest professionals that the Mountain Views Supervisory District has ever had the pleasure to hire,” said Keri Bristow, who chairs the Mountain Views school board.
However, the Claremont portion of her resume still follows her.
“I really don’t think the hiring district did their due diligence in hiring her,” Candace Crawford, a member of the Claremont school board, said by phone Monday.  
Current Claremont Superintendent Timothy Broadrick declined to weigh in on her specific performance, as he started his position after she left. But he was direct about who is responsible for the district’s finances.
“The business administrator and I are always responsible. Period,” Broadrick told the Valley News. “It’s any business administrator’s job and responsibility to know that the books are right, or if they’re not, to be the one who raises the alarms.”
The superintendent of Mountain Views, Sherry Sousa, said the hiring committee reviewed 17 applicants and chose Henry for her experience in public school finance.
“If there have been problems about Mary executing her position, the (Claremont) board would have had cause for termination,” Sousa said. “If the licensing board in New Hampshire believed that Mary had done something incorrectly or in violation of a license, it would have been rescinded. … That did not happen, and that gave us cause to pursue her as a candidate.”
“We know we have the best candidate for the position,” Sousa added.
What happened in Claremont
Claremont’s fiscal crisis didn’t start with Henry, and it didn’t end when she left. Broadrick said the district’s books had been in disarray for roughly seven years and that Claremont hadn’t completed an annual audit since around 2020 or 2021 — spanning two or three business administrators before Henry.
“It wasn’t that some new problem emerged — it’s that they ran out of cash,” he said, and compared it to checking a bank balance without accounting for checks already written.
Henry said she was told when she was hired in July 2023 that Claremont was five years behind on audits and already in a fiscal emergency. She traces the deficit to two sources: money returned to taxpayers after a prior tax rate was miscalculated, and unbudgeted special-education placement costs. The bulk of it, she said, ties to 2020 and 2021 audits she said she flagged to the district’s auditor in May 2025.
One of her first moves in Claremont, she said, was digitizing a paper-only system, which added to the district’s confusion: “Everything was to be scanned into the system and was paid. (But) nothing was, and everything was by paper and by hand, and you were constantly trying to find things.”
Henry wasn’t the only administrator to leave Claremont. Superintendent Christopher Pratt resigned in September 2025, and several others left around the same time.
“I can’t answer for other people and why they left,” Henry said. “I don’t think there is one administrator left from when I was there.”
The leaked letter
An internal SAU #6 “findings of fact” letter dated October 2025, a month before she left the district, outlined a dozen allegations against Henry, ranging from improper insurance paperwork to unreconciled bank statements.
Due to the separation agreement between Henry and the district, the document was never approved for public release, but it was leaked anyway — months later, Henry said, when a Claremont resident posted it to Facebook in January.
“I don’t know how they got their hands on it,” she said. Neither Henry nor Mountain Views officials could say who leaked it, though both believe it was released to damage her reputation.
Since none of the findings were adjudicated and SAU #6 had not made the letter public or confirmed its contents, Sousa declined to address the substance of the letter. Analyzing the findings “line by line,” she said, was “a rabbit hole that can be contested and has been contested, and it’s not proven for cause of termination, nor has it impacted her license.”
Henry said she was never formally notified of a license investigation. “In the state of New Hampshire, they have to tell me they’re investigating me and put me on notice,” she said.
“I was never put on notice that there was an investigation.”
Her New Hampshire license expired at the end of June 2026, and she is working toward Vermont certification, which requires a year in her current role before she can apply.
A district that’s all-in
Mountain Views officials describe a hands-on onboarding and finance plan: weekly check-ins between Henry and Sousa; continued contact with her mentor and predecessor, Jim Fenn; and a six-month evaluation planned for December or January.
Bristow, the board chair, told the Valley News that the board had held off on a statement while coverage played out, but was unambiguous.
“Why did Claremont try to destroy the person who was trying to fix the problem?” she said, adding that it’s “very infuriating to me that we have to put out fires like this when what we’re really trying to do here is build a new high school, middle school (and) keep moving forward with our successes in literacy and mathematics.”
The board didn’t wait long. On Aug. 20, Bristow sent a message to district families that said there was a “poisonous attempt” by “a relatively small group of individuals” to ruin Henry’s career. It closed with an endorsement from Fenn: “They’ve hired one of the most accomplished and talented Directors of Finance and Operations to support our District’s schools that you’ll find anywhere — in New England or beyond.”
Henry said the scrutiny weighs less on her than on the people around her. “The worst part of all of this isn’t about how much this has come back on me,” she said. “It’s about how much it’s coming back on others — this district, my family.”
Asked why she’s staying in public education rather than returning to the private sector, Henry didn’t hesitate: “I contemplated it. I looked into it. I want to be here, and I’m not going to let someone take away what I work so hard for, and what I want to do with my life.”
Before Claremont, Henry was a business administrator at the Fall Mountain Regional (2022-23), Hillsboro-Deering (2020-22) and Winchester (2018-20) school districts in New Hampshire. She holds a master’s degree from Plymouth State University, a bachelor’s in accounting and finance from Granite State College, and a certificate in education finance from Georgetown University. She also served for roughly a decade on the Fall Mountain Regional School Board.
“I was not terminated from Claremont. We negotiated out of my contract,” Henry told the Valley News.
Claremont, meanwhile, still hasn’t replaced her. The district’s business administrator job has been open since Henry left.
“The job has been posted since January. We are actively looking for a business administrator,” Claremont board member Crawford told the Valley News. “Things are much better than they were a year ago. Things have stabilized, and I encourage people to apply.”
Crawford said the vacancy isn’t unusual. “If you look around the state, we are not unique,” she said. “There are many schools with vacant business admin positions.”
The New Hampshire School Administrators Association currently lists at least nine open financial positions at schools across the state.

title: State approves funding to kickstart 122nd Fighter Wing modernization
description: The State Budget Committee on Thursday approved $1 million to help the Indiana Air National Guard’s 122nd Fighter Wing in Fort Wayne land a future F35-A base. Indiana Brigadier Gen. Matt Brown told the panel of lawmakers the 122nd is “locked in a fierce multi-state competition to secure the next-generation F-35 fighter jet, a designation […]
text:
An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 122nd Fighter Wing takes off at the 122nd Fighter Wing, Fort Wayne, Indiana, July 30, 2026. Training sorties were an essential part of the wing’s readiness to respond to a critical aerospace defense tasking. (Photo by U.S. Air National Guard Tech. Sgt. David Sherman)The State Budget Committee on Thursday approved $1 million to help the Indiana Air National Guard’s 122nd Fighter Wing in Fort Wayne land a future F35-A base.
Indiana Brigadier Gen. Matt Brown told the panel of lawmakers the 122nd is “locked in a fierce multi-state competition to secure the next-generation F-35 fighter jet, a designation that would solidify Fort Wayne’s fighter role in defense economic impact for decades.”
In June, Indiana’s entire congressional delegation sent a letter to the U.S. Air Force urging it to consider the Fort Wayne base for two new F-35A units. The letter highlighted the adaptability of the 122nd Wing and guaranteed the same seamless transition to F-35’s as its recent conversion from using the A-10 to F-16 in the last year.
But Brown said other states are investing heavily to improve their chances. For instance, the Michigan Legislature recently approved $152 million to upgrade the Selfridge Air National Guard Base.
“While Fort Wayne is one of nine F-16 wings competing and will score exceptionally high in performance and readiness, our outdated infrastructure will hold us back in the final scoring,” Brown said. 
He described two projects Thursday that will jumpstart base modernization.
The first costs $517,000 and covers the final design work on a revamped squadron operations building. It will include a mission planning cell, a secure vault area and maximizing the weapon system’s full capability. Federal funds covered the initial 35% concept phase, but the money is needed to position the base to secure an $8.8 million dollar federal construction investment.
The second project costs $500,000 for a comprehensive area development plan to map out future F-35 infrastructure requirements. One part of the roadmap will include mitigating a high-risk security and logistics challenge caused by a bisecting Norfolk Southern railroad.
“Established in 1947, the Fort Wayne base must look beyond its current F-16 operations and plan now for the next generation of aircraft,” Brown said. “Because he National Guard Bureau doesn’t provide federal planning funds until after the final basing decisions are made, Indiana must invest now to remain competitive for the headquarters U.S. Air Force basing decision, which is occurring in the next 18 months.”
The investments, he said, will help position the 122nd to secure an F-35 aircraft delivery by 2034, ensuring the long-term credibility of the Indiana Air National Guard.

text:
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon sits with kindergarteners, first and second graders at the Sweet Briar School near Mandan, North Dakota, on Aug. 27, 2026. 
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)The top U.S. education official on Thursday visited a small rural school in the rolling hills west of Mandan, part of her national education tour.
Education Secretary Linda McMahon visited the Sweet Briar School, joined by U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, R-N.D., and Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, who was North Dakota’s K-12 superintendent from 2013-2025.
School board members, state lawmakers, State Superintendent Levi Bachmeier and others watched as McMahon, Fedorchak and Baesler moved between grades and chatted with the approximately 25 students in kindergarten through eighth grade.
Trump, McMahon promote school voucher program as students return to class

One girl showed McMahon her classroom’s hydroponic garden on the wall. Older students told the secretary about their sports. McMahon sat among kindergarteners, first and second graders, and posed for photos with the students and teachers by the playground. 
The students are split between a 1936 stucco schoolhouse and a newer building. The school community is small enough that a few students are siblings or cousins. At least two teachers count their own children among their pupils.
McMahon’s visit is part of her 50-state “Returning Education to the States Tour. Education is “not one size fits all,” she told reporters, flanked by Fedorchak, Baesler and Bachmeier near the playground.
“Look at the school where we’re standing here today,” she said. “This is an obvious example of an innovation that is education for the students in the place where they live, and the president certainly believes the best education is that that’s closest to the child, and I think we can see evidence of that clearly here today.” 
North Dakota is McMahon’s 41st state since she took office, she said.
U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon visits the Sweet Briar School near Mandan, North Dakota, on Aug. 27, 2026. At right is Assistant Secretary of Elementary and Secondary Education Kirsten Baesler, who was North Dakota’s K-12 superintendent from 2013-2025.(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
“My goal is to see what is taught, how it’s taught, what are the reactions of the students, where are we making the greatest progress, etc., because states are the innovators,” McMahon told reporters.
Baesler and Fedorchak touted the Education Freedom Tax Credit, which rolls out in January and North Dakota will participate in. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill last year created the tax credit, which provides up to $1,700 per taxpayer for cash contributions made to nonprofits known as scholarship-granting organizations that give the funds to families for education expenses, including private K-12 school tuition.
“The key piece here is that that scholarship-granting organization is going to be granting those scholarships to parents to use that money and those dollars how they choose – it’s a choice – to help benefit the education,” Fedorchak told reporters.

title: Burlington artist, dug Nap, struck and killed e-bike rider in crosswalk, new court filing alleges.
description:
Fatal crash brings outpouring of grief for 16-year-old who died as filing in case states that an “attentive driver” should have seen the crosswalk flashing lights and stopped “before crashing into” her.   
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington artist, dug Nap, struck and killed e-bike rider in crosswalk, new court filing alleges..
text:
Doug Knapp appears in Chittenden County Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Knapp is charged with negligent operation of a motor vehicle with death resulting in the death of cyclist Shiloh Skalka. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON – A Burlington folk artist pleaded not guilty Thursday to a charge alleging he struck and killed a 16-year-old cyclist in a crosswalk with warning lights flashing.
Douglas Knapp, 79, faces a misdemeanor offense of negligent operation of a motor vehicle resulting in the death of 16-year-old Shiloh Skalka, a high school student from Burlington, on July 16, who had been riding her e-bike,
Knapp, through his public defender Austin Howard, pleaded not guilty to the offense during an arraignment in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington. If convicted of the charge, Knapp faces up to two years in jail. 
Judge Robert Katims released Knapp on conditions requested by the prosecution, including that he not drive a motor vehicle. Knapp’s next court hearing is set for Oct 27
Skalka’s death has led to tributes in her honor and calls for enhanced bike safety protections. A ride in Skalka’s honor and vigil earlier this month drew hundreds of people, Seven Days reported.
Several of Skalka’s family members, friends and other community members filled several rows of seats in the courtroom Thursday, and declined to comment following the hearing.
Knapp, a well-known Burlington folk artist using the name dug Nap, did not speak during the hearing or after it. 
Instead, Howard, his attorney, made a brief statement on his client’s behalf to reporters outside the courtroom. 
“First, and most importantly, he wants to extend his sincere condolences to the Skalka family,” Howard said of Knapp, who was seated on a bench next to Howard in a courthouse hallway. 
Howard also said that the defense had only recently received the state’s charging documents, 
“Our investigation is just beginning,” the defense attorney said, adding, “Mr. Knapp looks forward to engaging in the process and letting that process play out.“
Chittenden County Deputy State’s Attorney Kelton Olney referred questions from reporters regarding the investigation to the charging documents. 
“Obviously,” Olney added, “it’s very early in the prosecution but the state is pleased that the court imposed the conditions that the state requested, which in this case include a prohibition on driving a motor vehicle on a public highway.”
Knapp was issued a citation by Burlington Police to appear in court on the misdemeanor charge late last month. However, few details were made available at that time regarding what took place leading up to the fatal crash.
A 14-page charging affidavit made public following Knapp’s arraignment Thursday outlines the police investigation leading to the charge that included taking statements from witnesses and analyzing video footage captured from cameras near the scene. 
Burlington Detective Cpl. Padric Hartnett wrote in the filing that the crash took place on the afternoon of July 16 at the intersection of Pine and Locust streets. 
Hartnett added that the investigation showed Skalka was traveling east to west on her e-bike on Locust Street and stopped at the pedestrian crosswalk. Skalka then activated the crossing signal and waited about 3 seconds before entering the roadway, Hartnett wrote.  
While crossing the intersection, Hartnett wrote, Skalka, who was wearing a helmet, was struck seconds later by a Dodge Grand Caravan, driven by Knapp, and traveling south on Pine Street. 
“It is reasonable to believe an attentive driver would have noticed the amber LED lights engaged and upon observing the cyclist in the crosswalk, come to a stop prior to crashing into them,” Hartnett wrote. “Knapp was also traveling at a constant speed just prior to crashing into (Skalka), which further indicates his inattention to the roadway and failure to yield.”  

Doug Knapp appears in Chittenden County Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Knapp is charged with negligent operation of a motor vehicle with death resulting in the death of cyclist Shiloh Skalka. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Skalka was taken to the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington where she later died from her injuries. 
Knapp told an officer at the scene that he was pretty shook, adding that all of a sudden Skalka was in front of him and “I’m hitting her,” the affidavit stated. Knapp also said he had no memory of seeing the crosswalk warning lights or if he hit the brakes of his vehicle, according to the affidavit.
Knapp said he hadn’t consumed any alcohol, and noted that he was on prescribed medication, though the officer did not ask him what that medication was, Hartnett wrote. 
Police later tried to interview Knapp about two weeks after the crash, the affidavit stated, but he told the investigator that based on an attorney’s advice he would not provide a further statement. 
“Knapp was asked if he was on phone during the time of the crash to which he stated he did not have his phone, it was at his studio and not in the vehicle at the time of the crash,” Hartnett wrote.
Hartnett added that it appeared from video footage that Knapp’s vehicle was moving at a consistent speed, estimated at 28 mph in the 25-mph zone leading up to the crash.

title: IRS delays filing, paying of taxes for residents in 22 Nebraska counties after wildfires and storms
description: LINCOLN — The U.S. Internal Revenue Service is postponing the filing and paying of 2026 taxes for affected Nebraskans and businesses in 22 counties due to wildfires and storms this year. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced the delay Thursday as a result of five separate state disaster declarations. Affected taxpayers now have until Feb. 1, […]
text:
Gov. Jim Pillen surveys burned land in Nebraska on Saturday, March 14, 2026. One person died as four major fires continued to burn in western and central Nebraska. (Photo courtesy of the Governor's Office)LINCOLN — The U.S. Internal Revenue Service is postponing the filing and paying of 2026 taxes for affected Nebraskans and businesses in 22 counties due to wildfires and storms this year.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announced the delay Thursday as a result of five separate state disaster declarations. Affected taxpayers now have until Feb. 1, 2027, to file their tax returns and pay any taxes originally due during the disaster periods. Four of the five disasters are due to wildfires between March and June. The fifth is due to severe storms in May.
“When a disaster strikes, surviving the immediate aftermath takes priority,” Pillen said in a statement.
The counties with the approved delay: Arthur, Buffalo, Custer, Dawes, Dawson, Fillmore, Frontier, Gage, Garden, Grant, Howard, Jefferson, Keith, Lincoln, Morrill, Nemaha, Red Willow, Richardson, Saunders, Sioux, Thayer and Thurston.


Federal legislation now allows the IRS to grant a governor’s request for delay based on a governor-declared disaster or emergency. Before, a federal declaration, which can take longer, was needed. 
This is the first time Nebraska has requested the relief under the new law.
Pillen said this year has “undoubtedly” weighed heavily on those who experienced losses and/or damage from the fires and storms just months ago.
Said the governor: “This determination from the IRS will hopefully provide a little respite to Nebraskans in those counties who were affected by allowing them the time to meet their tax obligations without incurring additional penalties.”
Additional counties could be added to the previously declared disaster areas. Residents and businesses in those counties would also be eligible for postponement. Individuals who receive late filing or payment notices during the postponement can call the IRS to have the agency abate the penalty.
More information on each disaster is available from the IRS at https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/around-the-nation-nebraska.

title: US Justice Department challenges 4 more states over in-state tuition for immigrants
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Justice on Thursday sued Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington over laws that allow immigrants in the country without legal status to pay in-state college tuition in the states where they live.President Donald Trump’s administration has now sued 21 states over such laws, which enable noncitizen students who meet certain requirements access to in-state tuition at public colleges and universities, regardless of their immigration status. The lawsuits argue that these policies allow students without legal status to pay drastically lower tuition for public education than U.S. citizens from other states. They also come as the administration aims to curb benefits that could be extended to immigrants more broadly. “Over 30 years ago, Congress made clear that States cannot put illegal aliens before our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said in a statement announcing the four additional lawsuits. “By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, Washington, Oregon, New Mexico, and Arizona are pushing citizens to the side and ignoring federal law. No more.”Advocates for the policy of allowing in-state tuition regardless of immigration status say it does not bestow any advantages not available to the students’ peers in their home states. Meanwhile, in five of the DOJ’s lawsuits — against Texas, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Illinois — courts have already struck down the state laws. Illinois was the only one of those states that did not join with the federal government but instead defended its laws.Lawsuits are also pending in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Kansas, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Virginia.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: U.S. Rep. Edwards denies misconduct in plea to colleagues to avoid censure
description: The U.S. House could vote on Edwards' censure as early as next week.
text:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) listens during a  House Budget Committee meeting on Capitol Hill on May 16, 2025 in Washington, D.C.  (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards, a Republican representing western North Carolina, is asking his colleagues to reject his censure after a U.S. House Ethics Committee report accused him of inappropriate conduct towards two young women working in his office. 
Edwards said in a 22-page letter Thursday that the committee made an “extraordinary analytical leap” in classifying his behavior as sexual harassment. 
The bipartisan House Ethics Committee found “substantial evidence” that Edwards created a “hostile work environment” through a pattern of “inappropriate actions” towards the two staffers, according to a press release from earlier this month. As a result, the panel recommended Edwards’ censure. 
In his letter, Edwards argued that his actions, which the committee claimed “could be interpreted as romantic,” do not amount to sexual harassment. 
“An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition. A gift is not sexual misconduct. A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct. Socializing with a colleague is not sexual misconduct. Caring deeply about someone with whom you have worked and come to know for years is not sexual misconduct,” Edwards wrote. 
In its report, the House Ethics Committee found Edwards gave the two young female staffers gifts including jewelry worth over $1,000 and “designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.” 
The panel also said he wrote one staffer a poem that he read aloud at her going-away party, which several staffers said made them feel uncomfortable. On another occasion, Edwards skipped a House vote to decorate a Christmas tree with a female staffer, according to the Ethics review.
Edwards said in his letter that his staffers have given him gifts such as a custom-made NFL jersey, bourbon and whiskey, a taxidermy animal, and a planned skydiving trip. He called out the Ethics Committee for only including one example of “reciprocal gift-giving” in its report. 
NCGOP selects Balkcom as NC-11 candidate after US Rep. Edwards’ withdrawal

“Instead, the report extensively discusses gifts I gave the women even though some of them predated our time in Congress and some of them were provided as job related tools,” he said.
The congressman gave members of his staff, both male and female, gifts such as wine, olive oil, rum, Kennedy Center tickets, and “even a handgun to a male staffer,” Edwards wrote in his letter.
“Those facts are directly relevant to whether gifts to these two women demonstrated romantic interest or reflected a broader pattern of generosity toward people with whom I worked closely,” he continued. 
The House is expected to vote on Edwards’ censure when it returns from recess on Aug. 31. 
Edwards, who has represented North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District since 2023, dropped his bid for reelection following the Ethics probe. His withdrawal left western North Carolina Republicans scrambling to find a replacement and his colleagues saying he made the right choice. 
The North Carolina Republican Party selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom of Henderson County to fill Edwards’ spot on the ballot against Democrat Jamie Ager. President Donald Trump endorsed Balkcom on Truth Social earlier this month.

title: About $7.6B in New Mexico capital outlay funds remained unspent in recent months, new report says
description: About $7.6 billion intended for more than 6,400 big-budget projects across New Mexico remained unspent at the end of last fiscal year, according to a new Legislative Finance Committee analysis. State lawmakers at a Thursday hearing said they want to see local communities spend more of the capital outlay money the Legislature awards them.
text:
Construction crews work on underground pathways for a pipeline that has received a combination of state capital outlay and federal funds and is planned to serve 73,000 rural New Mexicans with drinking water. (Courtesy of Eastern New Mexico Water Utility Authority)About $7.6 billion intended for more than 6,400 big-budget projects across New Mexico remained unspent at the end of last fiscal year, according to a new Legislative Finance Committee analysis.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
LFC fiscal analyst Ella Hatfield and Director Charles Sallee gave lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee an update on last fiscal year’s capital outlay projects, a term that refers to major construction projects and significant one-time purchases.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in March signed off on nearly $1.3 billion in spending for such projects, which ranged from building pickleball courts to State Police facilities.
State lawmakers at Thursday’s hearing said they want to see local communities spend more of the capital outlay money the Legislature awards them.
Sen. George Muñoz (D-Gallup), who serves as vice chair of the interim Legislative Finance Committee, said the state has made progress to that end but acknowledged there is still more work needed.
“The problem, still, is people want money, but they don’t know how to expend it,” he said at the hearing. “Maybe there ought to be a penalty. We’ll give you the capital, but if you don’t complete your project, there should be some type of penalty.”
Sallee acknowledged that problem and pointed lawmakers to House Bill 247, passed during the most recent legislative session, which limits how many times stalled projects can get reauthorized state funding.
“As you were looking at those projects, it was like sand through an hourglass. Every time you came back, they were taking another one off their list,” he said.
The new LFC report, which focused on the final months of the fiscal year that ended in June, identified more than 950 projects statewide with a price tag of at least $1 million and assigned each a grade of “green,” “yellow” or “red.” Green projects are “on track,” meaning they are nearing completion or are in the construction or design phases, whereas red projects have reported no activity or face “significant” delays.
Nearly half of those projects earned a green rating in Thursday’s report.
The report gave just 7% of projects costing $1 million a “blue” rating, meaning they had been completed. Those included more than $10 million spent on renovations for the Albuquerque Rail Yards, $3.5 million spent on gym construction for the Taos Municipal Schools District and $1.2 million spent on Cochiti Pueblo housing renovations.
Nearly one in four of the 951 appropriations discussed in the report fell in the red category. Multimillion-dollar projects with a red grade included $45 million meant for highway projects in southern New Mexico; $29 million for statewide school bus replacements and $18 million for the Santa Fe Magistrate Court.
They also included the Santa Fe Southside Teen Center construction, for which only $40,000 has been spent out of the project’s $1.8 million budget; a Santa Fe Midtown infrastructure project, which still has nearly half of its $1 million budget; and a San Juan County splash pad project which hasn’t spent any of its $1.5 million budget.
State Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Santa Fe) told Hatfield and Sallee that she was frustrated by how many of the slowgoing projects fell in her district.
“It is rather frustrating, especially when you work really closely with the community,” she said. “All we can do is appropriate the money. We can’t do the contracting, we can’t do the building. When that money doesn’t get spent, it looks like what we’ve done has been for naught.”

name: WyoFile
title: Vance and son hike scenic Forest Service trail in Jackson Hole
description:
Veep traverses classic hiking, skiing and cycling route at public, non-motorized recreation spot above Wilson.
The post Vance and son hike scenic Forest Service trail in Jackson Hole appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Vice President JD Vance hiked down a popular Jackson Hole trail on the Bridger-Teton National Forest on Wednesday, pausing for 20 minutes with his son, Ewan, to learn about the area’s natural history from a Forest Service ambassador.
Ambassador Randy Roberts was covered in dirt from pulling weeds near Crater Lake on the Old Pass Road above Wilson when Vance’s Secret Service entourage arrived and asked him to show them around. Bears frequent the area; one bit a hiker on the butt earlier this month and the gumshoes wanted a brief tour and a bit of advice.

Forest Service Ambassador Randy Roberts works seasonally and is employed by the nonprofit Friends of the Bridger-Teton. (Courtesy photo)

When Roberts and the agents returned to the lake, Vance and his son were near the water enjoying the surroundings.
Vance’s 9-year-old son Ewan was inquisitive, Roberts said, asking whether there were fish in the pothole feature that’s about 40 yards in diameter.
There aren’t, but Roberts explained how one might tell by spotting a rise. They threw pebbles in the water to create their own concentric circles of ripples.
“That’s what the fish creates when he comes up to get an insect,” Roberts said he explained.
The nature talk on a bench went on for 20 minutes — about beavers, about the Scouts of America who built the bench and so on.
“We were talking so much we forgot to make introductions,” Roberts said. Then, the vice president said, “Hi, I’m JD,” Roberts said, and they shook hands.
The encounter wasn’t planned, Roberts said.
“He and his kid were just typical visitors to the area that had your typical visitor statements and appreciation for the beauty,” Roberts said.
“To me it was kind of great to see a father and son having a tremendous time on the Old Pass Road,” he said. “That’s what it’s all about up there — creating memories.”
Protesters gather
Local law enforcement, the Secret Service and the White House would not say why the vice president was in Jackson Hole or which members of his family might have been along. Vance visited the valley in 2025 to raise funds and reportedly was doing the same this year.
The FAA restricted aircraft Wednesday and Friday from the vicinity of Jackson Hole Airport and over a residential area during the vice president’s apparent three-day visit.
The idyllic forest setting contrasted with a protest at Teton Village where perhaps 20 demonstrators gathered to denounce Vance and Trump administration policies. Protesters believed the vice president would be at the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort ski-area base, but Vance was hiking instead.
Protesters gather at Teton Village on Aug. 26, 2026, to protest Vice President JD Vance and Trump administration policies. The group assembled during Vance’s visit to Jackson Hole. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Jules Shelton, a server at a Jackson restaurant, said she was at the protest “to show JD Vance and all his friends they can’t fly under the radar.” She objected to, among other things, the Trump administration’s policies toward public lands.
“They can’t use our town as an ultra-wealthy playground and have us not blink an eye,” Shelton said.
Eva Dabill, a photographer, was at the village “in protest of JD Vance, his insane loser-y pedophilic friends, their politics and everything they stand for.”
Kent Spence celebrated his birthday at the protest, rallying for public lands and democracy, he said, “while Trump tries to steal our elections.”
Musician Phil Round was demonstrating against the administration’s public land and environmental policies, which he called “an abomination.”
Craig Logan, an organizer with the Indivisible network, said he was fighting against the MAGA agenda of stripping public lands, fighting illegal wars, oppressing the LGBTQ community and diminishing reproductive health care rights for women.
Fuzzy Bunny
Vance was at Crater Lake in the middle of the afternoon when he encountered Roberts, a seasonal employee of the nonprofit Friends of the Bridger Teton. A non-motorized trail network below Mount Glory weaves between stands of conifer forests and meadows and is used in the summer by mountain bikers, hikers and equestrians, and by backcountry and cross-country skiers in the winter.
The paths include the History Trail, an old wagon route into Jackson Hole where valley innkeepers used boulders as billboards to advertise their establishments. Mountain bikers shred Lithium, Fuzzy Bunny and Jimmy’s Mom, among other up- and downhill paths.
Another route, the Old Pass Road, is a paved one-laner that served for decades as a motor road over the Teton Range via 8,431-foot-high Teton Pass. The Bridger-Teton made the trail network area off-limits to motorized travel some decades back.
It is not clear how Vance got to Crater Lake, but several vehicles followed him on the hike down, a stroll of about a mile and a half dropping some 700 vertical feet.
After the hike, Vance and his entourage took off in a motorcade of more than a dozen vehicles, none of which flew the customary vice president’s white limousine flag.
Vance was stepping into his limousine when he paused, got back out and said “Hey, thanks, Randy,” Roberts said.
Bridger-Teton National Forest Ambassador Randy Roberts shows souvenirs he got from the Secret Service after giving a nature talk to Vice President JD Vance and his son who hiked up part of Teton Pass on Aug. 26, 2026. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
“He could have just gotten in the car and zoomed off,” Roberts said. “He was really polite and gracious.”
The ambassador had been burying a stinky moose carcass one day, rubbing elbows with the veep the next, he said. He relived the previous 24 hours while in bed that evening, thinking, “was that real?”
Tennessee Watson and Rebecca Huntington contributed to this story.

title: Pediatric group wins early legal battle against DeSantis administration and its Medicaid rates
description: An administrative judge has refused to dismiss the state’s largest pediatric care provider’s allegations the DeSantis administration miscalculated Medicaid rates to cover the costs of applied behavioral analysis for children with autism. Division of Administrative Hearings Judge W. David Watkins ruled Wednesday that Pediatric Associates has legal standing to[...]
text:
Pediatrics Associates wins an early legal battle with the DeSantis administration over Medicaid reimbursement rates and how the state changed the rates to include the costs of providing applied behavior analysis for people with autism and special needs. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
An administrative judge has refused to dismiss the state’s largest pediatric care provider’s allegations the DeSantis administration miscalculated Medicaid rates to cover the costs of applied behavioral analysis for children with autism.
Division of Administrative Hearings Judge W. David Watkins ruled Wednesday that Pediatric Associates has legal standing to challenge Medicaid reimbursement rates for applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services the Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) first put in place in February 2025 and readjusted that November. 
A final hearing in the case has been scheduled for Oct. 1-2.
Pediatric Associates, which claims to treat about 15% of Florida’s pediatric Medicaid population, quickly released a statement praising Watkin’s order.
“DOAH rejected all of AHCA’s arguments for dismissing the case and ruled that Pediatric Associates has the right to challenge them, pointing to the agency’s acknowledgment that its funding changes could predictably cause harm,” the company said in a prepared statement. 
“AHCA’s flawed rate-setting methodology that led to our lawsuit has already drained millions in funding from Florida’s pediatric care system. Our goal is to protect access to everyday pediatric care depended on by more than two million Florida children on Medicaid. We are confident in our position, and we continue to urge AHCA to correct these actuarial errors and resolve this crisis for Florida families.”
The ruling came as a legislatively mandated 10-member task force reviews the state’s healthcare delivery system to “improve care experience and service continuity for enrollees and families receiving ABA services, while safeguarding long term program sustainability.”
The task force, which held its first meeting earlier this month, must submit its recommendations — along with the pros and cons of each proposal — to the governor and Legislature by Dec. 31.

Why does Florida spend so much money on treatment for children with autism and special needs?

In its legal challenge, Pediatric Associates asserted the rates have reduced pediatrician payments by nearly $300 million over 20 months and were adopted in violation of state and federal statutes.
In its motion to dismiss filed with the state Division of  Administrative Hearings on July 14, AHCA argued in part that Pediatric Associates lacked standing to challenge the rates because the state doesn’t pay it directly. Instead, the company gets paid by managed care organizations (MCO) under state contract.
Because of that, AHCA argued that any financial harm the providers might experience is outside the Medicaid statute’s “zone of interests.”
Watkins disagreed.
“But the fact that Pediatric Associates’ financial harm flows through MCO intermediaries does not defeat standing, especially at this stage, because Pediatric Associates need only allege that its injury predictably results from the Challenged Rules,” he wrote.
Additionally, Watkins said, AHCA’s position that Medicaid statute protects only the state’s interests is “irreconcilable” with a 2019 ruling from the Florida 1st District Court of Appeal that healthcare providers have standing to challenge Medicaid rate-making methodologies.
 All about ABA

ABA includes therapy for adults, children with autism, and special-needs children that focuses on individualized interventions to help control challenging behaviors. The idea is to improve the quality of life for children with special needs and their families.
Florida in 2025 switched its ABA delivery model to require managed care plans to cover services for children. Previously, patients, once authorized, saw the Medicaid ABA provider of their choice and the state paid for the services. Since 2025, the care must be provided by the state-contracted plans, and ABA providers who want to continue working with their clients must negotiate contracts with the plans in their regions.
AHCA relied on its contracted actuarial consultants to calculate how to modify rates (by age cohort and geographic location) to include provision of ABA services 
Pediatric Associates’ administrative challenge argues the actuarial consultants made several math mistakes, such as when they spread the costs for ABA services equally across the nine Medicaid regions and across all age groups.
The challenge alleges the new rates “dramatically reduced funding for pediatric care — primary, specialist, and acute — by as much as 20 to 30% in some counties. Overall, Florida has experienced a roughly 15% drop in reimbursement for core pediatric care — approximately $15 million per month in cuts to essential funding — even as the cost of providing this care has risen,” the suit alleges.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lax recordkeeping prompts state audit of Hinds District Attorney’s Office, the first on record since 2013
description: Poor recordkeeping was one reason acting Hinds DA Brad McCullouch asked the state auditor to review finances under former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens, who pleaded guilty in June to a federal corruption charge.
text:
Days before Brad McCullouch would be appointed the Hinds County district attorney in July, he sat down in a tan Shaquille O’Neal executive chair in a mostly empty corner office on the fifth floor of the Hinds County Courthouse. 
Prompted by a public records request from Mississippi Today, McCullouch decided to look for financial and payroll records. He tried to find invoices, accounting software, usernames and passwords for the office’s bank accounts, and audits. 
What he found instead, he said, was a black three-ring binder of checks that date back to January 2026. 
The apparent lack of recordkeeping was one reason McCullouch said he asked the state auditor’s office to review the Hinds DA’s finances under former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens, who pleaded guilty in June to a federal corruption charge and left office soon after.
“I’m realizing that it’s basically one person who is paying all the bills, and I’m thinking, ‘We need somebody to look at all this,’” McCullouch said.
Patchwork of financial oversight
The siloed documentation persisted due in part to a system of patchwork financial oversight for district attorney offices in Mississippi. Regulatory agencies that are supposed to receive financial reports complain of a lack of enforcement power, and accountability depends on the initiative of a particular district attorney.
Once completed, McCullouch’s requested review will be the first audit of the Hinds DA’s office the auditor’s office has recorded since at least 2013, according to Jacob Walters, a spokesperson for the auditor. 
District attorneys in Mississippi also face no penalties if they do not notify the state treasury of the existence of bank accounts holding public money, even though state law says district attorneys should file an annual report with this information. 
The Hinds DA’s office has not filed such a report to the state treasurer’s office since 2017, according to a treasury spokesperson. 
Along with audits, these filings are among the few mechanisms that exist in Mississippi to hold district attorneys accountable for how they spend self-generated funds, such as drug seizure money or fees from pre-trial intervention programs. 
These reports also would have been useful to McCullouch. In his role as Owens’ second-in-command, the Madison attorney said he knew of a few bank accounts the office had at Trustmark, because he was a co-signor. 
Brad McCullouch, a Madison attorney appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves as Hinds County district attorney in July, discusses proposals he believes could reduce crowding at the jail. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
After taking the reins, McCullouch went to Trustmark with an assistant district attorney, who suggested he ask the bank for all the DA’s accounts. 
That’s how he learned the DA’s office had seven accounts at Trustmark, some of which McCullouch didn’t know about. 
McCullouch said he hopes to have an independent audit of the office completed by the time he leaves his post after the Nov. 3 special election. 
In a text message to Mississippi Today, Owens wrote that he paid for an independent audit of his office so he could provide a copy to the Mississippi State Health Department as part of a grant application. Mississippi Today has not retrieved that audit from MSDH by press time. 
“To my knowledge there was no independent audits done in our office in the four years before I was elected,” Owens wrote. 
The missing audits and treasurer reports for the Hinds DA’s office span the terms of two district attorneys in Hinds County, Owens and his predecessor, the late Robert Shuler Smith. 
Smith, who served as Hinds DA from 2008 to 2019, also drew legal scrutiny during his controversial tenure. The Mississippi Attorney General’s Office unsuccessfully pursued various criminal charges against Smith for years, notably accusing him of illegally advising criminal defendants.  
But office paperwork was disorganized under Smith, some former prosecutors told Mississippi Today. Paper files routinely went missing. When Owens was elected in 2019, he implemented an online case management system. 
Records from 2021 and 2024 show that Owens followed reporting requirements for state funding for prosecutor salary supplements by responding to emails from a Department of Finance and Administration employee who was checking which offices were receiving the extra pay. 
Dearth of documents
It is difficult to say how much money is under the purview of the Hinds DA’s office, because of the complexity of the funding for district attorney offices in Mississippi and the dearth of documents. That’s one reason why an audit could be so useful in understanding the finances of one of the most powerful institutions in public life, said Amanda Beck, an accounting professor at Georgia State University who specializes in government auditing. 
“It’s public property so the public deserves to know how that money has been spent,” she said. 
District attorney’s offices in Mississippi are funded through a mix of state, county and self-generated money. Oversight exists for state and county funds: District attorneys must report how they spend this money to the state Department of Finance and Administration or to local county governments. 
But virtually no such enforceable checks and balances exist for self-generated funds, due to the loopholes in state law. Unlike other public funds, this money is solely managed and overseen by the district attorney’s office. 
Plus, little guidance exists for district attorneys in Mississippi on how to comply with state regulations. Stephanie Wood, the current president of the Mississippi Prosecutor’s Association, said the organization does not provide training to district attorneys on how to comply with state oversight laws. 
Hal Kittrell, a longtime district attorney in the 15th Circuit Court District in south Mississippi, said his office voluntarily pays for an independent audit every year. He doesn’t know why or when the audits started. He said it is just something the office has always done, ever since Kittrell was an assistant district attorney nearly 30 years ago. 
“There’s 23 DAs and 23 ways of doing things,” he said. 
The patchwork oversight for district attorneys means just one person knows the whole scope of a district attorney’s finances: The district attorney, said Sen. Brice Wiggins, a Republican from Pascagoula who chairs the Senate Judiciary A Committee. 
“If you have never served (as a district attorney) you don’t know and would never know how those funds come in and what would go out,” Wiggins said. 
Audits required but not always done
Because district attorneys receive state funding, Mississippi statute requires the auditor’s office to audit district attorney’s offices. 
While state law mandates the auditor’s office to annually audit state government offices, the law does not specify a schedule for district attorney offices. The law also does not provide for a punishment if district attorney’s offices fail to obtain or file audits. 
“There’s no penalty if it’s not getting done, so it’s basically not a law,” said Walters, the auditor’s spokesperson. 
When Walters opened a filing cabinet containing audits of district attorneys’ offices in Mississippi to check for records, the folders for other offices contained multiple documents. But he said the folder for the Hinds DA’s office contained just one – a contract for a 2013 audit. 
The audit, however, was never filed with the auditor’s office. 
David Ewing, the owner of the accounting firm that signed the 2013 contract, said he couldn’t find the final copy of the report in his files, which led him to speculate the audit wasn’t submitted to the auditor’s office because it was never completed. He said his firm hasn’t attempted to audit the Hinds DA’s office since 2013. 
Without more stringent requirements, the state auditor relies on district attorneys to self-report suspected wrongdoing in their offices. Past instances of financial crimes involving district attorney employees often involve the office’s self-generated funds. 
Since fiscal year 2018, the auditor has taken enforcement action in just two cases against district attorney’s offices, according to a review of the auditor’s annual reports. Both instances involved DA employees embezzling from the office’s self-generated funds. 
Walters said some funding for district attorneys is covered by audits of county governments. But these can be out of date: The most recent audit the state auditor has on file for Hinds County was in 2022. 
All eyes on Hinds DA audit
Kittrell said he thinks district attorneys across the state will be looking for the outcome of the Hinds DA audit so they can ensure their independent audits are up to par. He noted that the elected offices are unique compared to other government entities in Mississippi, since district attorneys are not quite state offices, but not local agencies, either. 
“We’re kind of an oddity among any agency that I know,” he said. 
District attorneys are not only virtually unchecked in how they spend their self-generated funds. Mississippi’s top prosecutors are also given special powers to pick and choose crimes to prosecute in their circuit court. 
This power wasn’t lost on Owens: He frequently remarked on it to undercover FBI agents who were investigating him. At least one comment that made it into the 2024 federal indictment bore resemblance to McCullouch’s recent realization after his search for financial records turned up short. 
“I’m not trying to overemphasize this, you guys, but my ability to prosecute people… there’s only one me,” Owens was quoted saying in the indictment.

name: Daily Montanan
title: NorthWestern customers report ‘significant increase’ in bills, PSC reviewing complaints
description: Customers of NorthWestern Energy are reporting significant increases in their power bills in August 2026. The Montana Public Service Commission is reviewing complaints. (Photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)
text:
After facing costly heating bills this winter, a new report says consumers shouldn’t expect relief for the summer months, as electric prices and temperatures continue to rise. (Photo by Dave Cummings/New Hampshire Bulletin)The Montana Public Service Commission is looking into a “significant increase” in some NorthWestern Energy bills for August.
“Hundreds of NWE customers are expressing confusion about recent increases in their energy bill,” said a news release from the PSC.
PSC spokesperson Michael Turner said Wednesday the agency typically directs customers who have concerns to first contact the utility, but in this case, it is taking complaints directly.
“Given the volume of public concern, we believe it is important to hear directly from customers so we can better understand the scope and nature of the broader issue, regardless of whether the customer contacted NorthWestern Energy first,” Turner said in an email.
He said the situation was initially reported in East Helena but appears to extend statewide.
Turner also said many customers who are reaching out to the PSC said they already talked with NorthWestern Energy and were told their higher bills were “likely attributable to increased energy use, including air-conditioning use.”
The PSC is creating a case for each call or email it receives and asking NorthWestern Energy to explain the situation on each account, Turner said. It will determine next steps based on the responses.
The PSC is asking people to contact the agency via email at pschelp@mt.gov and provide the account-holder name and service address; scanned copy of the front and back of their bill; and any other relevant documentation.
“Once received, our team will contact NWE regarding each specific case and forward all submitted documentation as part of (the PSC’s) ongoing efforts to help resolve the matter,” the news release said.
The PSC has approved rate increases for NorthWestern Energy in recent years, although in a recent case, not as much of an increase as the utility requested.
In an email, NorthWestern Energy spokesperson Jo Dee Black said the utility typically sees an increase in questions about higher-than-expected bills after long periods of hot and cold weather.
“Changes in weather are often the primary driver of changes in a customer’s energy bill,” Black said.
NorthWestern encourages customers to contact the company if they receive a bill that is higher than expected.
“Our customer service representatives are available by phone and at our Montana walk-in offices to review bills, explain energy-use information and discuss resources to help customers manage their energy costs,” Black said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Schools superintendent backs Kanawha County protocol for special education and Hope Scholarship
description: West Virginia’s top school official says Kanawha County Schools’ procedure regarding students with disabilities returning to the public schools and the Hope Scholarship is legally sound.  Michele Blatt, state schools superintendent, sent a letter to Attorney General JB McCuskey on Wednesday saying that once a child with disabilities exits the public school s[...]
text:
West Virginia Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt speaks before lawmakers at the state Capitol in Charleston Jan. 7, 2025. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia’s top school official says Kanawha County Schools’ procedure regarding students with disabilities returning to the public schools and the Hope Scholarship is legally sound. 
Michele Blatt, state schools superintendent, sent a letter to Attorney General JB McCuskey on Wednesday saying that once a child with disabilities exits the public school system, their special education services cease under federal law. 
Should a student choose to return to public schools, a reevaluation for disability status is required, according to Blatt. This applies to students who left public schools to use the Hope Scholarship, the state’s education voucher program. 
“The West Virginia Department of Education and West Virginia’s local school systems support the right of parents to determine the educational pathway that best meets the needs of their child,” Blatt said in a statement to West Virginia Watch. “At the same time, parents need to consider the benefits, responsibilities and limitations associated with each education option when making these important decisions. We remain committed to providing accurate information and supporting families as they navigate those choices.”
McCuskey sent a letter on Aug. 18 to Blatt taking issue with the Kanawha County Schools procedure that he said impacted students who had left public schools to use the Hope Scholarship. He worried that the protocol violated federal and state law and could subject those students “to discipline without state and federal protections.”
Blatt disagrees with McCuskey’s legal analysis of the KCS procedure and says schools cannot implement an Individualized Education Plan for a student who is no longer enrolled in and attending the public school under federal education law. 
KCS has already responded that their protocol, while not an official policy, is in accordance with federal and state law. The county school system has been sending a letter to parents of students with disabilities explaining their procedure for returning to public schools since 2024.
Blatt said the state education department has worked collaboratively with KCS to revise their letter to parents to clarify that filling out a notice for a child to use the Hope Scholarship specifically does not constitute the revocation of special education services. 
“However, the corrected notice should also accurately communicate that the student’s withdrawal from public enrollment is the basis on which special education services cease,” Blatt said. 
“We have no evidence that Kanawha County has denied any services or that a student was adversely affected by the issuance of the letter in question. In the exercise of our general supervisory authority, we will continue to work statewide to ensure that all students are being served within the state and federal statutes and regulations,” she wrote in her response to McCuskey.
The Department of Education has not received any formal complaints regarding this matter, Blatt said.
“ … We understand parents may question how federal special education requirements apply in different educational settings,” Blatt said in a statement. “We encourage families to contact the WVDE or their local school system so that we can provide information, answer questions and assist when concerns arise. Many concerns can be resolved through a conversation, and the WVDE also provides a formal state-level complaint process for parents who wish to pursue the matter further.”
“In the future, I encourage the Attorney General to call the WVDE or county board of education to quickly resolve matters or provide parents with the appropriate contact information,” she added.
Blatt said the education department will develop and disseminate statewide guidance addressing the nuances between Hope Scholarship for private schools, Individualized Instruction Programs, homeschooling and more in relation to special education services.
If a student enrolls in a private school that participates in an agreement with a county board of education, Blatt said some special education services may be available to the student as funding allows.
There are more than 25,000 students using the Hope Scholarship this school year, and the program gives students around $5,400 this school year to pay for education outside of public schools. The majority of funds are spent at private religious schools, which are not legally required to provide special education services or follow IEPs under federal law.
