name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Trump has widened scope of anti-immigrant policy in second term
text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Treasury’s recent proposed regulation to limit refunds for certain tax credits based on immigration status is the latest move by the Trump administration to restrict noncitizens’ access to federal benefits.In President Donald Trump’s return to the White House, he has employed a governmentwide approach to fulfilling his immigration agenda that includes not only the central campaign promise of mass deportations, but curtailing what few federal benefits some immigrants had. Those actions include pushing out foreign-born workers from the trucking industry, barring noncitizens from accessing government-subsidized housing even for families that include U.S. citizens, and pressuring banks to restrict immigrants' access to opening accounts or borrowing money.Previous presidents generally restricted management of immigration to the departments of Homeland Security, State or Justice. But in Trump’s second term, several unrelated federal agencies have undertaken initiatives meant to disadvantage immigrants.“What's been unique about this administration is beginning to incorporate agencies that have never before been involved in immigration,” Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an analyst with the immigration think tank Migration Policy Institute, said.In Trump’s second term, the Department of Transportation, Department of Housing and Urban Development, Small Business Administration and Federal Communications Commission are among the agencies that have sought to carry out the president’s immigration crackdown.Administration officials have said the benefits of federal programs should be reserved for U.S. citizens.An executive order Trump signed in February 2025 to limit immigrants from receiving benefits, said it was necessary to “prevent taxpayer resources from acting as a magnet and fueling illegal immigration to the United States, and to ensure, to the maximum extent permitted by law, that no taxpayer-funded benefits go to unqualified aliens.”In an Aug. 26 statement to States Newsroom, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the “Trump Administration is putting Americans first.”“As promised, President Trump secured the border, cracked down on illegal immigration, and put Americans first,” Rogers said.Pace acceleratingTrump’s first administration was partially defined by its aggressive immigration policy, including visa restrictions, a travel ban from certain countries, a higher bar for asylum cases in immigration court, and forcing asylum seekers to remain in Mexico while their asylum cases were pending. But the rate at which the second Trump administration is pursuing immigration-related actions is far surpassing the first, according to an analysis from the Migration Policy Institute. In its first year, the administration took more than 500 immigration actions, including executive orders and regulations, compared to 472 actions in all four years of the first administration, according to MPI’s analysis.Welfare restrictionsFederal public benefits are generally denied to “not qualified” immigrants, under a welfare reform law enacted during the Clinton administration known as the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, or PRWORA.The law limits certain public benefits for individuals who do not meet a specific immigration status or eligibility requirements. Over the years, Congress has expanded certain immigrant categories and federal agencies have interpreted which programs are covered under PRWORA.But Trump reversed that trend.Last February, he signed an executive order directing federal agencies to review any programs that benefit immigrants and reverse any expansions. Following the order, the departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, Education, Labor, HUD and the IRS either rescinded notices that clarified eligibility or issued reinterpretations of PRWORA.HHS in July 2025 designated 13 additional programs, including the early-childhood Head Start program, that are subject to PRWORA qualifications. HUD in October restricted certain housing programs and grants based on immigration status. USDA now considers certain licenses, grants, payments and loan programs to fall under the law’s requirements.The Labor Department updated a policy that now forces noncitizens with temporary work authorization to go through reverification every three months in order to participate in a program to help access employment or education.And the Department of Education issued a notice that certain higher education programs, such as Pell grants, loans and workforce programs fall under “federal public benefits.” A preliminary injunction currently prevents the Trump administration's new interpretation of PRWORA from taking effect.The FCC, which is supposed to operate as an independent federal agency but has shown a deference to Trump during his second term, issued a proposed rule in April that would limit the Lifeline program, which provides a discount on phone services for low-income consumers, to U.S. citizens and immigrants with a “qualified” status. That group includes lawful permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, certain survivors of trafficking and victims of abuse. All other immigrants, including those with some form of legal status, are considered “not qualified.” Livelihoods at stakeWhile the second Trump administration has expanded efforts to limit benefits, it has also moved to restrict access to the workforce in a couple of policies.The SBA in March banned noncitizens from applying for small business loans. And the DOT issued a rule that limits the types of visas which can be used to obtain a Commercial Driver's License for foreign-born truck drivers while pushing for veterans to fill the void. That approach was novel, David Bier, the director of immigration studies of the libertarian think tank the Cato Institute, said.“There were certainly some benefits that they attempted to restrict more on the welfare side of things,” Bier said of the first Trump administration. “But I can't think of an instance where they attempted to try to use their regulatory authority to prevent people from being able to engage in certain occupations that they would otherwise be eligible for if they were authorized to work.”Restrictions in GOP megabillThe massive tax cuts and spending package that the Republican-controlled Congress passed last year also limits safety net programs for immigrants.The “big, beautiful” law restricted eligibility for immigrants in Medicaid, Medicare, the Children's Health Insurance Program, Affordable Care Act coverage, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.

 






Economic assistance application for SNAP, TANF and Medicaid through the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

The bill struck several categories of non-citizens who were previously eligible for SNAP, such as immigrants with longstanding humanitarian status like refugees, asylees, parolees and those with suspended deportation status. It also implemented tighter proof-of-citizenship or immigration verification requirements for Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, while also discouraging states from covering insurance for immigrants until that status is verified. The law also bars several other groups of immigrants from ACA subsidies. Immigrants with asylum or a pending claim, in the country on a humanitarian basis, who hold Temporary Protected Status or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status, or who an immigration judge has deemed their home country too dangerous to return are ineligible, under the law.The Trump administration’s focus on limiting safety net programs to noncitizens has produced a chilling effect. An estimated one in ten adult immigrants stopped participating in government benefits for food, housing or healthcare because they were afraid to enroll in benefits they qualified for, according to a report from the Migration Policy Institute.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ICE agent Christian Castro, charged in Minneapolis shooting, released from Texas jail
description: Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January, was released from a Texas county jail early Thursday morning.  Castro has been the subject of a rare interstate extradition battle between Minnesota and Texas, as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign paperwork facilitating[...]
text:
Christian Castro's mugshot. (Cameron County Sheriff’s Department)Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January, was released from a Texas county jail early Thursday morning. 
Castro has been the subject of a rare interstate extradition battle between Minnesota and Texas, as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign paperwork facilitating Castro’s transfer to Minnesota, where he is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. 
U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas paved the way for Castro’s release in a Wednesday decision denying Minnesota’s request to force Abbott to facilitate the extradition, or at least keep Castro in custody until the matter is settled. 
Castro was arrested by the Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, on May 29. A Texas law prevents law enforcement agencies from holding fugitives with pending extradition requests for more than 90 days. 
Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño told the Reformer Castro was released at 6:59 a.m. Thursday.
Castro is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison submitted affidavits to the court showing that Castro was in a romantic relationship with a woman in Mexico, and owns property there, presenting a possible flight risk. Cameron County, where Castro was jailed, is on the U.S.-Mexico border. 
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who charged Castro, said in a Wednesday press conference that the next steps in the legal process become much more complicated if Castro flees the country.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Four years after Tennessee “trigger law,” poll shows Tennesseans favor abortion ban exceptions
description: Tuesday marked the anniversary of Tennessee’s so-called “trigger ban,” the extreme anti-abortion legislation that went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion through 1972’s Roe v. Wade.  Tennessee law makes abortion a felony except in circumstances where the life of the mother is in danger or […]
text:
Four years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion, polls show Tennesseans of all political stripes favor more exceptions to Tennessee's abortion ban. Photo taken of protests in Nashville on the June 2022 day of the Court's ruling. (Photo:John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tuesday marked the anniversary of Tennessee’s so-called “trigger ban,” the extreme anti-abortion legislation that went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to an abortion through 1972’s Roe v. Wade. 
Tennessee law makes abortion a felony except in circumstances where the life of the mother is in danger or she faces serious bodily injury. That means no exceptions for rape, incest or the mental health of the mother and none for life-limiting fetal diagnosis. In other words, if your baby is sure to die, you are still barred from abortion.
Tennessee’s law is one of the most draconian in the country. Four years later, it seems reasonable to ask how Tennesseans are feeling about it.
In January of this year, the Tennessee Freedom Circle administered the first statewide poll measuring Tennesseans’ views on reproductive health policy since the end of Roe. 
We polled 600 likely 2026 general election voters, a population that closely mirrors the 2024 presidential vote in Tennessee, with 64% of respondents identifying as Republican and 73% identifying with the Make America Great Again movement. The most surprising revelation from that poll was how little the majority of Tennesseans actually know about abortion law in our state. 
Many of our respondents were astonished to learn that our abortion law has so few exceptions. Seventy two percent of them told us that they support exceptions for rape and incest and 71% support an exception when the fetus cannot live outside the womb. When we initially asked them how they felt about Tennessee’s abortion law, 49% said they supported it. Once they learned how restrictive it was, 55% opposed it. These statistics tell us that Tennesseans want common sense, not extremist, reproductive health policies. 
Tennesseans also understand that reproductive freedom is about more than abortion. Our respondents overwhelmingly support keeping in vitro fertilization, IVF, legal: 73% of voters, including majorities of Republicans and voters who identify as pro-life, believe IVF should remain legal. Two-thirds of voters oppose new restrictions on genetic testing that could threaten access to IVF. 
Four years after Tennessee enacted one of the most restrictive abortion laws in the nation, these polling results demonstrated that we don’t have to understand reproductive health care policy as a purely partisan issue. And our lawmakers are starting to understand that. 
Last year, the Tennessee General Assembly passed the Fertility and Contraception Protection Act that protects contraception and IVF, becoming the first state in the South to do so. This year, our legislators expanded access to contraception by passing legislation allowing patients covered by applicable health plans to obtain a 12-month supply of prescription contraception at one time. 
At the same time, Tennessee Freedom Circle and its partners worked to successfully oppose extreme proposals, including HB 1528, which would have expanded Tennessee’s wrongful death statute by redefining “person” to include an unborn child beginning at fertilization. Why were we successful? We think it’s because everyone — Democrats and Republicans — are realizing that Tennesseans want a more compassionate, medically grounded approach to reproductive healthcare than is represented by the extremist law triggered by the Dobbs decision. We may have learned a lot in four years.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri power grid faces costly upgrades as AI data centers drive electricity demand
description: A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments. text:
(Getty Images)A new federal report shows the electric grid across much of the country is strained, requiring thousands of miles of new power lines and billions of dollars in investments.
The National Transmission Needs Study shows that approximately 4,000 miles of powerlines will need to be replaced each year for the next few decades.
The federal report notes that most of the country’s transmission infrastructure was built in the 1960s and ’70s and is now reaching the end of its useful life and that currently, “operational challenges of the electric grid are evolving in complexity and magnitude.”
Threats from severe weather, increasing demand for electricity and additional wind and solar generation coming online all compound the need for new powerlines nationwide.
“Significant transmission investment is needed to cost-effectively meet future demand through 2050,” the report states.
The federal analysis points to projections that show U.S. electricity consumption rising 16% to 25% by 2034.
Increasing electricity demand is due in large part to the rapid development of data centers needed to support artificial intelligence technologies.
During a visit to Jefferson City on Monday, Department of Energy leaders said they believe operators of forthcoming AI data centers will pay their fair share.
Katie Jereza is the assistant secretary of the federal Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity. She pointed to President Donald Trump’s voluntary ratepayer protection pledge that’s been signed by tech companies, utilities and governors.
“The whole principle is that the data centers will pay for the infrastructure upgrades for their generation, not the families,” Jereza said.
Jereza said the federal government will soon announce funding for what’s called “reconductoring.”
“Which is basically … restringing the lines,” Jereza said. “So you’ve got old conductors, and now we’re going to put in new ones that can carry more electrons through from generation to delivery.”
As technology companies build AI data centers across the state, Missouri lawmakers have passed legislation with new consumer protections in an attempt to ensure the company’s large energy needs don’t increase residents’ utility bills.
“We feel like the transmission element is something that largely gets glossed over, but it’s a huge cost that ultimately is borne by ratepayers,” said Geoff Marke, chief economist with the Missouri Office of Public Counsel, the state’s consumer advocacy department.
He said he’s concerned the cost for the vast infrastructure upgrades needed will fall to the average energy consumers.
“If the proper cost allocation is not in place there, then yes, I do think residential customers will be exposed more than they otherwise would be,” Marke said.
The national study of powerlines comes as a group of nine electric transmission utilities, including Ameren and Evergy, are asking federal energy regulators for the right of first refusal to build and operate new multi-state, large-scale powerlines. The energy companies say pausing the competitive bidding process will speed up needed grid upgrades.
But Marke said competition reigns in overspending.
“Incumbent utilities have the vast majority of the transmission investment,” Marke said. “Opening that up to requests for proposals or just competitive bidding will just force everybody to be more professional and curb those costs.”
Jezera said whether competition brings the cost of new transmission lines down depends on a variety of factors, including location.
“There are parts of the country where it has worked really well. It has gone faster and reduced the cost, and then in other areas it hasn’t worked as well,” she said.
This story was originally produced by KBIA.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming school finance committee moves toward funding solutions
description:
Lawmakers continued work this week to address funding for Wyoming’s K-12 public education system after a judge ruled that the state failed to provide sufficient resources for key areas.
The post Wyoming school finance committee moves toward funding solutions appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CHEYENNE—State lawmakers continued work this week to address funding for Wyoming’s K-12 public education system, attempting to close shortfalls identified by courts in critical areas, including school safety, nutrition and technology.
The Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration heard testimony and public comment on how to tackle these issues.
In February 2025, Laramie County District Court Judge Peter Froelicher issued a 186-page order finding that the Wyoming Legislature had unconstitutionally underfunded public schools. The judge ruled that the state failed to provide sufficient resources for key areas, such as nutritional programs, school resource officers and technology.
The state appealed the decision to the Wyoming Supreme Court, which issued a stay pausing the lower court’s mandate while the state’s appeal proceeds. When the committee began its work, the stay had not yet been issued, and no final ruling has been made to date.
Co-Chair Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, expects the court to pay attention to the committee’s actions in the coming months.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the committee heard from consultants with Picus Odden and Associates, who presented proposals to ensure these programs are funded in compliance with the state Constitution.
School safety
The court order determined that “all Wyoming public school students are entitled to the benefit of SROs.” Not every school is required to have its own full-time school resource officer, but the order does require students to have access to SRO services.
Picus Odden estimated that 172.5 SRO positions are necessary to meet the requirements, at a cost of $15.8 million annually for personnel alone, and $17.1 million annually in total, including professional development, equipment and supplies.
The model, based on the recommendations provided by Picus Odden, proposed one SRO for each high school, one for every two middle schools and one for every three elementary schools.
During interviews, school district personnel emphasized how professional development allows SROs to work effectively and the necessary equipment allows them to perform their responsibilities.
Currently, school districts contract with local sheriff’s offices or police departments to provide SRO services.
Teton County Sheriff’s Office School Resource Officer Andrew Roundy lets Jackson Hole High School seniors back into school during the lunch hour in March 2018. As a resource officer, Roundy was present at the school whenever students were in the building, as well as during special local events. (Ryan Dorgan/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
Manny Fardella, a Cheyenne Police Department officer and president of the Wyoming School Resource Officers Association, spoke on behalf of SROs in the state and about his experience in Laramie County. He disagreed with the notion that SROs are simply there to be security.
“Our school resource officers are more than a security guard. We become part of a school family. To many, we become members, trusted people,” he said.
Jeremy Smith, the business manager for Sheridan District 1, spoke about making sure this funding would not be categorical, meaning that it could only be spent on SROs. Smith stressed that this funding could also be put toward additional district-specific safety needs.
The committee requested that a bill be drafted based on Picus Odden’s recommendations, but did not include professional development or equipment.
Food service programs
The court’s ruling determined that the school funding model not including a nutrition component was unconstitutional because “nutrition is an essential component of a quality education.”
To remedy this, Picus Odden’s proposed options would ensure all students have adequate access to food by covering the difference between food service revenues and expenditures. The consultant’s research estimated the difference during the 2024-25 school year was $17.8 million.
The first proposed option was to provide employee benefits such as health insurance and retirement contributions to food service staff, as they are currently excluded from both. This option would cover about $9 million in district food service costs.
This option would only cover about half of the current statewide difference and would provide limited or no support to districts that contract for food services, meaning it would have to be combined with another option.
The second option would reimburse districts a fixed percentage of food service expenditures; reimbursement rates vary from 10% to 30%. The state could set the rate to reflect the difference between revenues and expenditures statewide.
However, due to the difference varying widely by district, this approach would not cover the difference for 29 of the state’s 48 districts.
The combination of options one and two would leave shortfalls in 25 districts uncovered, according to Picus Odden.
Fort Washakie School second grader Dale Siers eats corn at lunchtime on Farm to School Day. The corn came from 1890 Farms in nearby Riverton. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
The final option would fund food services using the same general approach used to determine funding for other school resources. Under this approach, the Legislature would determine the variables used to calculate the appropriate level of funding. Under Picus Odden’s recommended assumptions, $17.1 million would be provided for food service worker staffing and $5.8 million to food service director staffing, for a total of $22.9 million.
Option three would leave 12 districts with shortfalls uncovered, Picus Odden officials said.
Public comment on the subject was divided, with some preferring the combination of options one and two, and others exclusively preferring option two because their districts contract for meals.
Brian Farmer, the executive director of the Wyoming School Boards Association, explained why there is no perfect fix for this issue.
“There is wide variability, and it’s really challenging because you can come up with something that works great for parts of the state but not necessarily others,” he said.
The committee unanimously requested a bill draft using option two, at a reimbursement rate of 30%, which equates to $17.5 million.
Technology
Judge Froelicher’s order also stated that a computer must be provided for every student, though there has been concern from local communities and parents regarding the amount of screen time students experience. Picus Odden took those concerns into account and provided eight different choices to address them.
The options ranged from the recommended 1:1 ratio for all grades to a 1:3 ratio for all grades and included options five and six, which provide no computers to students in kindergarten through second grade.
The recommendation from Picus Odden is a comprehensive estimate to provide computers at a 1:1 ratio for students and school staff at $208.95 per Average Daily Membership. Also known as ADM, this is the state’s way of calculating student enrollment. Additional operational costs for networks and learning management systems are estimated at $235 per ADM, for a total of $443.95 per ADM, leading to a $16.7 million total cost statewide. The options provided variability concerning the ratio and whether computers would be given to students in kindergarten through third grade.
Kalie Bocek, a senior at Tongue River High School, does school work on the computer. (Sheridan School District #1)
Sheridan County’s Smith noted how this funding could be best used for each district.
“I think having a tech director position in every district would help solidify how we actually operate in real life,” he said.
The committee agreed to request a bill draft with no computers for grades K-2, and a 1:1 ratio for grades 3-12, at a cost of $395 per ADM. State Sen. Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, also asked that the bill draft include a minimum of one tech director and a part-time tech specialist for every district, based on testimony provided.
Next steps
The recalibration committee will meet Oct. 21 and 22 in Casper to continue discussions and make changes to the bill drafts as necessary.
Sen. Salazar expressed optimism about progress the committee had made, but acknowledged the primary task was ensuring compliance with the judge’s order.
“I think it’s important to go forward because I want to give the third branch of the government the understanding that we are trying to do the right thing in regard to the order,” he said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico psilocybin program opens permitting applications for psychedelic mushroom producers
description: New Mexico’s Medical Psilocybin Program recently opened up applications for producers of the psychedelic mushroom, marking a significant step toward the therapeutic program becoming fully operational.
text:
he New Mexico Department of Health Center for Medical Cannabis and Psilocybin on Aug. 17, 2026, began accepting applications from potential producers to grow mushrooms for the program. (Photo provided by Rudick Law Group)New Mexico’s Medical Psilocybin Program recently opened up applications for producers of the psychedelic mushroom, marking a significant step toward the therapeutic program becoming fully operational.
“We’re no longer talking about a piece of legislation and some rulemaking. This is real, this is happening and it’s being operationalized right now,” Santa Fe-based psychedelic attorney Victoria Cvitanovic told Source NM. 
The program was created last year with the signing of Senate Bill 219, which created the medical psilocybin program, an advisory board and legalized use of the psychedelic in controlled, therapeutic settings. Qualifying conditions currently include major treatment-resistant depression, post traumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders and end-of-life care. 
The New Mexico Department of Health Center for Medical Cannabis and Psilocybin began accepting applications last week from potential producers to grow the mushrooms for future program participants. Cvitanovic told Source that the application is intended to ensure the psilocybin “produced for this program in New Mexico is both safe and medically beneficial for patients, as well as that this doesn’t cause safety issues for people in New Mexico generally.”
According to the permit requirements, applicants must provide a state business license; proof of registration with the New Mexico Secretary of State and the Taxation and Revenue Department; facility safety documents; proof of ownership of the facility or a signed statement from the landowner; proof of compliance with city and county zoning requirements; and verification that psilocybin products will only be produced and tested in New Mexico.
“I think it’s notable that the application balances both the safety of the patients who will be receiving the end product and the safety of people who may live in areas of the state where someone is granted a license to produce psilocybin,” Cvitanovic said. “These applications are open to anyone, but they are fairly extensive because of the high stakes of producing a controlled substance, specifically for very limited medical use.”
She said she believes that most applicants will have an agricultural and entrepreneurial background, but likely only a small number of “highly qualified” applications will meet the requirements. A DOH spokesperson told Source NM in an email that there is currently no deadline for applications and that they will be reviewed in order of submission.
Cvitanovic said she recommends those considering applying to be a producer confer with a lawyer and accountant and get documentation together to submit the most complete and compliant application as possible. However, they should also consider whether their plans are operational if a permit is granted.
SB219 set a deadline of Dec. 31, 2027 for the psilocybin program to be implemented; however, the state committed to expediting the timeline by a year, aiming to open the program to its first patients by the end of 2026.
“The state is working really hard to operationalize this program as quickly as possible,” Cvitanovic said. “People are suffering and they want to address that suffering.”
She added that the program’s rulemaking process is not complete and more permit applications will open up down the line for testing and for qualified clinicians. A “buildout and inspection period” will also likely follow before treatment begins with patients. She encouraged people interested in participating in the program to speak with their behavioral health providers about becoming certified to facilitate the treatment.
“Programs like this are only as strong as the clinicians and therapists and other people who choose to participate in them. This is hard work, and it is not risk free, but it has the ability to change the lives of thousands of New Mexicans who are suffering,” Cvitanovic said.

title: Federal agencies threaten to punish two Kansas school districts over gender-inclusive policies
description: LAWRENCE — The U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Education announced a plan for increased enforcement measures against two Kansas school districts for their gender-inclusive policies.  In April, the department found four public school districts — Olathe, Shawnee Mission, Topeka and Kansas City, Kansas — were in violation of federal Title IX civil[...]
text:
The Lyndon Baines Johnson Department of Education Building in Washington, D.C., stands on Nov. 25, 2024. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)LAWRENCE — The U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Education announced a plan for increased enforcement measures against two Kansas school districts for their gender-inclusive policies. 
In April, the department found four public school districts — Olathe, Shawnee Mission, Topeka and Kansas City, Kansas — were in violation of federal Title IX civil rights protections. Reasons included allowing students to change their name or pronouns used at school without clear communication to parents and allowing transgender students to use the restroom, locker room and changing room that aligns with their gender identity.
On Tuesday, the Education Department announced it would work alongside the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division to take “enforcement measures” against the Olathe and Shawnee Mission school districts for failing to comply with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, or FERPA.
The Education Department said that failure to comply could lead to legal action and potential loss of federal funding.
“These policies encourage schools to conceal from parents whether their child uses different pronouns and even permits schools to print a different name on students’ diplomas without parental knowledge or consent,” the release said. “Withholding such sensitive information from parents when they request their children’s records is a clear violation of FERPA.”
The Education Department issued letters Wednesday to local and state education agencies with reminders about FERPA guidelines as a new school year begins. A news release from the department said the reminder comes amid “rampant reports” of schools withholding records related to a child’s gender or gender transition from parents. 
The Education Department said it proposed resolution agreements with Olathe and Shawnee Mission school districts earlier this year, and that the Shawnee Mission district never agreed to a resolution. 
In a letter addressed to the Education Department’s Student Privacy Policy Office, the Shawnee Mission school district’s legal representation said the office’s findings did not violate FERPA. The letter also said the office’s findings ignored that the district requires proof of parental involvement in official student name change requests.
“Nothing about SMSD’s approach to student names, pronouns, or gender violates or even implicates FERPA,” the letter said. “SMSD has been and remains in compliance with FERPA.”
The Olathe district signed a “voluntary resolution agreement” in May outlining the district’s commitment to giving students access to gender-specific facilities “strictly on the basis of sex.” The agreement was rejected by the Education Department. 
The Olathe district has said throughout the department’s investigation there have been no Title IX or FERPA violations in its schools, and outlined district communication with the department as well as any legal correspondence on its website.
“The unfortunate continuation of this drawn-out political display continues to rob time and resources from the work that matters most as a public school system: educating our children,” said a district press release. “Olathe Public Schools will continue to defend the integrity of its people and practices, and remains committed to serving students, supporting families, and complying with all applicable federal and state laws.”
The Education Department announced Tuesday that its Student Privacy Policy Office entered a resolution agreement with the Topeka school district to uphold parental rights and come into compliance with federal law. 
The agreement’s guidelines include not creating gender support plans, allowing any gender support plans on file to be reviewed by parents, adding FERPA content into staff training and revoking any guidance that prevents schools from keeping parents informed about their students.

title: The NC candidate who wanted to use “Mortellus” on the ballot says the state’s response is incomplete
description: North Carolina ballots must have candidates’ legal names or nicknames, and must include last names unless legally, the candidates have just one name, the state Board of Elections decided last week.  The State Board of Elections voted unanimously that candidates cannot forgo putting surnames names on ballots if they have them.  The decision stemmed from […]
text:
State Board of Elections member Siobhan O’Duffy Millen (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina ballots must have candidates’ legal names or nicknames, and must include last names unless legally, the candidates have just one name, the state Board of Elections decided last week. 
The State Board of Elections voted unanimously that candidates cannot forgo putting surnames names on ballots if they have them. 
The decision stemmed from a request for declaratory rulings from Mortellus, a candidate for Soil and Water District Board of Supervisors in Rutherford County, whose legal name is Terrayle Amorello. Mortellius is a religious name and is how they are known in the community, they said in the request for a declaratory ruling. 
In their discussion last week, elections board members said they would stick with state law.
Candidates must have surnames on the ballot, said Siobhan Millen, a Democrat on the state board. Election officials  must have the ability to make changes if there is an error, she said.
In an interview this week, Mortellus, who uses they/them pronouns, said they may ask the state Office of Administrative Hearings to determine whether the board made the right decision.  
When Morellus filed to run, they wanted to use their single name, but offered to have “Mortellus” in parentheses before or after their legal name. They did not want Motellus displayed as a nickname. 
“I simply asked if my faith name could be before my birth name rather than in the middle,” they said. “I didn’t want it  to be perceived as a nickname when it is in fact something holy.” 
They were first publicly listed as a candidate as NLN Mortellus, or “no last name,” with the single name appearing on the ballot. 
State board members said they did not want to delve into religion. . 
“I don’t want to second-guess anyone’s religious beliefs,” said board member Stacy “Four” Eggers IV, a Republican. 
In the process of receiving instructions from the state elections staff on how their name would appear, Mortellus’ name on the ballot was changed from the mononym to Mortellus Amorello. 
In the interview, they said the board failed to answer the question about religious names and didn’t say whether a county or state elections board could alter accepted candidate records without cooperation from the candidate. 
“I don’t feel like they answered my questions,” they said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: The teenage girls behind a $25 minimum wage fight in rural Alaska
description: This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th. Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. In one of the most remote towns in America, a group of teenagers is fighting to put an initiative on the November ballot that would raise the minimum wage for the […]
text:
Teens Kaya Kent and Sara James are among many youth in Nome, Alaska fighting for a $25 minimum wage. (EMILY SCHERER FOR THE 19TH)
This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th.  Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
In one of the most remote towns in America, a group of teenagers is fighting to put an initiative on the November ballot that would raise the minimum wage for the largely Native population of Nome, Alaska.
The idea took hold earlier this year when the six young women were invited to a conference in California as part of a Native youth leadership group they’d joined at their high school. There, they listened to Saru Jayaraman, who heads a national effort to raise the minimum wage, speak about the work being done city by city to secure higher pay. They kept looking at each other as she spoke. We should do this in Nome, they thought.
“We were just talking amongst ourselves, and we were like, ‘There’s people in Alaska who work for their whole lives, and their minimum wage doesn’t change at all to support their children and their elders, and their whole family,’” said Alora Stasenko, one of the women leading the effort who graduated this spring. Another student leader, Renee Brown, was working part-time at the local preschool and saw how many of her coworkers lived out of renovated shipping containers and walked to work in harsh conditions. The low in Nome reached -26 degrees Fahrenheit last year.
“We decided that money was a problem, and that we wanted to help get, not just a few people, but everybody, what they need,” Stasenko said.
Nome, a town of about 3,700 on Alaska’s Seward Peninsula, just 150 miles off the coast of Russia, is perhaps best known for its history as a gold rush town and as the ending point of the Iditarod Sled Dog Race. The next nearest town is 70 miles away, and supplies need to be shipped or flown in. That makes living expensive. The minimum wage is $14 an hour, but the cost of living is about 69 percent higher than the national average. Gas often tops $6 a gallon. Milk is $10 a gallon. Grocery stores are rarely full and so expensive that many people hunt for their food.
“It takes a while to go out on boats or snow machines or trucks or four-wheelers, and you have to buy your ammo and your guns and all your equipment to go out. Everything gets expensive,” Stasenko said. “I grew up living a very subsistence lifestyle.”
In her freezer: caribou, fish and walrus that she helped hunt herself.
Stasenko and the other students were gripped by the idea that raising the minimum wage in Nome could help give people there a better quality of life. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology Living Wage Calculator sets the living wage there — how much one person working full-time needs to support themselves — at nearly $24 an hour. A family of four would need two working adults earning about $28 an hour each to stay afloat.
Jayaraman was impressed when the students followed up with her after the conference. It was the first time in her decades of activism that she had been approached by high schoolers to start a campaign.
With her guidance, the students formed the Nome Living Wage For All Alliance and convened a call with some of the town’s largest employers to discuss interest in a ballot initiative. They settled on a goal of raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour. They’re proposing a phase-in period, giving large corporations until 2029 to raise wages and small businesses until 2032. Already, the town’s top employer, Norton Sound Health Corporation, sets its minimum wage at $25 an hour, so raising the floor would only apply to about 15 percent of workers in the city.
They submitted a ballot petition to the city in May, which was approved, and now need to collect 108 signatures — representing a quarter of ballots cast in the 2025 local election — to get their proposal on the ballot in November. They have until the end of the month to collect enough signatures.
“They’ve initiated this conversation in Nome,” said Jayaraman, who added that the story of the group’s work has also inspired other organizers around the country. “Whether they make it on the ballot this November or not, they’ve already had such profound impact on the national movement, on young people all over the country, on workers in other states.”
Because Nome is also a larger regional hub, part of the hope is that improving wages there could also help raise them in neighboring towns where conditions are even harsher — where stores often lack meat or fresh produce and there is no running water.
Over the summer, Brown, one of the student organizers, spoke at a national mobilization event in Washington, D.C. about the hope she had that Nome’s movement “will not only improve the lives of our community members, but will inspire our fellow classmates and peers across Alaska to believe in the power of effort, advocacy and determination.”
“Our efforts will help Nome pioneer a new kind of American dream — one where dignity is the baseline and every resident can afford to stay on our golden beaches,” Brown said.
Most of the organizers spent much of the end of their senior year at Nome-Beltz Middle High School strategizing. Kaya Kent, another organizer, said she remembers talking excitedly about it with Stasenko during classes.
“I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I was checking my email constantly, and I was waking up thinking about the campaign,” Kent said.
A $500 million-plus project to turn Nome’s dock into the nation’s first deepwater Arctic port just kicked off, and though it will likely bring in money for all the businesses that traverse through there, the organizers want to make sure the people of Nome can benefit, too.
Even those already earning more than $25 an hour — like Kent’s mother, who works in an administrative position at the local hospital — are still struggling to live comfortably in Nome, Kent said.
“If it’s like that for my mom, who’s able to make $40 an hour, I can’t imagine what it’s like for the people that are making way, way less than that,” she said.
It’s an effort that is about fundamental survival, and it mirrors a lot of what’s driving Gen Z students to get engaged politically, Jayaraman said. Some tell her that they support raising the minimum wage because it’s fundamental to them being able to take on any other causes.
“They tell me, ‘This is the thing that’s giving me hope because I can’t envision a future unless I can have one job and earn enough to maybe one day have my own place, maybe think about having a family. I can’t imagine working on any of these other issues I care about, whether it’s climate or immigration or anything else, unless I can survive and my family can survive.’”
Still, getting a tight-knit town that has subsisted on its own to embrace a lofty idea made popular in cities like New York, Los Angeles and Chicago has not been easy. There’s concern over how businesses will be able to absorb the increased personnel costs. There’s dismissiveness because the effort is being led by young women — people say they’re just high schoolers who need to take an economics class, Kent said.
Plus, she added, “with a lot of Nome, change is scary for them.”
But the arguments against a minimum wage hike in Nome are similar to those heard across the country, Jayaraman said. Primarily, it’s the worry that it will lead to rising costs. Minimum wage increases have led to some modest employment loss and some added costs to businesses — but these are often offset by rising revenues. Extensive research that’s been done on minimum wage initiatives over the years has also found significant positive benefits for workers, and particularly low-wage ones.
“What the girls are saying is, ‘We need money to survive costs going up,’” Jayaraman said. For many people in America now, “that argument that it’s going to make costs go up and therefore we can’t do it, they’re like: ‘Costs have already gone up. What are you talking about? The only thing that hasn’t gone up is my paycheck.’”
Kent starts every conversation when she goes out to collect signatures with the same question: “How much money do you make?”
She and the other students are rushing to collect signatures before their deadline is up. Admittedly, it’s been tough to do with most of them out of town or preparing for college this summer. Stasenko already moved to Washington state to attend Shoreline Community College, where she’s studying accounting and playing college volleyball.
Kent will soon move to Colorado to attend Fort Lewis College. As she’s made her final push for signatures, she’s been thinking about how this effort might ensure that if she ever comes back home to make a life, she can.
Before all of this started, she and the other students had never done any activism like this. For Kent, taking it on has helped solidify what she wants to do with her life. When she gets to Colorado this fall, she’ll major in political science.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Regulatory process launched for 30 more years of trans-Alaska oil pipeline operations
description: Forty-nine years after it began transporting crude oil from Prudhoe Bay, the Trans Alaska Pipeline System is due for a regulatory renewal that will allow it to keep operating on federal lands into future decades. The U.S. Bureau of Land Management has kicked off the process to renew the right-of-way agreement for the pipeline. About […]
text:
A vehicle drives past the trans-Alaska pipeline near Galbraith Lake on the Dalton Highway, Alaska. Pump Station 4 is visible in the background. Fedearl regulators are beginning the process of granting a renewed right-of-way agreement to allow 30 more years of operations. (Photo by Craig McCaa/U.S. Bureau of Land Management)Forty-nine years after it began transporting crude oil from Prudhoe Bay, the Trans Alaska Pipeline System is due for a regulatory renewal that will allow it to keep operating on federal lands into future decades.
The U.S. Bureau of Land Management has kicked off the process to renew the right-of-way agreement for the pipeline.
About half of the territory that the 800-mile pipeline system crosses is federal land, so a federal authorization is required. The rest of the territory is state or Native-owned land; the state is also due to issue its own right-of-way renewal.
In a statement, Kevin Pendergast, the BLM’s Alaska state director, predicted a robust future for operations of the pipeline system. It will carry new oil from federal land units, including the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, where the Trump administration has pushed for oil drilling, he said.
“Nearly 50 years after its construction, the Trans Alaska Pipeline is still an engineering marvel and only growing in its importance to Alaska’s economy and global energy markets,” Pendergast said in the statement. “We are acting now to secure the pipeline’s future as we work to unlock the energy resources of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and the Coastal Plain of Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.”  
The Trans Alaska Pipeline System was first authorized in 1974. It was built over the following three years.
The prior federal renewal was made final in 2003 by the administration of President George W. Bush. It was completed just prior to the scheduled 2004 expiration of the original right-of-way agreement that allowed the system to be built and operated on federal lands.
The prior BLM approval process officially kicked off in November of 2000 and involved a full environmental impact statement that evaluated subjects like the impacts of aging on the structure, long-term changes to permafrost and oil spill risks.
This time, the Trump administration is planning a much shorter review. The BLM is preparing an environmental assessment, a less-comprehensive review than an environmental impact statement.
Brenda Younkin, the Department of the Interior’s deputy assistant secretary for land and mineral management, said this renewal process will take much less time. That is in keeping with Secretary Doug Burgum’s new rules for shorter and quicker environmental reviews, she said.
“We’re optimistic about being quick,” she said on Wednesday during a panel discussion at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association’s annual conference in Anchorage. “We better, or we’re going to be reporting to the secretary why not.”
The new rules include strict timelines and page limits for study documents, she said.

 Catching Our Eye

• Limbo rock. Limbo lower now. How low can you go? TiffinOhio’s Bonnie Lucas reports, “Fact check: Ramaswamy ad blames Acton for death of woman who lived and died in Kentucky, not Ohio.”
Vivek Ramaswamy’s newest television ad asks Ohio voters to blame Amy Acton for a woman’s isolation and death without telling them a central fact: the woman was a Kentucky resident who died in Kentucky.
The spot, paid for by Vivek Ramaswamy and Rob McColley for Ohio and tracked by the ad-monitoring firm Medium Buying, features Delhi Township Republican activist Linda Caudill speaking directly to the camera about her mother…
What the ad never tells viewers is where Caudill’s mother lived or where she died.

A central Ohio family who died in a fiery car crash is front and center in a political ad to boost U.S. Sen. Jon Husted − and their relatives want it taken down.
The spot from the National Senate Republican Committee highlights the deaths of Lynnea, Luke and 1-year-old Logan Soposki in an April multi-vehicle crash in Delaware County. Authorities said Modou F. Ngom, of Columbus, was driving a tractor trailer and rear ended the Soposkis’ vehicle, pushing it into other cars and across multiple lanes…
The ad also includes a photo of the Soposkis taken by a family friend, according to a statement from the family. And they never agreed for it to be used.
“This is not a statement about immigration policy, and we are not making one for any party or candidate,” the family said. “It is a statement about our family. Ohio’s Democratic candidate for governor has received an endorsement from a major statewide police agency. And she spoke out about her positions on some issues involving law enforcement, including qualified immunity and police cooperation with federal law and immigration enforcement.
Amy Acton was also asked about the controversial use of Flock cameras by police to solve crimes, something that has raised questions about privacy. When questioned specifically about police use of Flock cameras and the data they provide, Acton said she’d do a comprehensive overview of all our public safety and emergency response.

description: MADD Delaware, Police Agencies Team Up for Labor Day Impaired Driving Prevention Effort Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) Delaware is partnering with the Delaware Office of Highway Safety and law enforcement agencies statewide for “Saturation Saturday” on Aug. 29, an initiative aimed at preventing impaired driving ahead of the Labor Day holiday weekend. text:
MADD Delaware, Police Agencies Team Up for Labor Day Impaired Driving Prevention Effort
MADD Delaware and law enforcement agencies statewide are partnering for “Saturation Saturday” on Aug. 29 to promote impaired driving prevention ahead of Labor Day weekend. (Photo courtesy of MADD Delaware.)
Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) Delaware is partnering with the Delaware Office of Highway Safety and law enforcement agencies statewide for “Saturation Saturday” on Aug. 29, an initiative aimed at preventing impaired driving ahead of the Labor Day holiday weekend.
The coordinated enforcement effort will include increased DUI patrols across Delaware as part of a national push to reduce impaired driving crashes during one of the year’s busiest travel periods. The initiative coincides with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s “Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over” campaign.
According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Fatality Analysis Reporting System, 451 people were killed nationwide in drunk driving crashes during the Labor Day holiday period in 2024. In Delaware, drunk driving fatalities have increased by 3.2% since 2019.
MADD Delaware will work with Delaware State Police in New Castle, Kent and Sussex counties, as well as the Wilmington Police Department, New Castle County Police Department, New Castle City Police Department, Camden Police Department and Dagsboro Police Department, to support Saturation Saturday events and increased impaired driving enforcement.
Law enforcement officers are often the first line of defense against impaired driving. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, sobriety checkpoints can reduce drunk driving deaths by up to 20%.
“Impaired driving continues to be the leading cause of death on our roadways, stealing lives and leaving countless families to cope with unimaginable loss,” said Stacey D. Stewart, CEO of MADD. “MADD is proud to work alongside law enforcement to help prevent crashes, save lives, and remind drivers that impaired driving is never acceptable. Together, we can encourage responsible choices and make our roads safer for everyone.”
Saturation Saturday is part of ongoing efforts through NHTSA’s “Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over” campaign, which raises awareness about the dangers of impaired driving and supports high-visibility enforcement efforts throughout August and September.
“Preventing impaired driving requires a shared commitment from all of us. Saturation Saturday brings together MADD, law enforcement, and highway safety partners to send a clear message: impaired driving is preventable, and every driver has a responsibility to make a safe choice. As Labor Day weekend approaches, we encourage Delawareans to plan ahead, designate a sober driver, use a rideshare or find another safe way home,” said Sharon Bryson, director of the Delaware Office of Highway Safety.
“High-visibility traffic safety enforcement efforts serve as a deterrent to impaired driving crashes and prevent senseless deaths and injuries,” said Bryna Clark-Braverman, Regional Executive Director. “Together alongside law enforcement and NHTSA, MADD Delaware urges the public to have a plan for getting home safe – whether you’re driving, riding or hosting – as we approach Labor Day weekend.”

Wilmington Bride-to-Be Wins $100,000 Delaware Lottery Prize
A 32-year-old Wilmington woman claimed a $100,000 top prize in the Delaware Lottery’s 100X THE CELEBRATION instant game, marking the first major lottery win of her life. (Graphic by Milford LIVE)
A Wilmington woman is celebrating more than her upcoming wedding after winning a $100,000 top prize playing the Delaware Lottery’s 100X THE CELEBRATION instant game.
The 32-year-old Delaware native, who chose not to publicly release her name, claimed her prize Aug. 18 at Delaware Lottery headquarters in Dover. She told lottery officials the win was the first major prize she has received while playing the Delaware Lottery.
According to the Delaware Lottery, the woman said she was in disbelief after discovering she had won $100,000 and immediately contacted family members to share the news. She plans to use part of her winnings to help pay for her upcoming wedding.
The winning ticket was purchased at Naaman’s Beverage Mart Inc., located at 109 Naamans Road in Claymont.
“The Delaware Lottery couldn’t be happier for this winner, and it’s incredibly meaningful to us that her prize will help pay for her wedding celebration,” said Helene Keeley, director of the Delaware Lottery. “We love hearing stories about the ways Delawareans plan to use a lottery prize — whether that means having a little extra to help pay for a wedding, adding to their savings, or anything in between. As always, we encourage all Delaware Lottery players to enjoy playing responsibly. And we wish this bride-to-be and her partner a wonderful life together!”
The 100X THE CELEBRATION instant game launched in 2025 as part of the Delaware Lottery’s 50th anniversary celebration and originally featured two $100,000 top prizes. Players can also win prizes ranging from $20 to $20,000.
The $20 scratch-off game still had one $100,000 top prize remaining as of Aug. 19, according to the Delaware Lottery.

title: Kansas communities can learn from ‘painful’ data center lessons in other states, experts say
description: TOPEKA — Kansas communities exploring data center development must put policies in place to protect residents, the environment and long-term economic growth before building begins, national experts say. Mike Turner, a Loudoun County, Virginia, county official, learned about holding data centers accountable through “painful lessons.” Loudoun County is often c[...]
text:
An Amazon Web Services data center, located in Loudoun County, Virginia, is one of 253 data centers that have forced county leaders to create policies to protect the community. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)TOPEKA — Kansas communities exploring data center development must put policies in place to protect residents, the environment and long-term economic growth before building begins, national experts say.
Mike Turner, a Loudoun County, Virginia, county official, learned about holding data centers accountable through “painful lessons.”


Data centers
This story is part of our ongoing coverage of data centers in Kansas.
Read more.


Loudoun County is often called “data center alley,” with 70% of the world’s internet traffic going through 253 data centers located there. Turner wrote a white paper about what government entities should consider before approving a data center.
“The 15 best practices are based on six factors that you have to address before we say yes to a data center: sound, power, water, emissions, setback and appearance,” he said. “Right now, if you measured, we probably don’t pass five of the six. Our new ordinances that we’re crafting and have been crafting for the last two years do address all six.”
The county’s application process is about two years long, Turner said. Ordinances are adapted over time.
Kansans fear impacts of data centers despite promise of economic benefits

For example, Turner said the county decided data centers must have Tier IV backup generators, even though Tier II are the minimum acceptable standards.
“Tier IV diesel generators, the current, highest EPA standard for diesel generators, are much quieter and filter out more than 90% of all pollutants,” Turner’s paper said.
Best practices are learned over time, and Turner travels the country sharing them with other communities.
Kathryn Kline Tyndall led a team for the Bipartisan Policy Center in Washington, D.C., holding roundtable discussions nationwide, including in Kansas City, Missouri, about data center development.
She said it is easy for communities to feel a “David and Goliath” relationship as they talk with data center developers who have experience handling negotiations.
Being prepared and taking the time to learn from other communities can make a difference. One Maryland county planned ahead, talking about power needs, possible locations and other options, before a data center approached them, she said.
Although the Bipartisan Policy Center report wasn’t meant to make policy recommendations but to gather information, she said several roundtable attendees thought technical assistance for communities from state and federal levels might be needed.
“It was proposed that a state task force group would come into communities with some expertise and more experience and knowledge and help communities negotiate these deals,” she said. “I think something like that seems like it could be worth exploring.”
Turner’s 56-page white paper, which he has been updating since July 2024, isn’t a layman’s guide to data center development. It goes in depth on energy usage and power lines and even looks at possible future industry changes that would affect operations.


What is a hyperscale data center?
While data centers have been around for decades, the facilities being proposed today are much larger and often referred to as “hyperscale.” Definition of the term varies.
An IBM website said there are at least 5,000 servers in millions of square feet, while a Cisco site said “hyperscale refers specifically to an architectural approach that allows for extreme scalability and high performance.”
Mike Turner, an official in Loudoun County, Virginia, which has more than 250 data centers, defines hyperscale facilities as those using more than 100 megawatts of electricity continuously.
The three companies with the largest share of the hyperscale data center market are Amazon Web Services, with roughly 32%; Microsoft Azure, with about 23%; and Google Cloud Platform with about 10% share, according to IBM.


Water usage
Drought conditions in Kansas, as well as declining aquifers that threaten the state’s agriculture industry, make water usage a prime concern in Kansas.
Turner said Loudoun County’s 253 data centers use about 10% of the county’s potable water.
“Water has not been an issue for us, but then virtually all of our data centers are on closed-loop water systems,” he said. “In today’s day and age, I would not approve a data center on anything other than a closed-loop water cooling system.”
Closed-loop systems are recharged every few years, and Turner said communities need to know how that works and where the water will be discharged.
“You’ve got to address wastewater with your water authority,” he said. “Wastewater, whether it’s an open loop or closed loop system, is going to contain biocides, anti-corrosion chemicals, and heavy metals, and that’s all got to be cleaned out.”
The water utility will need to understand how to treat wastewater from the data center, Turner said. In Loudoun County, the wastewater is discharged into the Potomac River, “so it’s very clean,” he said.
Increased utility usage associated with data centers also causes increased water usage tied to power generation, according to a report from the sustainability advocacy group Ceres.
The effect of power generation on water varies in each state and even down to localities, depending on whether power generation comes from natural gas, renewable energy, coal or nuclear, the report said.
“Nationally, data centers rely heavily on water-dependent electricity generation,” the Ceres report said. “Natural gas supplies 40% of their electricity, followed by renewables (24%), nuclear (20%), and coal (15%). Though there are many renewable projects in the pipeline to meet the growing energy demands (65% of renewable power purchase agreements in the U.S. signed since 2021 have been dedicated to data center operations), these options are often limited by timing or transmission and distribution issues across the grid.”
 
Energy usage
Utility regulators at the Kansas Corporation Commission set a large load tariff in November for big power users like data centers in an attempt to make sure infrastructure costs aren’t passed along to residential and small business consumers. While one energy expert called the tariff a “model” for other states, one conservation organization expressed caution.
In a statement, Sierra Club said it signed on as one of the convenors on the large load tariff but was concerned because Evergy, the state’s largest electric utility, is building natural gas plants and delaying coal plant retirements to meet energy demands.
Turner’s paper notes negative effects on climate sustainability goals, and he explored changes that may occur as power grids are stressed and data center companies develop new ways to cool their systems.
Objections to data centers became louder in the last few years in Loudoun County, Turner said, and he believes most of the problem is about energy usage.
In Loudoun County, PJM Interconnection — a regional transmission organization that manages power transmission needs and energy markets like the Southwest Power Pool does for Kansas and the Midwest — determined that it had underestimated five-year infrastructure needs by a factor of 10, Turner said.
“We’ve got nine overhead transmission lines under construction in Loudon County right now, and it’s not going to be enough, in my opinion,” he said.
Southwest Power Pool made a similar projection, with energy usage in its 14-state area expected to grow by 96% over the next decade.
“Generally speaking,” he said, “my rule of thumb is every data center is going to come with an overhead transmission line, at least a single 230-kV line overhead, and a substation, at least one substation, maybe two. So you need to plan on all of that.”
Energy usage affects not just a single community but an entire region, said Kansas Health Institute analyst Emma Uridge, who worked on a team to examine the environmental footprint of data centers.
The East Coast and other areas have seen power failures, she said, and it is a concern that has to be looked at from a regional and statewide perspective.
“One solution that I’m seeing to respond to this is actually legislation that’s putting some responsibility on developers to make upgrades to the grid and any related infrastructure for them to successfully kind of connect to the grid when they come online,” she said. “I’ve been seeing policy that would require on-site renewable energy.”
 
Noise, light pollution
Noise and light pollution are handled through design perimeters and location, Turner’s paper said, and aren’t as challenging as the utility usage issues. As part of 15 best practices for communities, he recommends requiring significant setbacks from the road, berms and tree plantings, and other tactics.
Many of those are already used in economic development, such as for manufacturing plants, said Mike Morse, partner at Kansas Commercial Real Estate Services Inc. in Topeka and a proponent of a Compass Datacenter facility trying to open southwest of the capital city.
The city of Topeka recently passed a one-year moratorium on data center development to better research the issue.
Morse said Topeka has noise standards and other criteria that any developer has to meet. Compass has already done decibel testing to see what the noise level is at the property now, knowing it would need to comply with local regulations, Morse said.
The Bipartisan Policy Center’s Tyndall said roundtable discussions talked about noise and light pollution as hyperlocal issues. Sometimes, she said, it can be more about perception of a problem. One group went to a data center and it wasn’t loud, Tyndall said.
“This really brings home an important point that it’s not really about the numbers as much as it’s about the community perception on some of these pieces,” she said, adding that it turns back to having “honest faith conversations” about community concerns and being transparent.
 
Transparency
One of the primary challenges is lack of data about the actual effects data centers have on the electric grid and water resources, Uridge said. The KHI report found that “current corporate emissions reporting practices present a related challenge.”
For instance, one analysis found that some data centers may emit more carbon dioxide than publicly reported, the KHI report said.
“Despite existing policy frameworks, including the U.S. Energy Act of 2020, which mandates studies on data center energy and water use and development of efficiency metrics, voluntary disclosure of energy and water use by data center operators remains inconsistent, limiting the ability of researchers, regulators and public health professionals to fully assess the sector’s environmental footprint,” the report said.
Communities can change that through their practices, Turner said. He recommends allowing no nondisclosure agreements, for instance. He helped Newcastle County, Delaware, write an ordinance for a data center that wanted to build.
“The data centers have to live by those rules,” he said. “The key is does the local governing authority have the authority to enforce these rules with new data centers, and that’s critical. There are states that are taking local authority away and making the decision at the state level. That is a huge mistake because every data center application is a unique, community-based solution.”
